docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 21 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Bhūgola: Geography and Travel. It surveys the ways in which the land of the Indian subcontinent, and the wider world, were described, imagined, measured, mapped and travelled: the cosmography of the Purāṇas and of the Jain and Buddhist traditions; the spherical earth of the astronomers from Āryabhaṭa to Bhāskara II; the sacred geography of pilgrimage, Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Sikh and Muslim; Indian maps and plans; the accounts of foreign visitors from Megasthenes and the Chinese pilgrims to al-Bīrūnī, Ibn Baṭṭūṭa and the visitors to Vijayanagara and the Mughal court; geographical writing in Persian, from the Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam to the Āʾīn-i Akbarī and the Mughal road books; routes, rivers, mountains, coasts and islands; the historical regions, administrative divisions and boundaries of the subcontinent, from the janapadas to the linguistic states; the Indians who travelled abroad as merchants, monks, sailors and pilgrims; and the colonial surveys, including the Great Trigonometrical Survey and the Indian surveyors and explorers who worked for it.

The volume follows a few simple principles. Primary texts are quoted only where the wording and the reference are well established; figures are given only with a source; ancient texts are not read as “anticipating” modern science; Purāṇic cosmography is presented as cosmology, not as an encoded map of the modern world; and the calculations of the astronomers are reported as they stand, with the uncertainty that the length of the yojana introduces into any modern comparison. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such. Maps are drawn on a frame of latitude and longitude with a simplified coastline, and the diagrams of the Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist world-systems are labelled as diagrams of cosmology. The main secondary works on which the volume relies—among them the History of Cartography, Schwartzberg’s Historical Atlas of South Asia, Eck’s India: A Sacred Geography, Plofker’s Mathematics in India, Casson’s Periplus and Edney’s Mapping an Empire—are cited and listed in the bibliography, followed by a glossary, a chronology and a gazetteer of the places most often named.

No survey of this size can be exhaustive: readers should turn to the editions and studies cited, and check every quotation against a critical edition before use.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput, Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Transliteration and Names
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST): bhūgola, Jambūdvīpa, Arthaśāstra. Tamil words follow the conventions of the Tamil Lexicon (Madras), which marks the letters peculiar to Tamil, ḻ, ṟ and ṉ: tiṇai, Paṭṭiṉappālai, Cōḻa. Arabic and Persian words and names are given in a simplified scholarly form, with long vowels and the letters ʿayn (ʿ) and hamza (ʾ) marked and dotted consonants for the emphatic letters: Āʾīn-i Akbarī, ṣūba, Riḥla, al-Bīrūnī. Chinese names are given in pinyin (Xuanzang, Faxian), with older spellings where they are the titles of translations (Si-yu-ki).

Modern place-names are given in their current official or customary English spelling without diacritics (Varanasi, Prayagraj, Kodungallur), except where a place is discussed under its classical name (Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Ujjayinī); older forms such as Banaras, Calcutta and Madras are used for the period in which they were current. The gazetteer at the end of the volume gives the modern equivalents of the principal ancient names.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Bhūgola-Vidyā: India’s Geographical Imagination
docs.text:
mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṃ pṛthivyāḥ “The Earth is my mother; I am the son of the Earth.”

— Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 12.1.12, the Bhūmi Sūkta

The people of the Indian subcontinent have known, named, crossed and venerated their land in many different ways. The Vedic poets praised rivers and the Earth; the authors of the Purāṇas built an immense symbolic cosmos of ring-shaped continents around a golden central mountain; astronomers from Āryabhaṭa onwards treated the earth as a sphere and worked out latitudes and longitude differences; administrators described districts, roads and revenue; pilgrims, merchants, monks and sailors carried a practical knowledge of routes, seasons and harbours across South Asia and far beyond it. This volume, the twenty-first in the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā, surveys these traditions, together with the accounts of India left by foreign visitors and the modern survey that eventually mapped the subcontinent trigonometrically.

The aim is to describe these traditions accurately, in their own terms and in the light of current scholarship. Two temptations have to be resisted. One is the older colonial claim that pre-modern Indians had no interest in geography; the other is the more recent habit of reading modern science back into ancient texts, as if the Purāṇic continents “encoded” the modern map of the world or as if an ancient value for the earth’s size could be checked to the kilometre. Neither is supported by the evidence. What the evidence does show is a set of distinct and often sophisticated ways of thinking about space, place and travel, which deserve study as they actually were.

docs.title: 1.1 What Is Bhūgola-Vidyā?
docs.text:
The Sanskrit compound bhūgola joins bhū (earth) and gola (ball, sphere). It is a term of the astronomical (jyotiḥśāstra) tradition: in the Siddhānta texts the golādhyāya, the “chapter on the sphere”, explains the spherical earth set within the celestial sphere (khagola or bhagola) and the geometry that connects them. Bhāskara II (b. 1114 CE) gives the name Bhuvanakośa (“treasury of the world”) to the section of his Golādhyāya that sets the Purāṇic world-picture beside the astronomers’ spherical earth (Plofker 2009; Pingree 1981). In this narrow sense bhūgola-vidyā is mathematical and astronomical geography: the shape and size of the earth, latitude (akṣa), longitude difference (deśāntara), the length of daylight at different places, and the conversion of terrestrial distances into angular ones.

This volume uses the term more broadly, for at least four overlapping bodies of knowledge:

  1. Mathematical and astronomical geography: the spherical earth, its size, the reference meridian through Laṅkā and Ujjayinī, latitudes and longitude differences (Chapter 3).

  2. Cosmography: the Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist pictures of the universe, with Jambūdvīpa, Mount Meru and the concentric continents and oceans (Chapter 2). These are cosmologies, not maps of the physical earth.

  3. Sacred geography: tīrthas, kṣetras, pilgrimage circuits and the networks that linked them, in Brahmanical, Buddhist, Jain, Sikh and Muslim traditions (Chapter 4).

  4. Practical, administrative and trade geography: regions and peoples, roads, passes, rivers, ports and seasons, as known to rulers, revenue officials, merchants and sailors (Chapters 8–13).

Bhūgola, Khagola, Bhuvanakośa

Bhūgola: the earth-sphere of the astronomers. Khagola (also bhagola): the celestial sphere, on which the stars and planets appear to move. Bhuvanakośa: “treasury of the world”; the name given in the Purāṇas to their descriptions of the cosmos and its regions, and adopted by Bhāskara II for his discussion of the same material.

docs.title: 1.2 Sources of Indian Geographical Knowledge
docs.text: The sources are spread across genres, languages and some three thousand years. None of them is a “geography” in the modern sense; each has its own purpose, and its geographical content has to be read with that purpose in mind.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Vedic and Epic Sources
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (core composed c. 1500–1200 BCE) is set in the north-west of the subcontinent, in the region of the Indus and its tributaries. Its hymn in praise of rivers, the Nadīstuti (Ṛgveda 10.75), names rivers from the Gaṅgā in the east to the Kubhā (Kabul) in the west (Chapter 9). Later Vedic texts (c. 1200–500 BCE) show the centre of Vedic culture moving east into the Kuru–Pañcāla country of the Gaṅgā–Yamunā Doab and then towards Kosala and Videha (Witzel 1995). The Bhūmi Sūkta (Atharvaveda 12.1), a hymn of sixty-three verses to the Earth, describes her hills, plains, rivers and peoples “of many speeches”.

Atharvaveda (Śaunaka) 12.1.1

satyaṃ bṛhad ṛtam ugraṃ dīkṣā tapo brahma yajñaḥ pṛthivīṃ dhārayanti sā no bhūtasya bhavyasya patny uruṃ lokaṃ pṛthivī naḥ kṛṇotu

“Great truth, mighty order, consecration, austerity, sacred formulation and sacrifice uphold the Earth. May she, the mistress of what has been and what will be, make wide space for us.”

The two Sanskrit epics contain long lists of peoples, rivers and mountains: the geographical sections of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata (the Jambūkhaṇḍa and Bhūmiparvan), the Tīrthayātrāparvan of its third book, and the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa. These passages combine real names with mythical ones; they are valuable evidence for how the land was imagined and named, but they were not written as surveys, and their details cannot be checked on the ground as if they were (Section 1.3).

docs.title: 1.2.2 The Purāṇas
docs.text: Most of the major Purāṇas contain a bhuvanakośa: a description of the universe, of the seven ring-continents and oceans, of Jambūdvīpa and its nine regions, and of Bhāratavarṣa with its mountains, rivers and peoples. The fullest and most often quoted versions are in the Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Brahmāṇḍa, Matsya, Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhāgavata Purāṇas; they overlap heavily but differ in detail. Willibald Kirfel’s comparative study of these texts remains the standard analysis (Kirfel 1920); on the Purāṇas generally see Rocher (1986). The Purāṇic māhātmya literature, which praises particular sacred places, is a second large body of geographical material (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 1.2.3 The Arthaśāstra and Administrative Literature
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra attributed to Kauṭilya is a composite text which, in its present form, is best dated c. 50 BCE–300 CE; its traditional attribution to Cāṇakya, minister of Candragupta Maurya (c. 300 BCE), cannot be confirmed (Olivelle 2013). Its second book describes the settlement of new land, the hierarchy of administrative centres, the storehouse, mines, roads, ferries and the work of the superintendents of agriculture, shipping and trade. It is a prescriptive text, describing an ideal administration, but its vocabulary of land, water and routes is a precious record of practical geographical concepts. Its scheme for settling the countryside, its frontier posts and its theory of the circle of states are discussed with the other political geography in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 1.2.4 Grammar
docs.text: Pāṇini’s grammar, the Aṣṭādhyāyī (c. 4th century BCE), is not a geographical work, but because it gives rules for forming the names of places, peoples and their products, it preserves a large number of geographical names from the north-west and the Gangetic plain. Tradition, recorded by Xuanzang, makes Pāṇini a native of Śalātura near the Indus, in Gandhāra. One rule distinguishes the names of wells on the northern bank of the river Vipāś (the Beas) from those on other banks (4.2.74), a sign of the grammarian’s attention to local usage. V. S. Agrawala collected the cultural and geographical information in the grammar in India as Known to Pāṇini (Agrawala 1953).

docs.title: 1.2.5 Astronomical and Encyclopaedic Texts
docs.text: The astronomical Siddhāntas, from Āryabhaṭa’s Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) to Bhāskara II’s Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (1150 CE), contain the mathematical geography discussed in Chapter 3. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century CE) has a chapter, the Kūrmavibhāga (“division of the tortoise”), which arranges the regions and peoples of India in nine groups around the Middle Country, for use in astrological prognostication (Bhat 1981; Sircar 1971). The poetician Rājaśekhara’s Kāvyamīmāṃsā (early 10th century) includes a chapter on the regions of India for the use of poets (Section 12.2).

docs.title: 1.2.6 Inscriptions
docs.text: Inscriptions are among the most reliable geographical sources because they are dated and fixed in place. Aśoka’s edicts (r. c. 268–232 BCE) name the peoples on the frontiers of his empire and five Hellenistic kings in the west; their find-spots, from Kandahar to Karnataka, outline the empire itself. Samudragupta’s Allahabad pillar inscription (4th century CE) lists kings of Āryāvarta, of the forest tracts and of Dakṣiṇāpatha. Thousands of later land-grants define village boundaries by streams, trees, tanks and neighbouring villages, and are the closest thing to local maps that survives from early medieval India (Sircar 1971).

docs.title: 1.2.7 Travel and Pilgrimage Literature
docs.text: Foreign visitors—Greek, Chinese, Arab, Persian, Central Asian and European—left accounts of India (Chapter 6). Indian travellers left fewer formal travelogues, but there is a large literature of pilgrimage: the tīrthayātrā section of the Mahābhārata, the Purāṇic māhātmyas, the medieval digests on pilgrimage such as Lakṣmīdhara’s Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa (12th century), Jain tīrthamālās and Jinaprabhasūri’s Vividhatīrthakalpa (14th century), Sikh accounts of Guru Nānak’s journeys, and, from the eighteenth century, Persian and Urdu travel narratives by Indians who went to Mecca, Iran or Europe (Chapters 4 and 13).

docs.title: 1.3 Epic Geography
docs.text:
The two Sanskrit epics, composed and expanded over many centuries (roughly 400 BCE–400 CE), contain the earliest long descriptions of the land as a whole. In the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, before the great battle, the bard Sañjaya describes the earth to the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra: first the cosmic geography of Jambūdvīpa and Meru, then Bhāratavarṣa, with its seven principal mountain ranges, a long catalogue of rivers, and lists of the peoples of the Middle Country, the north, the south and the borderlands. In the Sabhāparvan, the Pāṇḍava brothers’ campaigns of conquest in the four directions and the peoples who bring tribute to Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal consecration provide further lists (Section 12.3.4). The Tīrthayātrāparvan adds the sacred places (Chapter 4).

In the Rāmāyaṇa, Rāma’s exile takes him from Ayodhyā across the Gaṅgā at Śṛṅgaverapura, to Citrakūṭa, through the forests of Daṇḍaka to Pañcavaṭī on the Godāvarī, and then south to Kiṣkindhā and the sea. In the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa, Sugrīva sends search parties in the four directions with descriptions of the lands they will pass. The places on Rāma’s route became pilgrimage sites, and the identification of others—above all Kiṣkindhā and Laṅkā—has been debated. The epics are therefore sources for how the land was named and imagined, and many of their names can be identified; but they were not written as geographical surveys, and their descriptions should not be treated as such.

docs.title: 1.4 Cosmography and Observational Geography
docs.text:
A recurring difficulty is the relation between two very different kinds of description. Purāṇic cosmography imagines the earth as a flat disc of concentric ring-continents (dvīpa) and ring-oceans (samudra) round Mount Meru, with Bhāratavarṣa as the southern region of the central continent, Jambūdvīpa. Its dimensions run to hundreds of thousands of yojanas, and its outer oceans are of sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curds, milk and sweet water. It is a cosmological and religious picture, not a map of the physical world, and attempts to identify its continents with Asia, Africa or the Americas have no basis.

The astronomers of the Siddhānta tradition, by contrast, treated the earth as a small sphere at the centre of the celestial sphere and calculated with it. Their geography was mathematical but thin: they needed latitudes and longitude differences for a limited number of places in order to compute local times of sunrise, eclipses and planetary positions.

Cosmography and Geography

Cosmography (Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist traditions): a picture of the whole universe, including heavens and underworlds, organised by religious meaning and by number. Mathematical geography (Siddhānta tradition): the earth as a sphere, described by angles and calculated distances. Descriptive and practical geography (epics, Purāṇic lists, inscriptions, administrative and travel literature): named regions, peoples, rivers, routes and places.

The two pictures were not easily reconciled, and Indian astronomers knew it. Their attempts to fit Meru and the continents into the spherical earth, al-Bīrūnī’s criticism of both sides and the debate that continued into the seventeenth century are described in Section 2.9. It is more accurate to speak of a long and sometimes uneasy coexistence than of a harmony in which the two never contradicted each other (Minkowski 2001).

docs.title: 1.5.1 Correcting Two Kinds of Distortion
docs.text: Colonial writers often asserted that Indians had no sense of geography or history. The work of historians of cartography, above all Joseph E. Schwartzberg’s long contribution on South Asian cartography to the History of Cartography (Harley and Woodward 1992) and his Historical Atlas of South Asia (Schwartzberg 1978), of Susan Gole on Indian maps (Gole 1989), of Irfan Habib on Mughal geography (Habib 1982), and of Diana Eck on sacred geography (Eck 2012), has shown that this was false. At the same time, Schwartzberg stressed that relatively few pre-modern Indian maps survive, most from after 1500, and that Indian cartography had purposes and conventions of its own. Honest scholarship has to avoid both the colonial dismissal and its mirror image, the claim that ancient Indians knew everything that modern geography knows.

docs.title: 1.5.2 Sacred Geography and Shared Space
docs.text: The networks of pilgrimage places that cover the subcontinent created, over many centuries, a shared sense of a land that extended far beyond any single kingdom. Eck argues that this “imagined landscape” was one of the main ways in which people in pre-modern India understood the subcontinent as a whole (Eck 2012). Pilgrimage networks were also plural: Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs and Muslims had their own sacred places and routes, often overlapping with Hindu ones, and access to many sacred sites was restricted by caste and gender in ways that must not be forgotten (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 1.5.3 Practical Knowledge
docs.text: Much of the most important geographical knowledge was never written down: the knowledge of herders, cultivators, boatmen, caravaneers, fishermen and pilots. It is known mainly through its effects (routes, tank systems, sailing seasons) and through the observations of outsiders and modern ethnographers. It deserves respect, but claims for it should be made on the basis of evidence rather than assumed.

docs.title: 1.6 The Vocabulary of Land, Water and Season
docs.text:
Sanskrit has a rich vocabulary for landforms and waters. Many of these words are already Vedic; the lexicon Amarakośa (mid-first millennium CE) groups them in its sections on earth, towns, mountains and waters. Table 1.1 gives a selection with their usual meanings. Like words in any language, they overlap; they were not a technical classification.

Table 1.1. Some Sanskrit words for land and water Term Meaning Term Meaning parvata, giri, adri mountain, hill nadī, sarit river śikhara, śṛṅga peak srotas stream, current droṇī valley saṅgama confluence sthalī dry land, upland kūla, taṭa bank, shore maru, dhanvan desert hrada, saras lake, pool anūpa wet, marshy land kūpa well aṭavī, araṇya forest vāpī, taḍāga tank, reservoir dvīpa island; “continent” in cosmography samudra, sāgara sea, ocean deśa region, country tīrtha ford; sacred place janapada territory of a people patha, mārga road, route

docs.title: 1.6.1 Land Types in Āyurveda
docs.text: The medical classics classify regions (deśa) as jāṅgala (dry, open country with sparse trees and little water), ānūpa (wet, marshy country) and sādhāraṇa (“common” or mixed). The classification concerns health: jāṅgala land is described as healthy and ānūpa land as productive of disorders of phlegm and wind. Francis Zimmermann showed that the word jāṅgala, from which English “jungle” derives, originally meant dry, open savanna, almost the opposite of its modern sense (Zimmermann 1987). The Arthaśāstra also distinguishes jāṅgala and ānūpa land in its rules on settlement and rainfall.

docs.title: 1.6.2 The Six Seasons
docs.text:
Indian texts divide the year into six seasons (ṛtu) of two months each (Table 1.2). The months are lunar-solar, so the correspondence with the Gregorian calendar is approximate.

Table 1.2. The six seasons (ṛtu) and their months Ṛtu Months Approximate period and character Vasanta (spring) Caitra, Vaiśākha mid-March to mid-May; flowering Grīṣma (hot season) Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha mid-May to mid-July; heat, then first rains Varṣā (rains) Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada mid-July to mid-September; the monsoon Śarad (autumn) Āśvina, Kārttika mid-September to mid-November; clear skies, harvest Hemanta (cool season) Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa mid-November to mid-January Śiśira (cold season) Māgha, Phālguna mid-January to mid-March

Bhagavadgītā 10.35cd

māsānāṃ mārgaśīrṣo ’ham ṛtūnāṃ kusumākaraḥ

“Of months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; of seasons, the maker of flowers [spring].”

The rains governed travel. Buddhist and Jain monks were required to stop wandering during the rainy season and to stay in one place (the Buddhist vassa, the Jain cāturmāsya); kings were advised to set out on campaigns after the rains, in autumn; merchants and sailors planned their journeys round the monsoon winds, whose calendar is set out in Chapter 11. The Arthaśāstra’s rain gauge is described with the other texts on water in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 1.7 Cities and Settlements
docs.text:
The first cities of the subcontinent belong to the Indus or Harappan civilisation, whose mature urban phase is dated c. 2600–1900 BCE, with earlier and later phases extending from c. 3300 to c. 1300 BCE. Harappan sites of all phases are spread from Shortugai on the Amu Darya in northern Afghanistan to Daimabad in Maharashtra (a Late Harappan site) and from Sutkagen Dor on the Makran coast to Alamgirpur near Delhi. The Harappans left no deciphered texts, so their geographical knowledge can only be inferred from what they built: streets broadly aligned to the cardinal directions, raised mounds, covered drains, and at Dholavira in Kutch a series of reservoirs cut into the rock to store the scarce water of an arid island. Their settlements spread across river plains, coasts, desert margins and hill valleys, and they traded with Mesopotamia and the Gulf by sea (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002; Wright 2010). The Harappan port at Lothal is discussed with the coasts in Chapter 11, and the question whether the Ghaggar–Hakra, along which many Harappan sites lie, was the Vedic Sarasvatī in Chapter 9.

Urban life returned to the subcontinent in the Gangetic plain from about the sixth century BCE, in what historians call the second urbanisation. Cities such as Rājagṛha, Pāṭaliputra, Śrāvastī, Kauśāmbī, Vārāṇasī and Ujjayinī, many of them fortified with ramparts and moats, grew at river crossings and on routes, and their names fill Buddhist and Jain literature. In the far south, the Caṅkam poems describe the capitals of the three Tamil kingdoms—Madurai of the Pāṇḍyas, Uṟaiyūr and the port of Pukār of the Cōḻas, and Vañci of the Cēras—with their markets, streets and harbours (Thapar 2002). The ideal city plans of the Arthaśāstra and the architectural treatises are described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 1.8 Names for the Land
docs.text:
The subcontinent has been called by many names, and their history is itself a piece of historical geography. Jambudvīpa, the central continent of the cosmologies, is used by Aśoka in the third century BCE for the land in which he spread the Dharma. Bhārata or Bhāratavarṣa, “the land of the descendants of Bharata”, is the name defined in the Purāṇas (Chapter 2) and remains the Sanskrit and Hindi name of the country.

Other names came from outside and from the Indus. The Sanskrit Sindhu, “river” and the name of the Indus, became Hindu in Old Persian, in which the inscriptions of Darius I name a province “Hindush”; from the Persian form came Greek Indos for the river and India for the land beyond it, Arabic al-Hind, and Persian Hindūstān. The Chinese called the country Shendu, Tianzhu and later Yindu; Xuanzang explained the last name as coming from indu, the moon. The Constitution of India of 1950 uses two of these names together: “India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.”

docs.title: 1.9 Landscapes in Tamil Poetry
docs.text:
A distinctive classification of landscapes comes from the classical Tamil poems of the Caṅkam anthologies (early centuries CE) and the grammar that describes them, the Tolkāppiyam. Love poetry (akam) is set in one of five landscapes or tiṇai, each named after a characteristic flower and each associated with a deity, a season and time of day, plants, animals, occupations and, above all, a phase of love (Table 1.3; (Ramanujan 1967; Zvelebil 1973)).

Table 1.3. The five landscapes (tiṇai) of classical Tamil love poetry Tiṇai Landscape Associations kuṟiñci mountains the god Murukaṉ; night; the lovers’ union mullai forest and pasture Māyōṉ (Kṛṣṇa); evening in the rainy season; patient waiting marutam cultivated river plains Vēntaṉ (Indra); dawn; quarrels caused by the husband’s infidelity neytal seashore Varuṇaṉ; nightfall; anxious waiting and lament pālai parched wasteland no fixed region; midday in summer; separation and dangerous journeys

The tiṇai system is a poetic convention, not a survey; a poem’s landscape is a code for its emotion. But the conventions rest on a precise observation of the different environments of the Tamil country—hills, forests, paddy fields, coasts and drought-stricken land—and of the plants, animals and ways of life that belong to each. The second great genre of Tamil poetry, puṟam (“exterior”), on war, kings and public life, also uses a set of tiṇai. In the tiṇai scheme, feeling, season and terrain are classified together, so that to name a hill flower is already to name a mood.

docs.title: 1.10 Geography in the Regional Literatures
docs.text: Sanskrit is only one of the languages in which Indians described their land, and the literatures of the regional languages are often closer to everyday experience. In Tamil, besides the landscape poetry of the Caṅkam anthologies, the “guide poems” (āṟṟuppaṭai) of the Pattuppāṭṭu direct a bard along the road to a generous patron, describing the lands, peoples and food he will meet on the way, and the hymns of the Nāyaṉmār and Āḻvār name hundreds of temple towns (Chapter 4). The Marathi Līḷācaritra (late thirteenth century), a biography of Cakradhara, founder of the Mahānubhāva sect and one of the earliest works of Marathi prose, records the places he visited in such detail that later scholars have used it to reconstruct the geography of the region in his time. The Assamese buraṅjīs, chronicles of the Ahom kingdom of the Brahmaputra valley, record routes, rivers, forts and the movements of armies and embassies, and the Bengali maṅgalkāvyas follow merchants down the rivers to the sea (Chapter 11). From the thirteenth century histories, gazetteers and travel accounts in Persian, and later in Urdu, described provinces, routes and cities (Chapters 7 and 13). The geographical knowledge of the subcontinent was multilingual, and this volume can give only a sample of it.

docs.title: 1.11 Social Space
docs.text:
Geographical description in the Sanskrit sources is not socially neutral. The normative texts define the land where Brahmanical norms apply and treat regions beyond it as impure; the law books describe a village in which those regarded as “untouchable” (such as the caṇḍālas) were to live outside the settlement. Faxian, around 400 CE, observed that caṇḍālas lived apart and had to announce their approach (Chapter 6). In many parts of India, villages were divided into separate quarters by caste, with Dalit hamlets—the cēri of Tamil villages, for example—set apart from the main settlement, often with separate wells and paths. Access to roads, water and temples was unequal.

This social geography belongs to the history of Indian space as much as the cosmologies of the Purāṇas or the calculations of the astronomers. It was also one of the main targets of social reformers from the nineteenth century onward: B. R. Ambedkar’s Mahad satyāgraha of 1927 was fought over the right of Dalits to draw water from a public tank, that is, over who might use a particular place (Olivelle 2005; Thapar 2002). The same questions of access return in the chapter on pilgrimage (Section 4.13).

docs.title: 1.12 A Note on Method
docs.text:
Scholarly Note: How This Volume Treats Its Sources

  • Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship; traditional dates are labelled as such. Thus the Buddha is placed c. 480–400 BCE (short chronology), Śaṅkara c. 700–750 CE (the conventional 788–820 is traditional), and the Arthaśāstra c. 50 BCE–300 CE.

  • Quotations from Sanskrit and other texts are given only where the wording and reference are well established. Verse numbers vary between editions.

  • Units: the yojana and krośa varied in length between texts and regions. Modern equivalents are given only as rough ranges, and calculations that depend on an exact value of the yojana are treated with caution (Chapter 3).

  • Comparisons with modern science are offered as comparisons. Ancient texts are not read as anticipating modern discoveries.

  • Maps in this volume are drawn on a simple frame of latitude and longitude, with a simplified coastline. Places are plotted at their modern positions; positions that are uncertain are marked as approximate, and no modern boundaries are drawn.

docs.title: 1.13 Plan of the Volume
docs.text:
Chapter 2 describes Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist cosmography: Jambūdvīpa, Meru, the seven continents and oceans, and the world-picture of the Purāṇas, presented as cosmology. Chapter 3 turns to the spherical earth of the astronomers, the size of the earth, latitude and longitude. Chapter 4 examines sacred geography and pilgrimage, Hindu, Buddhist, Jain, Sikh and Muslim, including the Hajj from India. Chapter 5 surveys Indian maps and plans. Chapter 6 reads the accounts of foreign travellers from Megasthenes to Bernier and Tavernier, and Chapter 7 the geographical writing in Persian produced in India from the Delhi Sultanate to the early colonial period, with the Āʾīn-i Akbarī at its centre. Chapters 8–11 treat routes and trade, rivers, mountains, and coasts and islands. Chapter 12 turns to political and administrative geography: the janapadas and the normative regions of the early texts, the divisions of kingdoms in the inscriptions, the names of the historical regions, place-names, boundaries and frontiers, and the making of the linguistic states. Chapter 13 follows Indians abroad: merchants, monks, sailors and travellers. Chapter 14 describes the colonial surveys, including the Great Trigonometrical Survey and the Indian surveyors who worked for it, the growth of geography as a modern discipline, and the legacy of the earlier traditions in modern India. A gazetteer at the end of the volume gives the modern locations of the places most often named.

Some subjects are treated more thinly than they deserve. The oral and written geographies of the Himalayan and north-eastern peoples appear only in passing; Sikh sacred geography is followed only as far as the janamsākhīs, the principal gurdwaras and the Kartarpur corridor; the painted narrative scrolls of Rajasthan (phaḍ) and other folk spatial narratives are left aside; and before 1800 the only women travellers whose journeys are described are Gulbadan Begum and, in tradition, Mīrābāī. These are limits of this survey, not of the traditions.

Several neighbouring volumes of the series treat related subjects more fully: Indian astronomy, including the Siddhāntas used in Chapter 3, in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa; the Purāṇas as literature in Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa; Buddhist and Jain traditions, including the Chinese pilgrims’ accounts of Indian monasteries, in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā; architecture and the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala in Volume 16, Vāstu–Śilpa; trade, ports and seafaring in Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra; and the knowledge of Adivasi and folk communities in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On the historical geography of early India: Law (1954), Sircar (1971) and Cunningham (1871). On cartography: Harley and Woodward (1992), Schwartzberg (1978) and Gole (1989). On sacred geography: Eck (2012) and Bhardwaj (1973). On mathematical geography: Plofker (2009).

docs.title: Chapter 2: Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist Cosmography
docs.text:
uttaraṃ yat samudrasya himādreś caiva dakṣiṇam varṣaṃ tad bhārataṃ nāma bhāratī yatra santatiḥ “The land that lies north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains is called Bhārata; there dwell the descendants of Bharata.”

— Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.3.1

Many Hindu rituals still begin with a declaration of intent (saṅkalpa) that locates the worshipper in cosmic time and space. The priest names the current aeon, age and year and then the place: “in Jambūdvīpa, in Bhāratavarṣa, in Bharatakhaṇḍa…”, narrowing down to the local region and river. The formula is a small survival, in everyday religious practice, of the cosmography laid out in the Purāṇas: a universe of concentric ring-shaped continents and oceans round a golden central mountain, Meru, with the land of Bhārata as the southern part of the innermost continent.

This chapter describes that cosmography and the parallel Jain and Buddhist systems. They are best understood as cosmologies: pictures of the whole universe, ordered by number, symmetry and religious value, in which the known land of India was given its place. They were not attempts at a map of the physical earth that “failed”, nor coded descriptions of the modern continents. Within them, however, the description of Bhāratavarṣa itself—its mountains, rivers and peoples—does draw on real geographical knowledge, and the boundary between the two is one of the interesting features of the texts (Kirfel 1920; Sircar 1971; Eck 2012).

docs.title: 2.1 The Purāṇic Universe in Outline
docs.text:
The Purāṇic bhuvanakośa sections describe, with variations, a flat, circular earth-disc (bhūmaṇḍala) at the centre of which stands Meru. Round Meru lies the continent Jambūdvīpa, and round that, in alternation, six further ring-shaped continents and seven oceans. Beyond the last ocean lies a land of gold, then the mountain Lokāloka (“world and no-world”), which separates the lit world from outer darkness. Above the earth rise the heavenly worlds; below it lie the netherworlds and, below them, the hells.

Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.2.5–6: The Seven Continents and Seven Oceans

jambūplakṣāhvayau dvīpau śālmaliś cāparo dvija kuśaḥ krauñcas tathā śākaḥ puṣkaraś caiva saptamaḥ ete dvīpāḥ samudrais tu sapta saptabhir āvṛtāḥ lavaṇekṣusurāsarpirdadhidugdhajalaiḥ samam

“The continents called Jambū and Plakṣa, another, Śālmali, O Brahmin; Kuśa, Krauñca, likewise Śāka, and Puṣkara as the seventh: these seven continents are surrounded by seven oceans, of salt water, sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curds, milk and fresh water.”

Table 2.1. The seven continents and seven oceans of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa Continent (dvīpa) Named after Surrounding ocean 1 Jambūdvīpa jambū (rose-apple, Syzygium cumini) salt water (lavaṇa) 2 Plakṣadvīpa plakṣa (a fig tree) sugar-cane juice (ikṣu) 3 Śālmaladvīpa śālmali (silk-cotton tree) wine (surā) 4 Kuśadvīpa kuśa grass clarified butter (sarpis) 5 Krauñcadvīpa Mount Krauñca curds (dadhi) 6 Śākadvīpa śāka (teak) milk (dugdha, kṣīra) 7 Puṣkaradvīpa puṣkara (lotus) fresh water (jala)

Table 2.1 lists the continents and oceans, and Figure 2.1 shows their arrangement. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa’s account Jambūdvīpa is 100,000 yojanas across, each following continent is twice as wide as the one before, and each ocean is as wide as the continent it encloses. The numbers grow very large very quickly; they express immensity and order, not measurement. The order of the oceans was variously explained by commentators; the familiar ocean of salt water is the one nearest to human beings, and the Ocean of Milk, on which Viṣṇu reclines and which gods and demons churned for the nectar of immortality, lies far out in the system. H. H. Wilson’s annotated translation of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, though old, remains the most accessible English version of these chapters (Wilson 1864–1870).

Figure 2.1. The Purāṇic earth-disc as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (2.2–2.4) describes it, shown in half-section from Meru outward: Jambūdvīpa at the centre, then the seven oceans (of salt water, sugar-cane juice, wine, ghee, curds, milk and fresh water) alternating with the six further continents, the golden land and the world-bounding mountain Lokāloka, beyond which lies darkness. This is cosmology, not geography. The rings are drawn with equal widths for legibility; in the text Jambūdvīpa is 100,000 yojanas across and each continent is twice as wide as the one before, with each ocean as wide as the continent it surrounds.

Reading the Seven Continents

  • The scheme is symmetrical and numerical: seven continents, seven oceans, regular doubling.

  • It places the known land (Bhāratavarṣa) in the innermost continent and surrounds it with ever larger, more wonderful and less accessible regions.

  • Identifications of the outer continents with Asia, Africa, Europe or the Americas, which appear in some modern popular writing, have no support in the texts.

  • Some names of the outer continents (Śākadvīpa, Kuśadvīpa) were linked by later writers with real lands to the west, but these are interpretations, not the meaning of the cosmography.

docs.title: 2.2.1 Meru
docs.text:
At the centre of Jambūdvīpa stands Meru, a mountain of gold. In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa it rises 84,000 yojanas above the earth and descends 16,000 below; it is wider at the top than at the base, so that it is often compared to the seed-cup of a lotus whose petals are the continents. On its summit lie the cities of Brahmā and of the guardians of the directions; round it the sun, moon and stars revolve. Four buttress mountains support it on the four sides—in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa Mandara (east), Gandhamādana (south), Vipula (west) and Supārśva (north)—each crowned with a great tree, and four lakes lie between them (Kirfel 1920). The same Purāṇa uses the name Gandhamādana a second time, for the range that bounds the central region of Jambūdvīpa on the west (below); the two uses are both in the text and should not be confused.

The Gaṅgā, falling from heaven onto the summit of Meru, divides into four streams that flow to the four quarters: the Sītā to the east, the Alakanandā to the south, the Cakṣu to the west and the Bhadrā to the north. The Alakanandā flows into Bhāratavarṣa and becomes the earthly Gaṅgā. The name of the southern stream is also the name of one of the real headwaters of the Ganges in the Garhwal Himalaya, an example of the way the cosmography attaches itself to known places.

Meru is an axis mundi, a world-mountain at the centre of the cosmos, comparable in function to other world-centres in the religions of Asia. Some modern writers, following B. G. Tilak’s The Arctic Home in the Vedas (1903), have read the descriptions of Meru as a memory of the Arctic, where the sun circles the horizon. The idea rests on selected passages and has not been accepted by scholars of the Purāṇas. The astronomers, however, did locate Meru at the north pole of their spherical earth, where the gods see the sun for six months at a time (see below and Chapter 3).

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Nine Regions and the Mountain Ranges
docs.text:
Jambūdvīpa is divided into nine regions (varṣa) by mountain ranges that run east to west. South of Meru, separated by three ranges—Himavat (the Himālaya), Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha—lie Bhāratavarṣa, Kimpuruṣavarṣa and Harivarṣa. North of Meru, separated by the ranges Nīla, Śveta and Śṛṅgin, lie Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya and Uttarakuru. These six ranges are the varṣaparvatas. In the centre, round Meru, lies Ilāvṛta, with Bhadrāśva to its east and Ketumāla to its west, bounded in many accounts by the ranges Mālyavat and Gandhamādana (Table 2.2 and Figure 2.2).

Table 2.2. The nine varṣas of Jambūdvīpa Varṣa Position Separated by Bhārata southernmost Himavat Kimpuruṣa south Himavat and Hemakūṭa Harivarṣa south, next to Ilāvṛta Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha Ilāvṛta centre, round Meru Niṣadha and Nīla Ramyaka north, next to Ilāvṛta Nīla and Śveta Hiraṇmaya north Śveta and Śṛṅgin Uttarakuru northernmost Śṛṅgin Bhadrāśva east of Ilāvṛta Mālyavat Ketumāla west of Ilāvṛta Gandhamādana Figure 2.2. The nine regions (varṣa) of Jambūdvīpa in the Purāṇic scheme, with Meru at the centre and north at the top. Six east–west ranges divide the southern and northern varṣas; the Mālyavat and Gandhamādana ranges separate Ilāvṛta, round Meru, from Bhadrāśva in the east and Ketumāla in the west. Bhāratavarṣa is the southernmost region. A schematic diagram of the cosmology, not a map; the widths of the regions are not to scale.

The Himavat is plainly the Himālaya, and Uttarakuru, the land of the northern Kurus, keeps a name that appears already in Vedic literature. Beyond these, attempts to identify the ranges with the Karakoram, the Kunlun or the Tian Shan are guesses. It is more economical to see the system as a symmetrical construction that begins from the known northern mountains and extends the pattern outward.

docs.title: 2.3 Bhāratavarṣa: The Known Land
docs.text: The Purāṇas give Bhāratavarṣa special status. It is the only karmabhūmi, “land of action”, where deeds bear fruit and liberation can be sought; the other regions are bhogabhūmis, “lands of enjoyment”, where beings consume the results of earlier merit. The Viṣṇu Purāṇa says that the gods themselves envy those born in Bhārata. The same section is the most concretely geographical part of the cosmography.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Nine Divisions
docs.text: The Viṣṇu Purāṇa (2.3) divides Bhāratavarṣa into nine parts: Indradvīpa, Kaśerumat, Tāmraparṇa, Gabhastimat, Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gandharva and Vāruṇa, and a ninth, “this one, surrounded by the sea”. Other Purāṇas give similar lists. The ninth part is usually taken to be the subcontinent proper (called Kumārikā or Kumārīdvīpa in some texts); the others may reflect vague knowledge of islands and lands beyond it—Tāmraparṇa is an old name for Sri Lanka—but most of them cannot be identified (Sircar 1971).

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Seven Principal Mountain Ranges
docs.text:
The Purāṇas list seven principal ranges (kulaparvata) of Bhāratavarṣa, distinct from the Himālaya, which forms its northern boundary. Their usual identifications are given in Table 2.3.

Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.3.3

mahendro malayaḥ sahyaḥ śuktimān ṛkṣaparvataḥ vindhyaś ca pārīyātraś ca saptātra kulaparvatāḥ

“Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, the Ṛkṣa mountain, Vindhya and Pāriyātra: these are the seven principal mountain ranges here [in Bhārata].”

Table 2.3. The seven kulaparvatas and their usual identifications Kulaparvata Usual identification (with degree of certainty) Mahendra hills of the Eastern Ghats in southern Odisha (the name survives in Mahendragiri); fairly secure Malaya southern Western Ghats in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, the sandalwood hills; secure Sahya northern and central Western Ghats (the Sahyādri); secure Śuktimat uncertain; placed by different scholars in central India, Chhattisgarh or Bihar Ṛkṣa uncertain; often taken as the eastern Vindhya or the Satpura hills Vindhya the Vindhya hills of central India; secure in general, though the ancient name covered more than the modern range Pāriyātra western Vindhya and Aravalli hills; probable

The Purāṇas also list the rivers that rise in each range, and these lists contain many real river names: the Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī and Kṛṣṇaveṇī from the Sahya, the Tāmraparṇī from the Malaya, the Narmadā and others from the Ṛkṣa or Vindhya. They are the most reliable part of the Purāṇic description and were used by D. C. Sircar and others to reconstruct the historical geography of early India (Sircar 1971; Law 1954). The lists of peoples (janapada) that follow are more mixed: they combine names of contemporary peoples with older names preserved from earlier lists, and arrange them by direction.

Geographic Insight: Empirical Knowledge Inside a Cosmological Frame

The description of Bhāratavarṣa shows real knowledge of the mountains and rivers of the subcontinent. That knowledge is placed inside a cosmological frame whose outer parts are imaginary. Reading the whole cosmography as a map, or dismissing the whole as fantasy, both miss this layered character. Even within Bhāratavarṣa, identifications should be given with their degree of certainty.

docs.title: 2.4 Myths of Origin and Lists of Peoples
docs.text:
The Purāṇas explain the shape of the world through stories as well as numbers. In the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Book 5), King Priyavrata, dissatisfied that the sun lit only half the earth at a time, drove his shining chariot round the earth seven times behind the sun; the ruts left by its wheels became the seven oceans, and the land between them the seven continents, which he divided among his sons. In other Purāṇas, Priyavrata’s sons are given the seven continents to rule, and his grandson Nābhi and great-grandson Ṛṣabha (also honoured by Jains as the first tīrthaṅkara) rule Jambūdvīpa; Ṛṣabha’s son Bharata gives his name to Bhāratavarṣa. Such stories connect cosmic geography with royal genealogy. F. E. Pargiter tried to extract a political history of early India from the Purāṇic genealogies (Pargiter 1922); his chronology is no longer accepted, but his collation of the lists is still consulted.

The description of Bhāratavarṣa in the Mārkaṇḍeya, Vāyu, Matsya and other Purāṇas includes long lists of peoples (janapada) arranged by region: those of the Middle Country, the north and north-west, the east, the south, the west, the Vindhya and the mountains. Some lists also describe the land as a tortoise lying on the waters, with peoples assigned to its head, flanks, feet and tail, a scheme related to Varāhamihira’s Kūrmavibhāga (Section 3.4). Many of the names are those of real peoples—Kurus, Pañcālas, Kosalas, Magadhas, Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Andhras, Coḻas, Pāṇḍyas, Keralas, Gāndhāras, Kāmbojas—but the lists accumulated over centuries and include names that had ceased to be current when the texts reached their present form. Historians therefore use them with care, alongside inscriptions and other dated evidence (Sircar 1971; Law 1954).

docs.title: 2.5 The Vertical Cosmos: Worlds Above and Below
docs.text:
The Purāṇic universe is also vertical. Above the earth are the worlds called by the names of the vyāhṛtis, the sacred utterances recited with the Gāyatrī: bhūḥ (earth), bhuvaḥ (the intermediate space) and svaḥ (heaven). The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (1.5.1) already speaks of these three utterances and adds a fourth, mahaḥ. The Purāṇas extend the series to seven upper worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapas and Satya (the world of Brahmā). Table 2.4 sets the upper and lower worlds side by side.

Below the earth lie seven netherworlds (pātālas). Their names differ between the Purāṇas; the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (5.24) lists Atala, Vitala, Sutala, Talātala, Mahātala, Rasātala and Pātāla. They are inhabited by serpents (nāgas), daityas and dānavas, and are described as places of great beauty and luxury, lit by the jewels in the serpents’ hoods; the Viṣṇu Purāṇa has the sage Nārada report that they are more delightful than heaven. The hells (naraka), places of punishment, lie further below.

Table 2.4. The seven upper and seven lower worlds Upper worlds (loka) Lower worlds (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.24) Satya (Brahmaloka) Atala Tapas Vitala Jana Sutala (ruled by Bali) Mahar Talātala Svar (heaven of Indra) Mahātala Bhuvar (intermediate space) Rasātala Bhūr (earth) Pātāla (the serpent world)

docs.title: 2.6 Jain Cosmography
docs.text: Jain cosmography is related to the Purāṇic system but is a separate and highly systematic tradition, set out in canonical and post-canonical works such as the Śvetāmbara Jambūdvīpaprajñapti, Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra (chapter 3) and the Digambara Tiloyapaṇṇatti attributed to Yativṛṣabha (Caillat and Kumar 1981; Dundas 2002).

docs.title: 2.6.1 The Shape of the Universe
docs.text: The occupied universe (loka) has the shape of a standing person with arms akimbo, the lokapuruṣa: broad at the base, narrow at the waist and broad again at the chest. The lower world contains the hells; the upper world, the heavens, with the abode of liberated souls (siddhaśilā) at the top. The middle world (madhyaloka), a thin disc at the waist, is the world of humans and animals.

docs.title: 2.6.2 Innumerable Continents and Oceans
docs.text:
The middle world consists not of seven but of innumerable (asaṃkhyāta) concentric continents and oceans. Jambūdvīpa, 100,000 yojanas across, is at the centre; it is surrounded by the Lavaṇa (salt) ocean, then by the continent Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, the Kāloda ocean and the continent Puṣkaravara, and so on, each twice as wide as the last. Human beings can live only in Jambūdvīpa, Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and the inner half of Puṣkaravara, which is divided by the circular mountain Mānuṣottara: the “two and a half continents” (aḍhāī dvīpa, Sanskrit ardhatṛtīya dvīpa), the world of humans (Figure 2.3a).

Within this region there are five Merus: one in Jambūdvīpa, two in Dhātakīkhaṇḍa and two in the habitable half of Puṣkaravara. Jambūdvīpa itself is divided into seven regions (kṣetra) by six east–west ranges: Bharata in the south, then Haimavata, Hari, Videha (round Meru), Ramyaka, Hairaṇyavata and Airāvata in the north. The arrangement, as Jain painters showed it, is drawn in Figure 5.1.

Hindu and Jain Cosmography Compared

  • Number of continents: seven in the Purāṇas; innumerable in Jain texts, with human life confined to two and a half of them.

  • Meru: one in the Purāṇas; five in the Jain world of humans.

  • Regions of Jambūdvīpa: nine varṣas in the Purāṇas; seven kṣetras in Jain texts.

  • Lands of action: in Jain cosmography Bharata, Airāvata and the parts of Videha outside the two Kuru lands are karmabhūmis, where Jinas are born and liberation is possible; the rest are bhogabhūmis. There are fifteen karmabhūmis in the two and a half continents.

  • Time: in Bharata and Airāvata time moves in great cycles of ascent and descent (utsarpiṇī and avasarpiṇī); in Videha it does not, so that a Jina is always teaching there.

Jain cosmography gave rise to some of the most elaborate diagrams in Indian art: painted cloths of the two and a half continents (aḍhāī dvīpa paṭa), of Jambūdvīpa and of the lokapuruṣa, mostly from western India and from the fifteenth century onward (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 2.6.3 Nandīśvaradvīpa
docs.text: Jain cosmography gives special importance to the eighth continent, Nandīśvaradvīpa, beyond the world of humans. On it stand fifty-two eternal temples of the Jinas, thirteen in each direction, where the gods gather to worship on festival days. Since humans cannot travel there, Jains have recreated it on earth: many Jain temples contain a shrine or a sculpted or painted representation of Nandīśvaradvīpa with its fifty-two shrines, so that worshippers can perform in miniature the worship that the gods perform in the far continent (Dundas 2002). It is a striking example of cosmography made into a ritual space.

docs.title: 2.7 Buddhist Cosmography
docs.text:
Buddhist cosmography shares Meru and Jambudvīpa with the other systems but arranges them differently. In the classical form set out in Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa (chapter 3, c. 4th–5th century CE), Meru rises from a great ocean and is surrounded by seven concentric rings of golden mountains with seas between them. In the outer ocean lie four continents, one in each direction: Jambudvīpa in the south, shaped like a cart or trapezium and narrower to the south (a shape that recalls the subcontinent); Pūrvavideha in the east, semicircular; Aparagodānīya in the west, round; and Uttarakuru in the north, square. Each has smaller islands beside it. The whole world-system is ringed by a wall of iron mountains (cakravāla), and countless such world-systems exist in space (Figure 2.3b; (Kloetzli 1983)).

Figure 2.3. Two schematic diagrams of cosmology, north at the top, not to scale. (a) The Jain world of humans, the “two and a half continents” (aḍhāī dvīpa): Jambūdvīpa, the Lavaṇa ocean, Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, the Kāloda ocean and the inner half of Puṣkaravara, bounded by the circular mountain Mānuṣottara. Each of the two outer continents is divided into an eastern and a western half by two north–south ranges and has two Merus, so that the human world has five. In the texts the widths are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 8 hundred thousand yojanas. (b) The Buddhist world-system of the Abhidharmakośa: Meru within seven rings of golden mountains, and in the outer ocean the four continents, each with its characteristic shape, enclosed by the wall of iron mountains (cakravāla).

This four-continent model travelled with Buddhism to Tibet, China, Japan and Southeast Asia, where it shaped temple plans and painted cosmological diagrams. Human beings, in this scheme too, live in Jambudvīpa, the continent where Buddhas appear.

docs.title: 2.8 Cosmic Space and Cosmic Time
docs.text:
The saṅkalpa formula with which this chapter began places the worshipper in time as well as space, and the Purāṇic cosmos is as vast in time as in extent. In the classical scheme, a cycle of four ages (yuga)—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali—lasts 4,320,000 years, the ages shortening in the ratio 4:3:2:1 and the moral quality of life declining with them. A thousand such cycles make a kalpa, a single day of Brahmā, followed by a night of equal length in which the worlds are dissolved. The present Kali age is reckoned by astronomers and almanac-makers to have begun in 3102 BCE; this epoch is a calculated one, adopted in astronomical texts such as the Āryabhaṭīya, not a historical date.

Jain cosmology has a different scheme: in the lands of Bharata and Airāvata, time turns in a wheel of two half-cycles, one ascending (utsarpiṇī) and one descending (avasarpiṇī), each divided into six spokes, in which human stature, lifespan and virtue rise and fall; twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras appear in each half-cycle. In Videha, by contrast, conditions do not change: they remain like those of the period in which Jinas appear, so that a Jina is always present somewhere in Videha.

These immense time-scales are sometimes compared with the age of the universe in modern cosmology. The comparison is of the same kind as the identification of the continents with the modern map: the numbers are products of a cosmological arithmetic built on multiples of a few base values, not measurements, and their resemblance to modern figures is coincidental (Plofker 2009; Rocher 1986).

docs.title: 2.9 Cosmography Meets Astronomy
docs.text:
From the time of Āryabhaṭa (499 CE), Indian astronomers worked with a spherical earth (Chapter 3). This created an obvious conflict with the flat earth-disc of the Purāṇas. Astronomers responded in several ways. Āryabhaṭa placed Meru at the north pole and reduced it to a mountain only one yojana high (Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 11). The Sūryasiddhānta and later texts locate Meru at the north pole, the gods on it and the demons at the south pole, and explain that each sees the sun for half the year. Some placed the other continents of the Purāṇas on the unseen southern half of the globe; others treated the Purāṇic dimensions as true in some other way or simply set them aside (Plofker 2009).

Al-Bīrūnī, who studied Sanskrit sources in the early eleventh century, devoted several chapters of his book on India to the Purāṇic description of the earth, the seven continents and Meru, and set them against the views of the astronomers, criticising both where he found them inconsistent (Sachau 1910). In later centuries the question “which is right, the Purāṇa or the Siddhānta?” was debated in Sanskrit treatises; the argument was still lively in the seventeenth century (Minkowski 2001), and in the nineteenth century the encounter with European astronomy added a third voice.

Historical Note: Ptolemy and the Purāṇas

The Geography of Claudius Ptolemy (c. 150 CE) lists the latitude and longitude of some eight thousand places and gives instructions for drawing maps on a projection (Berggren and Jones 2000). The Purāṇic bhuvanakośa, compiled over a similar span of centuries, does something quite different: it orders the cosmos. The comparison shows two different projects rather than one tradition being “behind” the other; India’s own counterpart to Ptolemy’s mathematical geography is to be sought in the Siddhāntas.

docs.title: 2.10 Cosmography in Stone
docs.text:
Cosmography shaped architecture as well as texts. The Hindu temple is often understood as an image of Meru: Varāhamihira’s list of temple types in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā begins with the type called Meru, and later architectural texts and inscriptions compare the temple’s towering superstructure (śikhara, “peak”) to the cosmic mountain, rising above the sanctum that houses the deity. The great temples of Khajuraho, with their clusters of subsidiary towers rising to a central summit, have been read in this way by historians of art (Kramrisch 1946).

The same idea travelled to Southeast Asia. At Angkor Wat in Cambodia (twelfth century), the central towers represent the peaks of Meru and the surrounding moat the cosmic ocean; at Borobudur in Java (around 800 CE), the terraces of the Buddhist monument have been interpreted as a three-dimensional maṇḍala and an image of the cosmic mountain. In Bali, temple towers with many roofs are still called meru. Jain temple complexes, with their representations of Nandīśvaradvīpa and of the samavasaraṇa—the assembly hall in which a Jina preaches, arranged in concentric rings—likewise turn cosmography into built space.

docs.title: 2.11 The Afterlife of Purāṇic Geography
docs.text: Purāṇic names have had a long afterlife, from Aśoka’s use of “Jambudvīpa” in his Minor Rock Edict I to “Bharat” in Article 1 of the Constitution of India (Section 1.8). The saṅkalpa formula, recited in many households and temples, still places each ritual in Jambūdvīpa and Bhāratavarṣa. These are continuities of name and of religious imagination; they should not be mistaken for evidence that the Purāṇic universe is a description of the physical earth.

docs.title: 2.12 Purāṇic Geography in the Colonial Classroom
docs.text:
In the nineteenth century the Purāṇic world-picture became a battleground. Christian missionaries and some colonial educators used the contradiction between the Purāṇic earth and modern geography as an argument against Hinduism as a whole: if the sacred texts were wrong about the shape of the earth, they argued, they could not be trusted on anything else. Some officials tried a different approach. Lancelot Wilkinson, political agent at Sehore in central India in the 1830s, encouraged pandits to study the Sanskrit astronomical Siddhāntas, which already taught a spherical earth, as a bridge to modern astronomy. Among those he encouraged was the young Bāpū Deva Śāstrī, who later became the teacher of mathematics and astronomy, Sanskrit and European, at the Sanskrit College in Banaras. Bāpū Deva’s translation of the Sūryasiddhānta and Wilkinson’s translation of Bhāskara’s Golādhyāya, revised by Bāpū Deva, were published together in 1861 (Bāpū Deva Śāstrī and Wilkinson 1861).

Indian responses varied. Some traditional scholars defended the Purāṇic account, reading it as a description of a different order of reality or of a vaster cosmos than the astronomers’ earth; some reformers rejected the Purāṇas altogether, as Dayānanda Sarasvatī, founder of the Ārya Samāj, did in favour of the Vedas; and many educated Indians simply accepted modern geography while continuing to use the Purāṇic names and the saṅkalpa in ritual. The debate is a chapter in the history of how Indian intellectuals came to terms with modern science, and many of its arguments recur in modern debates over “Vedic science”.

docs.title: 2.13 Modern Readings of the Purāṇic Map
docs.text:
Since the eighteenth century, European and Indian writers have repeatedly tried to read the Purāṇic continents as coded descriptions of the real world. The most famous episode involved Francis Wilford (1761–1822), an officer of the East India Company and a member of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta. In a series of essays in Asiatick Researches he identified Purāṇic places with Egypt and the Nile and argued that the “white island” (Śvetadvīpa) and other “sacred isles in the west” were the British Isles. In 1805 he had to admit that the pandit who supplied his Sanskrit passages had forged many of them to suit what Wilford wanted to find. The affair damaged the reputation of Orientalist scholarship for a generation and is a lasting warning against reading one’s own expectations into ancient texts (Trautmann 1997).

Similar readings continue today: claims that the seven continents correspond to the modern continents, that Meru is the Pamirs or the North Pole, or that the dimensions of the Purāṇic earth encode the orbits of the planets. Such interpretations select a few details and ignore the rest; none has been accepted by scholars of the texts. The Purāṇic bhuvanakośa is best read as what it says it is: a description of the cosmos as its authors imagined it, combining inherited cosmological schemes with knowledge of the land of Bhārata.

docs.title: 2.14 Lemuria and Kumari Kandam
docs.text:
The most influential modern fantasy geography in India owes little to the Purāṇas. In 1864 the English zoologist Philip Sclater, puzzled that lemurs and their fossil relatives were found in Madagascar and in India but not in the lands between, proposed that a sunken land bridge had once joined them across the Indian Ocean, and called it Lemuria. Ernst Haeckel suggested that it might have been the cradle of humankind, and the Theosophists, above all Helena Blavatsky in The Secret Doctrine (1888), made the Lemurians one of the “root races” of human history. In the twentieth century continental drift and plate tectonics explained the distribution of the animals without any lost continent, and Lemuria disappeared from geology.

In the Tamil country it took on a second life. Medieval Tamil commentators had preserved a tradition that the sea had swallowed land in the far south. The commentary on the Iṟaiyaṉār Akapporuḷ, attributed to Nakkīrar and usually dated to about the eighth century, tells of three successive academies (caṅkam) of Tamil poets, the first two at southern cities that were later taken by the sea; Aṭiyārkkunallār, a later commentator on the Cilappatikāram, speaks of forty-nine territories (nāṭu) between the rivers Paḵṟuḷi and Kumari that the sea submerged. From the late nineteenth century Tamil writers combined these traditions with the European Lemuria and called the lost land Kumari Kandam (kumarik kaṇṭam), the “continent of Kumari”. In its fullest form it became the original homeland of the Tamils, and even of human civilisation, and its submergence a founding catastrophe of Tamil history; the story was repeated in political speeches, popular histories and some school textbooks.

Sumathi Ramaswamy’s study shows how the idea was assembled, from colonial science, occultism and Tamil scholarship, and what it did for those who held it: it gave devotees of Tamil an antiquity and a homeland independent of the Sanskritic north, and turned a loss into a claim (Ramaswamy 2004). As geography it has no basis. The sea did rise after the last ice age and covered coastal land round southern India and Sri Lanka (Section 11.5), but there is no geological or archaeological evidence for a sunken continent, or a lost civilisation, in the Indian Ocean. Like the Purāṇic continents read as modern ones, Kumari Kandam belongs to the history of how geographies are imagined. The Tolkāppiyam’s southern boundary of the Tamil land at Kumari, discussed in Section 12.5, is a different matter: it names a real place, the southern tip of the peninsula.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Kirfel (1920) remains the fundamental comparative study of Purāṇic cosmography; Sircar (1971) and Law (1954) use the Purāṇic lists for historical geography. On Jain cosmology see Caillat and Kumar (1981); on Buddhist cosmology, Kloetzli (1983). For the astronomers’ response, Plofker (2009) and Minkowski (2001); for Lemuria and Kumari Kandam, Ramaswamy (2004).

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Spherical Earth of the Astronomers
docs.text:
mṛjjalaśikhivāyumayo bhūgolaḥ sarvato vṛttaḥ “The earth-globe, made of earth, water, fire and air, is round on all sides.”

— Āryabhaṭa, Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 6 (499 CE)

The astronomer Āryabhaṭa tells us that he was twenty-three years old when 3,600 years of the Kali age had passed, that is, in 499 CE, the year usually taken as the date of his short Sanskrit treatise on mathematics and astronomy, the Āryabhaṭīya. He says that he set out the knowledge honoured at Kusumapura, usually identified with Pāṭaliputra (Patna). The work has 121 verses in four sections: the Gītikāpāda, which gives his astronomical parameters in a compact alphabetic notation; the Gaṇitapāda, on mathematics; the Kālakriyāpāda, on the reckoning of time and planetary motion; and the Golapāda, on the sphere (Clark 1930; Shukla and Sarma 1976).

The Āryabhaṭīya is not the first Indian text to treat the earth as a globe—older astronomical works, now known only from Varāhamihira’s summary in the Pañcasiddhāntikā, already did so, partly under the influence of Hellenistic astronomy—but it is the earliest surviving Indian treatise to set out a complete mathematical astronomy on that basis. From it, and from the works of Brahmagupta, Bhāskara I, Lalla, Bhāskara II and their successors, comes the mathematical geography of India: the spherical earth, its size, the reference meridian, latitude and the correction for longitude (Plofker 2009; Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 3.1 The Earth as a Globe
docs.text:
Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 6

vṛttabhapañjaramadhye kakṣyāpariveṣṭitaḥ khamadhyagataḥ mṛjjalaśikhivāyumayo bhūgolaḥ sarvato vṛttaḥ

“In the middle of the circular cage of the stars, surrounded by the orbits [of the planets], in the centre of space, is the earth-globe, made of earth, water, fire and air, round on all sides.”

The earth, in this model, is a small sphere at the centre of a much larger celestial sphere. It is unsupported: later astronomers, such as Bhāskara II, explicitly reject the older ideas that the earth rests on a tortoise, a serpent or elephants, and argue that it holds itself in place by its own power. People live all round it, and each sees himself on top (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 3.1.1 Rotation of the Earth
docs.text:
Āryabhaṭa’s best-known doctrine also has a geographical side. He held that the daily turning of the heavens is only apparent and that it is the earth that turns, and he described the effect from the standpoint of an observer at a fixed place on the globe: Laṅkā, the zero point of his mathematical geography (Section 3.2).

Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 9

anulomagatir nausthaḥ paśyaty acalaṃ vilomagaṃ yadvat acalāni bhāni tadvat samapaścimagāni laṅkāyām

“Just as a man in a boat moving forward sees stationary objects moving backward, so at Laṅkā the stationary stars [are seen] moving due west.”

For the geographer the point of the image is the observer’s place. On the equator, under the reference meridian, the stars rise due east and set due west; at any other latitude the same rotation is seen at a slant, and the astronomers’ rules for latitude, day length and local time all follow from that. How the doctrine should be read, how the following verse on the pravaha wind fits with it, and why most later astronomers, from Varāhamihira and Brahmagupta onward, rejected it are questions of the history of astronomy, treated in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa (Chapter 9). It is enough here that Āryabhaṭa’s rotating earth remained at the centre of the universe, so that it is not heliocentrism (Plofker 2009; Shukla and Sarma 1976), and that the dispute made no difference to mathematical geography: as al-Bīrūnī remarked, positions and times come out the same whether the earth or the heavens are taken to turn (Sachau 1910).

docs.title: 3.2 Laṅkā, Ujjayinī and the Reference Meridian
docs.text:
Calculations of planetary positions were made for a reference location. Indian astronomers chose a point on the equator called Laṅkā and the meridian that runs from it north through Ujjayinī (Ujjain) to Meru at the north pole. This Laṅkā is a mathematical point, not the island of Sri Lanka, which lies several degrees north of the equator and well east of Ujjain’s meridian; the name connected the point with the Laṅkā of the Rāmāyaṇa, imagined in the far south.

Āryabhaṭa states that Ujjayinī lies one-fifteenth of the earth’s circumference north of Laṅkā (Golapāda 14), that is, at 24° north; the modern latitude of Ujjain is about 23°11’. The Sūryasiddhānta names further places on the same meridian, among them Rohītaka (Rohtak) and the sacred lake at Kurukṣetra. The meridian of Ujjain, at about 75°47’ east of Greenwich in modern terms, remained the standard for Indian astronomers and almanac-makers (pañcāṅga) for more than a thousand years (Figure 3.1a). Ujjain also had a long association with astronomy: Varāhamihira worked in its region, and in the 1720s Sawai Jai Singh II built one of his observatories there.

Figure 3.1. The astronomers’ reference frame, schematic. (a) A section through the earth along the reference meridian, which runs from Laṅkā, a point on the equator, through Ujjayinī, put by Āryabhaṭa at one-fifteenth of the circumference (24°) north of Laṅkā, and through Rohītaka and Kurukṣetra to Meru at the north pole. \(\phi\) is the latitude. (b) The four cities imagined on the equator a quarter of the circumference apart, seen from above the north pole, with the earth turning eastward: when the sun rises at Laṅkā it is noon at Yavakoṭi, sunset at Siddhapura and midnight at Romaka. The cities are mathematical points, not places on a map.

Terms of Indian Positional Astronomy

Akṣa or akṣāṃśa: terrestrial latitude, equal to the height of the celestial pole above the horizon. Lamba: co-latitude (90° minus the latitude). Palabhā or akṣabhā: the “equinoctial shadow”, the noon shadow of a gnomon twelve units high on the day of the equinox; the ratio of this shadow to the gnomon is the tangent of the latitude. Deśāntara: “difference of place”; the correction to calculated times for a place east or west of the reference meridian. Laṅkā: the point on the equator under the reference meridian.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Finding Latitude
docs.text:
Latitude was found with the gnomon (śaṅku), a vertical stick usually reckoned as twelve aṅgulas high. Its noon shadow on the day of the equinox gives the latitude directly: if the shadow is \(s\) units long, the latitude \(\phi\) satisfies \(\tan\phi = s/12\). At Ujjain the equinoctial noon shadow is about five units (Figure 3.2a). Astronomical texts give rules for finding the latitude from shadows on other days, using the sun’s declination, and for finding the pole’s altitude from stars. Lists of latitudes for particular towns appear in some astronomical handbooks and in al-Bīrūnī’s works. Their accuracy varies from list to list and from town to town, so that no general figure for the accuracy of Indian latitudes can be given without examining each list.

A Worked Example: The Latitude of Ujjain

At Ujjain the noon shadow of a gnomon twelve aṅgulas high, on the day of the equinox, is a little over five aṅgulas long. Taking it as 5.1 units:

\[\tan\phi = \frac{5.1}{12} \approx 0.425, \qquad \phi \approx 23^\circ,\]

which is close to the modern latitude of Ujjain (about 23°11’). Āryabhaṭa’s figure of 24° (one-fifteenth of the circumference) is a convenient round value rather than the result of such a measurement.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Longitude Difference
docs.text: East–west position was harder to determine, as it was everywhere before accurate clocks. The Sūryasiddhānta and later texts compute the deśāntara from the distance of a place east or west of the reference meridian, measured in yojanas along the local parallel and converted into time. They also describe the principle of comparing the local times at which the same lunar eclipse is observed in two places. In practice distances were estimated rather than measured, and longitude differences were much less reliable than latitudes.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Day Length and Latitude
docs.text: Because the earth is a sphere, the length of daylight varies with latitude and season: at the equator day and night are always equal, while further north the summer days are longer and the winter days shorter. Indian astronomers computed this variation as the “ascensional difference” (cara), the correction by which the time of sunrise at a place differs from six hours before noon, and they gave rules for finding it from the latitude (through the equinoctial shadow) and the sun’s declination. Al-Bīrūnī discusses the Indian treatment of the inhabited earth and the experience of day and night at different latitudes, including the six-month day at Meru, in his chapters on the subject (Sachau 1910).

docs.title: 3.2.4 Ujjain in the Islamic and Latin Traditions
docs.text: Indian astronomy reached Baghdad in the eighth century, and with it the reference meridian through Ujjain. The channel was the Arabic version of a Sanskrit astronomical work brought to the court of the caliph al-Manṣūr by an Indian scholar; known as the Sindhind (from siddhānta), it introduced Indian parameters and methods, including the sine, into Arabic astronomy (Plofker 2009). In Arabic, the name Ujjayinī was written in a form that was later misread as “Arin”. The “cupola of Arin”, a point on the equator midway between the eastern and western limits of the inhabited world, became a standard reference in Arabic geography and was taken over into medieval Latin astronomy and geography. The idea of a central meridian at Ujjain thus travelled, in altered form, from India through the Islamic world to Europe—a small example of the circulation of geographical ideas.

docs.title: 3.3 The Size of the Earth
docs.text:
The astronomers gave the size of the earth in yojanas (Table 3.1). The figures differ from text to text because the yojana itself differed.

Table 3.1. The size of the earth in the astronomical texts Source Stated value Implied value Āryabhaṭa, Āryabhaṭīya (499) diameter 1,050 yojanas circumference about 3,299 yojanas; his yojana is 8,000 “man-heights” (nṛ) Sūryasiddhānta (present form c. 8th–10th c.) diameter 1,600 yojanas circumference \(\sqrt{10}\times1600 \approx\) 5,059.6 yojanas Brahmagupta, Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628) circumference 5,000 yojanas diameter about 1,581 yojanas (taking \(\pi = \sqrt{10}\)) Bhāskara II, Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (1150) circumference 4,967 yojanas diameter about 1,581 yojanas

The value 4,967 yojanas, sometimes attributed to Āryabhaṭa in popular writing, is Bhāskara II’s. Bhāskara also explains the principle by which the circumference could be found: measure the distance between two places on the same meridian, find the difference of their latitudes, and scale up to 360° (Figure 3.2b). This is the same principle that Eratosthenes used in the third century BCE and that the astronomers of the caliph al-Maʾmūn applied in the ninth century by measuring a degree in the Syrian desert. There is no record of an Indian expedition that carried out such a measurement.

Al-Bīrūnī, in the early eleventh century, used a different method. From a hill near the fort of Nandana in the Salt Range of the Punjab he measured the dip of the horizon and, knowing the height of the hill, calculated the radius of the earth (Figure 3.2c). He describes the measurement in his later astronomical works; it is a genuine field measurement made in the subcontinent, though by a visiting Central Asian scholar rather than an Indian astronomer.

Figure 3.2. The geometry behind the astronomers’ measurements, schematic. (a) Latitude from the gnomon: at noon on the day of the equinox the shadow \(s\) of a gnomon twelve units high gives the latitude \(\phi\). (b) The principle stated by Bhāskara II: if two places A and B on the same meridian are a distance \(d\) apart and their latitudes differ by \(\Delta\phi\), the circumference \(C\) follows by proportion. (c) Al-Bīrūnī’s method near Nandana: from a hill of known height \(h\), the dip \(\alpha\) of the horizon below the horizontal gives the radius \(R\) of the earth, since \(\cos\alpha = R/(R+h)\). The height of the hill is greatly exaggerated.

Why These Figures Cannot Be Checked to the Kilometre

  • The yojana was not a fixed unit. Most modern estimates for different texts fall roughly between 7 and 15 km, and some reckonings give more (Section 3.10). The Arthaśāstra’s yojana of 8,000 bow-lengths (dhanus) comes to roughly 13–15 km, depending on the length assumed for the finger-breadth (aṅgula).

  • Depending on the yojana chosen within that range, the figures in the table correspond to anything from about 23,000 km to about 76,000 km. (The modern equatorial circumference is about 40,075 km.)

  • It is circular reasoning to choose the yojana that makes a given figure come out close to 40,000 km and then to praise the figure for its accuracy. Statements such as “Āryabhaṭa’s circumference was within 1% of the true value” rest on exactly this procedure.

  • The astronomers’ figures were not derived from a recorded measurement. They are parameters of astronomical systems, consistent with the authors’ other values.

docs.title: 3.4 Varāhamihira and the Bṛhatsaṃhitā
docs.text:
Varāhamihira (fl. c. 550 CE), who worked in or near Ujjain, wrote the Pañcasiddhāntikā, a summary of five earlier astronomical systems, and the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, an encyclopaedia of omens and natural knowledge (Bhat 1981). Several of its chapters bear on geography.

  • The Kūrmavibhāga (chapter 14) arranges the regions and peoples of India in nine groups, as if on the body of a tortoise: the Middle Country and the eight directions. Each group is assigned to a set of lunar mansions, so that omens in those mansions can be applied to those lands. It is one of the most important lists of the peoples of early medieval India, though, like the Purāṇic lists, it combines current and archaic names (Sircar 1971).

  • Rain and weather (chapters 21–28): signs for predicting rain from clouds, winds and the behaviour of animals during the “pregnancy of the clouds” some months before the rains, and the measurement of rainfall in an āḍhaka vessel.

  • Earthquakes (chapter 32): classification of earthquakes by their signs and by the deity held responsible, with a mention of the older view that they are caused by winds or by the movements of great beings beneath the earth.

  • Water-finding (Dakārgala, chapter 54): rules for finding underground water from trees, termite mounds, soils, stones and animals.

Scholarly Note: The Dakārgala

The water-finding chapter is a practical text in a semi-arid land.
