It states, for example, that a particular kind of tree or termite mound indicates a vein of water at a given distance and depth, measured in puruṣas (man-heights). Such rules record accumulated experience of well-diggers. They have attracted modern interest, and some popular books present them as a method confirmed by modern hydrogeology; the published field studies do not show that. They are best read as a historical record of practical knowledge and as hypotheses, not as a tested method.

docs.title: 3.5 The Five Siddhāntas and the Meridian of Yavanapura
docs.text:
Varāhamihira’s Pañcasiddhāntikā (“Five Treatises”) summarises five astronomical systems current in the sixth century: the Paitāmaha, Vāsiṣṭha, Romaka, Pauliśa and Saura (Sūrya) Siddhāntas. The first two represent an older Indian tradition; the Romaka and Pauliśa, as their names suggest, derive from Greek astronomy, and the Saura is the most advanced. The Romaka used as its reference the meridian of Yavanapura, “the city of the Greeks”, generally taken to be Alexandria, and Varāhamihira gives the rule for converting its results to the meridian of Ujjayinī. The text thus records, in Sanskrit, an awareness that a different reference meridian had been used in the Greek world, and that time differences between distant places had to be taken into account (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009).

Varāhamihira’s work also preserves descriptions of the earth and the heavens from these systems, and his objection to the rotation of the earth (Section 3.1): if the earth turned, birds could not find their way back to their nests. Because the earlier treatises themselves are lost, the Pañcasiddhāntikā is the main evidence for the transitional period in which Hellenistic astronomy was absorbed into the Indian tradition.

docs.title: 3.6 Brahmagupta and Bhāskara II
docs.text:
Brahmagupta (b. 598 CE) wrote the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta in 628 at Bhillamāla (Bhinmal, Rajasthan), edited by Sudhākara Dvivedī in 1902 (Dvivedī 1902), and the handbook Khaṇḍakhādyaka in 665. He accepted the spherical earth, rejected its rotation, gave its circumference as 5,000 yojanas, and devoted a whole chapter to criticism of other astronomers, above all Āryabhaṭa. His work was translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the eighth century, and through that translation Indian astronomical parameters entered early Islamic astronomy (Plofker 2009).

Bhāskara II (b. 1114) wrote the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi in 1150. Its Golādhyāya includes a section called Bhuvanakośa in which he sets out the Purāṇic description of the world and reconciles it, as far as he can, with the spherical earth of the astronomers: Meru at the north pole, Laṅkā and three other cities 90° apart on the equator, and the continents of the Purāṇas on the southern half of the globe (Bāpū Deva Śāstrī and Wilkinson 1861). He also discusses the gnomon and other instruments in his chapter on instruments (Yantrādhyāya). The Siddhāntaśiromaṇi became one of the most widely studied astronomical texts in India.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Bhāskara II on the Earth’s Attraction
docs.text: In his Golādhyāya, Bhāskara II explains why the unsupported earth does not fall and why people on all sides of it do not fall off: the earth, he says, has a power of attraction (ākṛṣṭi-śakti) by which it draws heavy objects towards itself, so that they appear to fall; since the earth is surrounded on all sides by space, there is nowhere for it to fall to. The passage is sometimes presented as an anticipation of Newton’s law of universal gravitation. That is a misreading. Bhāskara offers a qualitative explanation of why bodies fall towards the earth, of a kind found in several pre-modern traditions; he does not propose that all bodies attract one another, nor a mathematical law, nor any connection between this attraction and the motions of the planets, which in his astronomy are explained quite differently (Plofker 2009). The passage is interesting in its own right as part of the astronomers’ defence of a spherical, unsupported earth.

docs.title: 3.6.2 The Four Cities on the Equator
docs.text: From Āryabhaṭa onward, astronomers imagined four cities on the equator, a quarter of the circumference apart (Figure 3.1b): Laṅkā on the reference meridian, Yavakoṭi to the east, Romaka to the west and Siddhapura on the opposite side. When it is sunrise at Laṅkā, it is noon at Yavakoṭi, sunset at Siddhapura and midnight at Romaka. The scheme is a teaching device for time differences on a rotating (or rotating-sky) sphere. The names connect it loosely with the known world—Romaka is Rome, Yavakoṭi (also called Yamakoṭi) a city in the far east—but the cities are mathematical points, not geographical claims.

docs.title: 3.7 The Sūryasiddhānta and the Almanac Tradition
docs.text:
The Sūryasiddhānta (“the Sun’s treatise”), presented as a revelation from the Sun to the demon Maya, is the best known of the Indian astronomical texts. A work of this name was among the five summarised by Varāhamihira in the sixth century, but the text that survives is a later revision, reworked over several centuries; its parameters were updated, and it became the standard authority for almanac-makers in much of India (Plofker 2009; Bāpū Deva Śāstrī and Wilkinson 1861). Its chapter on the earth gives the earth’s diameter as 1,600 yojanas and the rule for the correction for longitude, and names places on the reference meridian from Laṅkā through Ujjayinī, Rohītaka and Kurukṣetra to Meru. Its chapter on cosmography places Meru at the north pole and describes the four equatorial cities and the experience of day and night at different latitudes.

The Sūryasiddhānta and other Siddhāntas were used to compute the annual almanacs (pañcāṅga) that fix the dates of festivals, fasts and auspicious times. Because local sunrise, the length of day and the visibility of eclipses depend on latitude and longitude, almanac-makers had to adapt their calculations to the places for which they wrote, and regional almanacs carried this mathematical geography into daily life. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries a debate arose between those who kept the traditional parameters and those who wished to use modern astronomical values (dṛkpakṣa, “the side of observation”); both kinds of almanac are still published.

docs.title: 3.8 Indian and Greek Mathematical Geography
docs.text:
Indian and Greek mathematical geography shared the spherical earth, the gnomon, latitude measured by the pole’s altitude, and the use of eclipses to compare local times. The resemblances are not accidental. Greek astronomical ideas reached India in the early centuries of the common era through texts such as the Yavanajātaka and the older siddhāntas summarised by Varāhamihira; David Pingree argued that much of the early Indian mathematical astronomy derives from Hellenistic and Babylonian sources (Pingree 1976, 1981). Others, while accepting the borrowing, emphasise how quickly Indian astronomers transformed what they received, with their own trigonometry (the sine rather than the chord), their own parameters and their own computational methods (Plofker 2009).

The differences are as instructive as the similarities. Ptolemy’s Geography is a gazetteer of some eight thousand places with coordinates and a manual for drawing world maps on a projection (Berggren and Jones 2000). No Indian astronomical text attempts a world gazetteer or gives instructions for drawing maps; the Indian astronomers needed coordinates only for computing local times and planetary positions. Indian mathematical geography was therefore narrower in scope than Ptolemy’s, while in some computational techniques it went further.

docs.title: 3.9 Instruments and Observatories
docs.text:
Indian astronomers described a range of instruments for observing the sky and for teaching the geometry of the spheres. Āryabhaṭa, Lalla and Bhāskara II describe the armillary sphere (golayantra), a model of the celestial circles turning about the earth at the centre, which was used to demonstrate the relations between horizon, meridian, equator and ecliptic. The gnomon, the water-clock (ghaṭikā) and graduated circles and semicircles (cakra, dhanus) were used for measurement, and Bhāskara II describes an instrument of his own, the “board” (phalakayantra), for finding time from the sun’s altitude (Plofker 2009).

From the fourteenth century, the astrolabe of the Islamic world entered Sanskrit astronomy. The Jain astronomer Mahendra Sūri, at the court of Sultan Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq in Delhi, wrote the Yantrarāja (1370), a Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe, and astrolabes with Sanskrit as well as Arabic and Persian inscriptions were made in later centuries. Persian astronomical tables (zīj) were compiled at Indian courts, and Sanskrit astronomers translated and adapted Islamic works.

docs.title: 3.9.1 Observation in Kerala
docs.text: Indian astronomy is sometimes described as purely computational. The Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics shows otherwise. Parameśvara of Vaṭaśśeri (c. 1380–1460) recorded that he had observed eclipses and planetary positions over some fifty-five years, and he revised the traditional parameters to bring computation into agreement with observation in his system called Dṛggaṇita (“computation in accordance with sight”, 1431). His successors, including Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī, continued to discuss the relation between observation and theory (Plofker 2009). Such work depended on careful attention to the observer’s own latitude and longitude, since the visibility and timing of eclipses differ from place to place.

docs.title: 3.9.2 Sawai Jai Singh’s Observatories
docs.text:
The most spectacular instruments are the masonry observatories built by Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber and Jaipur (1688–1743) at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Vārāṇasī and Mathurā in the 1720s and 1730s. Their great sundial (samrāṭ yantra), hemispherical bowls (jayaprakāśa) and other instruments were designed to increase the precision of naked-eye observations by their sheer size. Jai Singh assembled Hindu, Muslim and European astronomers, had Greek and Arabic works translated into Sanskrit, compiled a Persian set of tables dedicated to the Mughal emperor Muḥammad Shāh, and sent a mission to Portugal that brought back European astronomical tables (Sharma 1995). The observatory at Jaipur was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.

Jai Singh’s project shows both the vitality of Indian astronomy in the eighteenth century and its limits: by the time his observatories were built, European astronomy was already using telescopes and a heliocentric model, which the Jaipur programme did not adopt. Within a few decades the surveyors of the East India Company were taking astronomical fixes of Indian towns with portable European instruments (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 3.10 The Yojana and Other Units
docs.text:
The basic units of distance in Sanskrit texts are the finger-breadth (aṅgula), the cubit (hasta or aratni, 24 aṅgulas), the bow-length (dhanus or daṇḍa, four cubits), the krośa or goruta, and the yojana. The words themselves show their origin in everyday life: goruta means the distance at which a cow’s lowing can be heard, krośa the range of a shout, and yojana probably the distance covered by a yoked team in a stage. Table 3.2 gives some of the definitions.

Table 3.2. Some definitions of the yojana Source Definition Rough modern equivalent Arthaśāstra 2.20 1 daṇḍa = 96 aṅgulas; 10 daṇḍas = 1 rajju; 2,000 dhanus = 1 goruta; 4 gorutas = 1 yojana yojana roughly 13–15 km Āryabhaṭa 1 yojana = 8,000 nṛ (man-heights) depends on the height assumed Xuanzang (7th c.) the yojana reckoned variously as 40, 30 or 16 Chinese li from about 7 to 18 km Al-Bīrūnī (11th c.) reports the yojana as 32,000 yards (8 of his miles) uncertain

The variety of definitions is not a defect peculiar to India; pre-modern units everywhere varied with region and purpose. It does mean that ancient distances and dimensions can be converted into modern units only within wide margins, and that arguments which depend on an exact conversion should be treated with suspicion.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Plofker (2009) is the best general account of Indian mathematical astronomy. For the Āryabhaṭīya see Shukla and Sarma (1976) and Clark (1930); for the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, Bhat (1981); for the transmission of Greek astronomy, Pingree (1976); for Ptolemy, Berggren and Jones (2000). The astronomy of the Siddhāntas as a whole is treated in Volume 12 of this series, Khagola Jyotiṣa.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Sacred Geography and Pilgrimage
docs.text:
ayodhyā mathurā māyā kāśī kāñcī avantikā purī dvārāvatī caiva saptaitā mokṣadāyikāḥ “Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā [Haridvār], Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā [Ujjain] and the city of Dvārakā: these seven grant liberation.”

— A widely quoted traditional verse

Of all the forms of geographical knowledge in pre-modern India, the one that reached the largest number of people was sacred geography. A dense network of sacred places—river fords, confluences, mountains, caves, groves, temple towns and the tombs of saints—covers the subcontinent. People travelled to them, sometimes over very long distances, and the texts that praised them named routes, rivers and neighbouring places. Pilgrimage thus helped to create a shared knowledge and imagination of the land far beyond the borders of any single kingdom (Eck 2012; Bhardwaj 1973).

The network was not the creation of one tradition. Brahmanical Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs and Muslims each developed their own sacred places and journeys, often in the same landscape and sometimes at the same sites. Nor was access equal: who could enter a temple, bathe at a ghāṭ or undertake a long pilgrimage depended on caste, gender and wealth. This chapter describes the main networks and the literature that recorded them.

docs.title: 4.1 The Idea of the Tīrtha
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word tīrtha comes from the root tṝ, “to cross over”. Its first meaning is a ford or a bathing place on a river. Already in the Mahābhārata it means a sacred place, often but not always beside water, where the boundary between the human and the divine is thought to be easily crossed, and where bathing, offerings to the ancestors and gifts bring great merit. By extension a holy person, a teacher or a parent can be called a tīrtha, and a Jain tīrthaṅkara is a “ford-maker” who has shown the way across the ocean of rebirth.

Some Terms of Sacred Geography

Tīrtha: ford; sacred place, especially one associated with water. Kṣetra: “field”; a sacred territory, often with defined boundaries, such as Kāśī-kṣetra or Kurukṣetra. Dhām: “abode”; a seat of a deity, used especially for the four great dhāms. Pīṭha: “seat”; above all the seats of the Goddess (śākta pīṭha). Māhātmya: a text in praise of a sacred place, describing its origin, sub-sites and merits. Yātrā: journey, pilgrimage; parikramā or pradakṣiṇā: circumambulation, keeping the sacred object to one’s right.

docs.title: 4.1.1 The Literature of Pilgrimage
docs.text:
The oldest extended account of pilgrimage in Sanskrit is the Tīrthayātrāparvan of the Mahābhārata’s third book, in which the sage Pulastya and later the Pāṇḍavas’ own journeys take the reader round the sacred places of the land. The Purāṇas contain a vast māhātmya literature; some, like the Kāśīkhaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa, are book-length descriptions of a single sacred city. From the twelfth century, scholars compiled digests on the rules of pilgrimage: Lakṣmīdhara’s Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa, part of his Kṛtyakalpataru, and later works by Vācaspati Miśra, Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa and Mitra Miśra. P. V. Kane’s History of Dharmaśāstra surveys this literature and lists many hundreds of tīrthas (Kane 1953).

These texts are religious, not travel guides, and their geography is often schematic. But they preserve local topography in detail, and the larger digests arrange tīrthas by region and river. Surinder Bhardwaj’s geographical study showed that Hindu pilgrimage places form a hierarchy, from places of all-India importance to regional and local ones, and that the distance pilgrims travel and the social groups they come from vary with the level of the place (Bhardwaj 1973).

docs.title: 4.2 Kāśī: The Paradigmatic Sacred City
docs.text:
Vārāṇasī, also called Kāśī (“the luminous”) and Banaras, is the most celebrated of Hindu sacred cities. It is held to be a mukti-kṣetra, a place where death brings liberation: according to the Kāśīkhaṇḍa and later tradition, Śiva whispers the “crossing” mantra (tāraka mantra) into the ear of the dying. The sacred territory is bounded by the Pañcakrośī road, a circuit of roughly 80 km which pilgrims walk in about five days, worshipping at a series of shrines (traditionally 108) on the way. Diana Eck’s study of the city traces how its sacred topography was described in the māhātmyas and how it can still be followed on the ground (Eck 1982); the geographer Rana P. B. Singh has mapped its pilgrimage circuits in detail (Singh 2009).

The city’s history is also one of destruction and rebuilding. The temple of Viśveśvara (Viśvanātha) was destroyed several times, most notably on Aurangzeb’s orders in 1669, when a mosque was built on part of the site; the present temple was built by Ahilyābāī Holkar of Indore in 1780. Kāśī was also an important centre of Muslim learning and crafts, and of Kabīr and Ravidās, whose critiques of caste and ritual were themselves part of the city’s religious life.

docs.title: 4.3 The Four Dhāms
docs.text:
The four dhāms are placed near the four extremities of the subcontinent (Figure 4.1):

  • Badrīnāth (north): a Vaiṣṇava shrine at about 3,100 m on the Alakanandā in the Garhwal Himalaya, open for about six months each summer.

  • Dvārakā (west): Kṛṣṇa’s city on the coast of Saurashtra, Gujarat.

  • Purī (east): the temple of Jagannātha on the coast of Odisha, famous for its annual chariot festival (rathayātrā).

  • Rāmeśvaram (south): the temple of Rāmanāthasvāmī (Śiva) on Pamban island, linked with Rāma’s crossing to Laṅkā.

Tradition associates the four dhāms with the philosopher Śaṅkara, who is said to have founded four monasteries (maṭha) in the four directions: Jyotirmaṭh near Badrīnāth, the Śāradā Maṭha at Dvārakā, the Govardhana Maṭha at Purī and the Śṛṅgeri Maṭha in Karnataka. Śaṅkara lived c. 700–750 CE; the conventional dates 788–820 are traditional. Historians regard the attribution of the four maṭhas to Śaṅkara himself as tradition rather than established fact; the institutional prominence of Śṛṅgeri, for example, dates from the Vijayanagara period in the fourteenth century, and the grouping of the four dhāms as an all-India circuit is probably later still. In the Himalaya a separate “little four dhāms” (choṭā cār dhām)—Yamunotrī, Gaṅgotrī, Kedārnāth and Badrīnāth—has become one of the most popular pilgrimages of modern India (Eck 2012).

Geographic Insight: The Four Directions

A pilgrim who visits the four dhāms crosses the subcontinent from the Himalaya to the southern sea and from the western to the eastern coast. The pattern of four cardinal shrines expresses, in religious form, an idea of the land as a single sacred whole bounded by mountains and sea, the same idea found in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa’s definition of Bhāratavarṣa (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 4.3.1 Purī and the Chariot Festival
docs.text: The temple of Jagannātha at Purī, begun in its present form under the Eastern Gaṅga king Anantavarman Coḍagaṅga in the twelfth century, is the focus of one of the most popular pilgrimages of eastern India. At the annual chariot festival (rathayātrā) in Āṣāḍha, the images of Jagannātha, his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadrā are drawn on huge wooden chariots along the main street of the town by crowds of devotees. The cult of Jagannātha has been described as inclusive—the deity is associated with tribal origins in Odisha, and food offered to him (mahāprasāda) is traditionally shared across castes—but the temple also maintains strict rules of entry, and non-Hindus are not admitted. Its history illustrates both the integrative and the exclusionary sides of sacred geography.

docs.title: 4.4 The Twelve Jyotirliṅgas
docs.text:
The twelve jyotirliṅgas (“liṅgas of light”) are Śaiva shrines where Śiva is believed to have manifested as a column of light. A popular hymn of remembrance, versions of which are attached to the Śiva Purāṇa, lists them as follows; their usual locations are given in Table 4.1 and Figure 4.1.

The Dvādaśajyotirliṅgasmaraṇa (popular hymn)

saurāṣṭre somanāthaṃ ca śrīśaile mallikārjunam ujjayinyāṃ mahākālam oṃkāram amaleśvaram paralyāṃ vaidyanāthaṃ ca ḍākinyāṃ bhīmaśaṅkaram setubandhe tu rāmeśaṃ nāgeśaṃ dārukāvane vārāṇasyāṃ tu viśveśaṃ tryambakaṃ gautamītaṭe himālaye tu kedāraṃ ghuśmeśaṃ ca śivālaye

“Somanātha in Saurāṣṭra, Mallikārjuna on Śrīśaila; Mahākāla in Ujjayinī, Oṃkāra [and] Amaleśvara; Vaidyanātha at Paralī, Bhīmaśaṅkara in Ḍākinī; Rāmeśa at the Bridge, Nāgeśa in the Dāruka forest; Viśveśa in Vārāṇasī, Tryambaka on the bank of the Gautamī [Godāvarī]; Kedāra in the Himālaya, and Ghuśmeśa at Śivālaya.”

Table 4.1. The twelve jyotirliṅgas and their locations Jyotirliṅga Usual location (and disputed claims) Somanātha Prabhāsa Pāṭan, Saurashtra (Gujarat) Mallikārjuna Śrīśailam, Andhra Pradesh Mahākāla Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh Oṃkāreśvara island of Māndhātā in the Narmadā, Madhya Pradesh Vaidyanātha Deoghar (Jharkhand); also claimed by Parli (Maharashtra), the “Paralī” of the hymn Bhīmaśaṅkara near Pune (Maharashtra); other sites, among them one near Guwahati (Assam), claim the name Rāmeśvara Rāmeśvaram, Tamil Nadu Nāgeśvara near Dvārakā (Gujarat); also claimed by Aundha (Maharashtra) and Jageshwar (Uttarakhand) Viśvanātha Vārāṇasī, Uttar Pradesh Tryambakeśvara near Nashik, at the source of the Godāvarī, Maharashtra Kedāranātha Garhwal Himalaya, Uttarakhand, at about 3,580 m Ghṛṣṇeśvara Verul, near Ellora, Maharashtra Figure 4.1. The four dhāms, the usual sites of the twelve jyotirliṅgas and the four sites of the Kumbh Melā, plotted by latitude and longitude. Rāmeśvaram is both a dhām and a jyotirliṅga, and Ujjain both a jyotirliṅga and a Kumbh site; Nāgeśvara near Dvārakā and Tryambakeśvara near Nashik are too close to their neighbours to be separated at this scale. Several jyotirliṅgas have rival claimants (Table 4.1); only the usual sites are shown. The coastline is simplified and islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted.

The disputes over location are themselves instructive. A sacred name in a text could be claimed by more than one place, and regional traditions competed for the prestige of a pan-Indian list. The twelve sites are spread from Saurashtra to the Himalaya and the southern sea, and popular writing sometimes presents the list as a deliberate plan to sanctify every kind of landscape; but the list was assembled over time, by the competition of places, and no text describes it as a design.

Several of these temples have long and troubled histories. The temple at Somanātha was raided by Maḥmūd of Ghazni in 1025–26, rebuilt and damaged more than once, and reconstructed after Independence, the new temple being inaugurated in 1951. Romila Thapar has shown how differently the event of 1026 was remembered in Sanskrit inscriptions, Persian chronicles, Jain texts and modern nationalist writing (Thapar 2004).

docs.title: 4.5 The Seats of the Goddess
docs.text:
The śākta pīṭhas are places associated with the body of the goddess Satī. In the best-known version of the myth, Satī dies at the sacrifice of her father Dakṣa; Śiva wanders the world carrying her body, and Viṣṇu cuts it into pieces with his discus, which fall to earth and sanctify the places where they land. Earlier Tantric texts, Hindu and Buddhist, know of four principal pīṭhas (Kāmarūpa, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri and Oḍḍiyāna); later lists give 51, 52 or 108. The list of 51 most often quoted, the Pīṭhanirṇaya attached to the Tantracūḍāmaṇi, is a late text. D. C. Sircar’s study of the lists remains the standard work (Sircar 1973).

The pīṭhas extend beyond the modern Indian state: Hiṅglāj in Balochistan (Pakistan), where local Muslims also venerate the goddess as Nānī, Guhyeśvarī in Kathmandu, and sites in Bangladesh and Tibet. Kāmākhyā in Assam, the pīṭha of the goddess’s yoni, is the most important in practice. The list is another example of a pan-Indian network built by linking many local goddess shrines to a single myth.

docs.title: 4.6 Rivers, Confluences and the Kumbh Melā
docs.text:
Rivers are goddesses, and their banks, sources and confluences are among the oldest tīrthas. A widely recited bathing verse invokes seven rivers to be present in the water (see Chapter 9). Prayāga, where the Gaṅgā and Yamunā meet and where tradition adds the invisible Sarasvatī, is the “king of tīrthas” (tīrtharāja).

The Kumbh Melā is held in rotation at four places—Haridvār, Prayāga (Prayagraj), Ujjain and Nashik–Tryambakeshwar—at intervals determined by the position of Jupiter and the sun. Its origin myth is the spilling of drops of nectar from the pot (kumbha) churned from the Ocean of Milk. The gatherings have grown enormously in modern times; the official estimates of attendance at the largest bathing days, which run into tens of millions, are announced by the organising authorities and cannot be checked independently. The history of the festival is less ancient than often claimed. Xuanzang described a great assembly at which Harṣa gave away his wealth at Prayāga in the seventh century, and bathing fairs at Prayāga and Haridvār are much older than the modern melā; but Kama Maclean has shown that the application of the name “Kumbh” to the Prayāga fair, and much of its present organisation, took shape in the nineteenth century, partly through the interaction of pilgrimage priests, ascetic orders and the colonial administration (Maclean 2008).

docs.title: 4.7 Circumambulation
docs.text:
Parikramā or pradakṣiṇā, walking round a sacred object with it on one’s right, is practised at every scale:

  • round a shrine or temple, along the ambulatory path;

  • round a sacred territory, such as the Pañcakrośī of Kāśī (about 80 km) or the caurāsī kos (“84 kos”) circuit of Braj, the land of Kṛṣṇa round Mathurā and Vṛndāvana;

  • round a sacred hill, such as Aruṇācala at Tiruvannamalai (about 14 km) or Govardhana in Braj;

  • round a mountain, above all Kailāsa in western Tibet (about 52 km at altitudes over 4,600 m);

  • round a river, as in the Narmadā parikramā, in which pilgrims walk from the source at Amarkantak to the sea along one bank and back along the other, some 2,600 km, a journey of months.

Long circumambulations produce an intimate knowledge of a landscape: its paths, crossings, villages, seasons and shrines. Pilgrims’ guides (paṇḍās), who kept registers of the families they served, were repositories of such knowledge.

docs.title: 4.8 Kailāsa and Mānasarovar
docs.text:
Mount Kailāsa (Tibetan Gangs Rin po che, 6,638 m) in western Tibet, with the lakes Mānasarovar and Rakas Tal at its foot, is sacred to four religions. For Hindus it is the abode of Śiva and Pārvatī; for Tibetan and other Buddhists it is the palace of the tantric deity Cakrasaṃvara; for Jains it is usually identified with Aṣṭāpada, where the first tīrthaṅkara, Ṛṣabha, attained liberation; and for followers of Bon it is the nine-storeyed sacred mountain of their founder’s tradition. The region is close to the sources of the Indus, the Sutlej, the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) and the Karnali, a tributary of the Ganges.

Kailāsa and Mānasa appear in Sanskrit literature from the epics onward, but the journey itself was long and hard. Indian pilgrims usually went from Kumaon over the Lipu Lekh pass or from Garhwal and Kinnaur over other high passes, and the Tibetan circumambulation was largely in the hands of Tibetan and Bhotiya traders and guides. Alex McKay has argued that the mountain’s present standing as the supreme Hindu pilgrimage goal owes a good deal to nineteenth- and twentieth-century developments: colonial travellers and officials, Hindu reformers and modern pilgrimage organisation (McKay 2015). Since 1981 the Government of India has organised an annual Kailash Mansarovar Yatra by agreement with China.

docs.title: 4.8.1 Amarnāth
docs.text: The cave of Amarnāth, at about 3,900 m in the mountains east of Srinagar, contains an ice formation worshipped as a liṅga of Śiva. Pilgrims visit it during the summer months, culminating at the full moon of Śrāvaṇa (July–August), approaching from Pahalgam or Baltal. Local tradition credits a Muslim shepherd family with the cave’s discovery, and Kashmiri Muslims have long provided porters, ponies and services to the pilgrims—one of many examples of shared involvement in sacred places. The pilgrimage has grown enormously since the 1990s and is now organised by a state board, with heavy security arrangements.

docs.title: 4.9.1 Buddhist Pilgrimage
docs.text: The Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 16) has the Buddha name four places that a faithful person should see: where he was born (Lumbinī), where he attained awakening (Bodh Gayā), where he first taught (Sārnāth, near Vārāṇasī) and where he passed away (Kuśinagara). Aśoka visited Lumbinī in the twentieth year of his reign and set up a pillar recording the visit; four further places associated with miracles were later added to make eight great sites. Pilgrims came from Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China, Korea, Southeast Asia and Tibet; the accounts of Faxian, Xuanzang and Yijing (Chapter 6) are pilgrims’ records. Burmese kings sent missions to repair the Mahābodhi temple at Bodh Gayā between the late eleventh and the thirteenth centuries, and the Tibetan monk Dharmasvāmin visited Bodh Gayā and Nālandā in 1234–36, after the destruction of the great monasteries (Roerich 1959). After a long decline, the sites were revived from the late nineteenth century, through archaeological excavation and the work of Buddhists such as Anagārika Dharmapāla, founder of the Mahā Bodhi Society (1891) (Huber 2008).

docs.title: 4.9.2 Jain Pilgrimage
docs.text:
Jain sacred geography is focused on the places where the tīrthaṅkaras were born, renounced the world, attained omniscience and liberation, and on great temple complexes built by lay donors. Śatruñjaya near Palitana and Girnār in Gujarat are covered with temples; Sammeta Śikhara (Parasnath hill, Jharkhand) is where twenty of the twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras are said to have attained liberation; Pāvāpurī in Bihar is the place of Mahāvīra’s liberation; Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Karnataka, with its colossal image of Bāhubali, is the focus of Digambara pilgrimage. Wealthy lay patrons (saṅghapati) led large pilgrim caravans (saṅgha-yātrā), and Jain writers produced pilgrimage literature: lists and hymns of sacred places (tīrthamālā) and Jinaprabhasūri’s Vividhatīrthakalpa (completed 1333), which gives historical and legendary accounts of many sites (Dundas 2002).

Figure 4.2 shows the principal Buddhist and Jain sites named here, with some of the Sikh, Muslim and regional centres described below.

Figure 4.2. Some pilgrimage places of the Buddhist, Jain, Sikh and Muslim traditions, three goddess pīṭhas, and regional centres named in this chapter, plotted by latitude and longitude. Braj stands for the circuit round Mathurā and Vṛndāvana; Hiṅglāj lies west of the frame in Balochistan (about 65.5° E). The selection is illustrative, not complete. The coastline is simplified and islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted.

docs.title: 4.9.3 Sikh Pilgrimage
docs.text: The janamsākhī narratives of the life of Guru Nānak (1469–1539) describe long journeys (udāsīs) to the east, south, north and west, including Mecca and Baghdad. Historians treat these narratives as hagiography whose details cannot be confirmed, but they show how the early Sikh community imagined its founder moving through the sacred geography of both Hindus and Muslims (McLeod 1968). The principal Sikh pilgrimage places are the Harimandar Sāhib (Golden Temple) at Amritsar and the five takhts, together with gurdwaras at places associated with the Gurus. Partition in 1947 left Nānak’s birthplace, Nankana Sahib, and Kartarpur, where he spent his last years, in Pakistan; since 2019 a corridor has allowed Indian pilgrims to visit Kartarpur without a visa.

docs.title: 4.10 Muslim Sacred Geography and the Hajj from India
4.10.1 Shrines of the Saints
docs.text: From the thirteenth century the tombs (dargāh) of Sufi saints became major centres of pilgrimage (ziyārat) in South Asia. The shrine of Muʿīn al-Dīn Chishtī (d. 1236) at Ajmer, visited by Akbar on foot, and that of Niẓām al-Dīn Awliyāʾ (d. 1325) in Delhi drew pilgrims from across the subcontinent, especially for the anniversary of the saint’s death (ʿurs) (Currie 1989). Such shrines were, and are, visited by Hindus and Sikhs as well as Muslims. Many places in India have overlapping sacred histories of this kind.

docs.title: 4.10.2 The Hajj
docs.text:
The pilgrimage to Mecca linked India to the Red Sea and Arabia. Before the age of steam, most pilgrims from India went by sea from the ports of Gujarat and the western coast—above all Surat, known in Mughal times as the “Gate of Mecca” (Bāb al-Makka)—to Jeddah or Mocha, using the monsoon winds; others travelled overland through Afghanistan and Iran. The Mughal emperors financed ships and pilgrims: Akbar appointed an official to lead the pilgrimage caravan in the 1570s, and his aunt Gulbadan Begum, author of a memoir of the early Mughal court, went on the Hajj with a party of royal women in 1576 and returned only in 1582. From the sixteenth century the Portuguese, who controlled much of the western Indian Ocean, required Indian ships to carry their passes (cartaz), and the safety of pilgrim ships became a political issue. In the nineteenth century steamships from Bombay transformed the journey, and the colonial government began to regulate it (Pearson 1994).

The Hajj was itself a source of geographical knowledge and of travel writing. Indian pilgrims returned with knowledge of Arabia, the Red Sea ports and the Ottoman world, and from the eighteenth century some wrote accounts of their journeys in Persian and later in Urdu (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.10.3 Shia Pilgrimage and Links with Iraq
docs.text: Shia Muslims in India also travelled to the shrines of the imams in Iraq and Iran, above all to Karbala and Najaf. The Shia rulers of Awadh in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries sent money to the shrine cities of Iraq, built canals there, and supported scholars and pilgrims; in India they built imāmbāṛās, halls for the commemoration of the martyrdom of Ḥusain, and replicas of the shrines of Karbala, so that the sacred geography of Iraq was in a sense reproduced in Lucknow and other Indian cities. Processions during Muḥarram carry taʿziyas, models of the tomb of Ḥusain, through the streets, and in many places Hindus as well as Muslims take part.

docs.title: 4.11 Regional Pilgrimage Traditions
docs.text: Alongside the pan-Indian networks, every region developed its own sacred geography, often created by the poets and saints of the regional languages.

docs.title: 4.11.1 The Tamil Shrines of the Hymnists
docs.text: In the Tamil country, the Śaiva poet-saints (Nāyaṉmār) and Vaiṣṇava poet-saints (Āḻvār) of the sixth to ninth centuries travelled from temple to temple and sang hymns to the deity of each place. Their hymns were later collected in the Tēvāram and the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. The places they sang about became canonical lists: some 275 Śaiva “places that received songs” (pāṭal peṟṟa talam) and 108 Vaiṣṇava “divine places” (divya dēśam), most of them in Tamil Nadu and Kerala (two of the 108 are heavenly). The hymns are full of the names and landscapes of particular places—the river, the paddy fields, the groves, the town—and so created a dense sacred map of the Tamil land (Peterson 1989).

docs.title: 4.11.2 The Vārī to Paṇḍharpur
docs.text: In Maharashtra the devotees of Viṭṭhala of Paṇḍharpur, the Vārkarīs, walk to Paṇḍharpur every year in the month of Āṣāḍha (June–July), accompanying palanquins (pālkhī) bearing the sandals of the saint-poets Jñāneśvar from Āḷandī and Tukārām from Dehu. The pilgrimage, which takes about three weeks, brings together people of many castes. The Vārkarī tradition honoured saints of low status—the tailor Nāmdev, the potter Gorā, the gardener Sāvatā, the woman servant Janābāī and the “untouchable” Cokhāmeḷā— but Cokhāmeḷā himself was not allowed into the temple, and is remembered by a shrine at its steps. D. B. Mokashi’s account of walking the pālkhī route conveys the experience of the pilgrimage (Mokashi 1987).

docs.title: 4.11.3 Pilgrimage Priests and Their Registers
docs.text: At major pilgrimage centres, hereditary priests (paṇḍās) served pilgrims from particular regions and castes. At Haridvār, Gayā, Prayāga, Kurukṣetra and elsewhere they kept registers (vahīs) in which visiting families recorded their names, ancestors and home villages, sometimes over many generations. These registers, still consulted by families tracing their ancestry, are an unusual record of pilgrims’ movements and of the geography of kinship. The priests also guided pilgrims round the sacred sites and, before modern transport, along the routes between them.

docs.title: 4.12 Local Sacred Geography
docs.text:
Below the level of the great pilgrimage centres lies the sacred geography that most people lived in every day: the village goddess (grāmadevatā) at the edge of the settlement, the shrine of the boundary or of the guardian deity, the sacred tree, the tank, the snake shrine, the memorial stones of heroes and of women who died as satī, and the tombs of local saints. Many of these sites are not mentioned in any Sanskrit text, and their priests are often not Brahmins. Their festivals mark the boundaries of the village and the turning of the agricultural year.

Local and pan-Indian sacred geography were connected in both directions. Local goddesses were identified with the great Goddess and given a place in the list of śākta pīṭhas; local heroes and deities were identified with forms of Viṣṇu or Śiva; and the māhātmyas often tell how a local sacred place became known to the gods and sages of the Purāṇas. At the same time, the great centres drew on their surrounding countryside for priests, pilgrims and patrons. The sacred geography of India is best seen not as a single system imposed from above but as many layers built up over time (Eck 2012; Bhardwaj 1973).

docs.title: 4.13 Caste, Gender and Access
docs.text:
Sacred geography was not equally open to all. Many temples excluded people of the castes regarded as “untouchable”, and in parts of the south they were barred even from the roads around temples. The struggle against these exclusions was a major part of modern Indian social reform: the Vaikom satyāgraha in Travancore (1924–25), the Guruvayur satyāgraha (1931–32), the Travancore Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 and B. R. Ambedkar’s Kalaram temple satyāgraha at Nashik (1930–35). Article 17 of the Constitution abolished untouchability, and later legislation opened Hindu temples to all Hindus. Other forms of exclusion remain contested, including restrictions on women’s entry to some shrines.

Gender shaped pilgrimage in other ways too. Women were among the most numerous pilgrims, and widows often settled in sacred cities such as Kāśī and Vṛndāvana, sometimes in great poverty. The bhakti saints included women who travelled, such as Mīrābāī, who according to tradition left Mewar for Vṛndāvana and Dvārakā. Ann Grodzins Gold’s study of pilgrims from a Rajasthani village shows women and men of several castes planning, financing and remembering their journeys, and the different meanings they gave to them (Gold 1988). For many women, pilgrimage was one of the few journeys that custom allowed, and it could bring both a measure of independence and the constraints of a widow’s life in a sacred city.

docs.title: 4.14 Rulers and Sacred Places
docs.text:
Sacred geography was shaped by royal patronage. Kings built and endowed temples, monasteries, mosques and shrines, granted villages for their upkeep, and issued orders protecting pilgrims. The Vijayanagara kings made rich gifts to the temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara at Tirumala; Mughal emperors and nobles made grants to Hindu temples as well as to Sufi shrines, and the great temple of Govindadeva at Vṛndāvana was built in 1590 by Akbar’s general Mān Singh of Amber. In the eighteenth century the Maratha queen Ahilyābāī Holkar of Indore (r. 1767–1795) paid for temples, ghāṭs, wells and rest-houses at pilgrimage places across India, from the Himālaya to the far south, including the rebuilding of the Viśvanātha temple at Kāśī. Rulers also destroyed or desecrated the sacred places of their enemies, and the memory of such acts has been used in modern politics.

Royal patronage helped to create pan-Indian networks: a donor in central India could build at Kāśī, Dvārakā and Rāmeśvaram, linking places hundreds of kilometres apart through a single act of piety. It also reinforced hierarchies, since rulers usually favoured the institutions and groups that supported them. The history of sacred geography is therefore also a political history (Eck 2012; Thapar 2004).

docs.title: 4.15 Pilgrimage in the Colonial Period
docs.text:
The East India Company inherited, from earlier rulers, the practice of taxing pilgrims at major centres such as Purī, Gayā and Prayāga, and for some decades administered the pilgrim tax and the finances of the Jagannātha temple at Purī. Evangelical critics in Britain attacked the Company for “patronising idolatry”, and the pilgrim taxes were abolished in 1840. Colonial officials were also concerned about the spread of cholera at great gatherings, and from the later nineteenth century sanitary regulations, quarantine and the policing of melās became part of the administration of pilgrimage (Maclean 2008).

The railways, built from the 1850s, transformed pilgrimage more than any earlier change. Journeys that had taken months on foot could be made in days, and the numbers travelling to Haridvār, Prayāga, Purī, Gayā and other centres grew enormously. Pilgrimage priests advertised their services along the railway lines, and new pilgrimage circuits developed. The railways also made it easier for Muslims from the interior to reach the ports for the Hajj, and for Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists to visit their sacred sites. The sacred geography of the subcontinent did not disappear under colonial rule; it was reshaped and, in many respects, intensified.

docs.title: 4.15.1 Printed Guides and Pictures
docs.text: From the later nineteenth century, cheap printed guidebooks to pilgrimage places appeared in Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Tamil, Gujarati and other languages, often combining a māhātmya with practical information on railway routes, lodgings and priests. Lithographs and, later, colour prints and photographs of sacred places and their deities circulated widely, and pilgrims brought them home together with the traditional souvenirs—water from the Gaṅgā in sealed pots, images, beads and sacred threads. Print, like the railway, made sacred geography more widely known and more standardised, while local oral traditions continued alongside it.

docs.title: 4.15.2 Gayā and the Rites for the Dead
docs.text: One of the oldest and most important pilgrimage places is Gayā in Bihar, where Hindus perform rites (śrāddha) for their ancestors, offering balls of rice (piṇḍa) at a series of sacred spots in and around the town, above all at the Viṣṇupada temple. The Gayāmāhātmya and the digests on pilgrimage describe these rites, and Gayā’s hereditary priests, the Gayāvāls, served pilgrims from across India. Gayā lies a few kilometres from Bodh Gayā, the place of the Buddha’s awakening, so that a Hindu and a Buddhist sacred landscape lie side by side.

docs.title: 4.16 Pilgrimage and Geographical Knowledge
docs.text: Pilgrimage was one of the main ways in which ordinary people in pre-modern India learned about places far from their own. Pilgrims followed established routes, used ferries and rest-houses (dharmaśālā, sarāy), travelled with merchants, and returned with news, objects and stories. The sacred geography of the tīrthas gave names and meanings to the land and linked distant regions into a single imagined space (Eck 2012). That space was plural, contested and unequal; but it was also one of the most powerful and enduring forms of geographical imagination that the subcontinent produced.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Eck (2012) and Bhardwaj (1973) are the essential introductions; Eck (1982) on Kāśī; Kane (1953) on the Sanskrit pilgrimage literature; Sircar (1973) on the śākta pīṭhas; Maclean (2008) on the Kumbh Melā; McKay (2015) on Kailāsa; Huber (2008) on Buddhist pilgrimage; Pearson (1994) on the Hajj from India.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Indian Maps, Plans and Diagrams
docs.text:
For a long time it was said that pre-modern India produced no maps. The claim was repeated by colonial writers and later by historians of science, and it rested largely on the fact that few Indian maps had found their way into European collections or been studied. The research that led to the History of Cartography, especially the long contribution on South Asia by Joseph E. Schwartzberg in the volume on traditional Islamic and South Asian societies (1992), showed that the claim was wrong, but also that the picture was more complex than a simple reversal (Harley and Woodward 1992).

Schwartzberg’s survey found a great variety of Indian maps and map-like representations: cosmographical diagrams, sacred and pilgrimage maps, route maps, maps of towns, forts and estates, architectural plans and a few nautical charts. At the same time it found that very few pre-modern Indian maps survive from before about 1500, that most surviving examples are from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries, and that Indian mapping served purposes and followed conventions different from those of the European and Islamic traditions. Susan Gole’s illustrated survey of Indian maps and plans complements his work (Gole 1989). This chapter follows their findings.

docs.title: 5.1 What Counts as a Map?
docs.text:
The editors of the History of Cartography (vol. 1, 1987) define maps broadly, as “graphic representations that facilitate a spatial understanding of things, concepts, conditions, processes, or events in the human world” (Harley and Woodward 1987). On this definition a cosmological diagram, a painted pilgrimage scroll, a temple plan or a diagram for a ritual are all maps, even though they lack scale, a consistent orientation or a grid of coordinates. The definition is useful because it lets us see the range of Indian spatial representation. It does not mean that every such object served the same purposes as a modern topographic map.

Main Kinds of Indian Maps (after Schwartzberg)

  • Cosmographical maps: Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist diagrams of the universe or of Jambūdvīpa.

  • Sacred and pilgrimage maps: pictorial maps of sacred sites, kṣetras and pilgrimage routes.

  • Route maps: strip maps or schematic maps of roads, with halting places and distances.

  • Maps of places: towns, forts, estates, villages and landholdings.

  • Architectural and ritual plans: temple and city plans, maṇḍalas.

  • Nautical charts: rare, and mostly late.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Jain Cosmographies
docs.text: The richest body of cosmographical maps is Jain. From about the fifteenth century, and in great numbers in the seventeenth to nineteenth, Jain artists in western India painted on cloth and paper the “two and a half continents” (aḍhāī dvīpa) of the human world, Jambūdvīpa with its seven regions and six mountain ranges, and the cosmic person (lokapuruṣa) whose body contains the whole universe (Chapter 2). The aḍhāī dvīpa paṭas are circular diagrams with Jambūdvīpa at the centre, the rings of Lavaṇa ocean, Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, Kāloda ocean and the inner half of Puṣkaravara around it, populated with mountains, rivers, Merus, fish and boats. They were made for instruction and contemplation in Jain temples and households and are now in many museum collections (Caillat and Kumar 1981; Harley and Woodward 1992).

docs.title: 5.2.2 Reading a Jain Map of Jambūdvīpa
docs.text:
A typical Jain painting of Jambūdvīpa shows a circle with Meru at the centre, surrounded by the ring of the Lavaṇa ocean. Six ranges cross the circle from east to west, dividing it into seven bands, each coloured differently: Bharata at the bottom (south), Airāvata at the top (north), and the broad central band of Videha around Meru. Rivers flow from lakes on the mountains; in Bharata the Gaṅgā and the Sindhu flow from the Himavat range, and the Vaitāḍhya range crosses the land, so that Bharata is divided into six parts—the six parts that a universal emperor (cakravartin) conquers in Jain narrative. Labels in Sanskrit, Prakrit or Gujarati name the features, and the dimensions given in the texts are sometimes written in. Figure 5.1 shows the layout in schematic form. The map is at once a diagram of doctrine, an aid to memory and a work of art (Caillat and Kumar 1981). An aḍhāī dvīpa painting extends the same scheme outward to the two further continents and their four additional Merus, in the arrangement drawn in Figure 2.3a; the oceans are usually filled with fish, crocodiles and boats, and the continents with ranges, rivers and shrines.

Figure 5.1. Schematic of the layout of a Jain painting of Jambūdvīpa, north at the top and not to scale, following the scheme of the Tattvārthasūtra (chapter 3) and the Jambūdvīpaprajñapti. Six east–west ranges divide the continent into seven regions (kṣetra); Meru stands in the broad central band of Videha, with the Kuru lands to its south and north. In Bharata the Gaṅgā and the Sindhu flow from the lake on the Himavat range to the ocean and, with the Vaitāḍhya range, divide the region into the six parts that a universal emperor conquers; Airāvata in the north mirrors it. Actual paintings add the lakes, rivers, forests, shrines and dimensions that the texts describe, and their colours and details vary.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Hindu and Buddhist Cosmographies
docs.text:
Hindu cosmographical maps are fewer and mostly late: painted diagrams of the Purāṇic earth-disc with its seven continents, of Jambūdvīpa and Meru, and, from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, a few terrestrial globes painted with the Purāṇic cosmos. In the Buddhist world, diagrams of Meru and the four continents were made in Tibet, Nepal, Burma and Thailand, and the same model was built into temple layouts and ritual offerings.

These objects are maps of a cosmos, not of the physical earth. Their value lies in what they show about how the world was imagined and taught; they should not be described as failed or symbolic attempts at world maps of the modern kind.

docs.title: 5.3 Sacred and Pilgrimage Maps
docs.text:
Many surviving Indian maps represent sacred places. They are usually pictorial: temples, tanks, rivers and hills are drawn in elevation, deities and pilgrims appear, and the scale is adjusted so that the most important shrine is largest. Examples include painted maps of the Jain temple-hill of Śatruñjaya, of Braj with its sacred groves and the caurāsī kos pilgrimage circuit, of the temple-town of Nāthdvārā, of Purī and of the routes to the Himalayan shrines of Garhwal. Some were made for pilgrims to take home, some for temples and patrons, some as guides. Their orientation varies: some put east at the top, some the direction of approach, some the main shrine at the centre with the rest arranged around it (Gole 1989).

Such maps share their logic with the māhātmya literature (Chapter 4): they represent a sacred place as a sequence of stations to be visited, rather than as a measured surface. Within that convention they could be very detailed and accurate in the relative positions of shrines, roads and water bodies.

docs.title: 5.4 Maps and Geographical Knowledge at the Mughal Court
docs.text: The Mughal court’s written geography—above all the province-by-province description and statistics of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī (1590s), the road books and the regional descriptions in Persian—is the subject of Chapter 7. This section is concerned with maps. Irfan Habib’s Atlas of the Mughal Empire (1982) turned the written data into a set of modern maps of Mughal political and economic geography (Habib 1982); the Mughals themselves left relatively few.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Mughal and Indo-Persian Maps
docs.text: Surviving Mughal maps are fewer than the written descriptions might lead one to expect. They include route maps, plans of forts and cities, and maps in Persian scholarly works written in India. Some manuscripts of Ṣādiq Iṣfahānī’s Shāhid-i Ṣādiq (1647) contain sectional maps on a grid of latitude and longitude (Section 7.5). In the eighteenth century large route maps and regional maps were made for Mughal successor states and for European patrons; the French officer Jean-Baptiste Gentil commissioned an atlas of the Mughal provinces from Indian artists in Faizabad in the 1770s (Gole 1989; Harley and Woodward 1992).

docs.title: 5.4.2 Globes and European Maps at the Mughal Court
docs.text:
European maps and globes reached the Mughal court through Jesuit missionaries and ambassadors from the late sixteenth century. Mughal painters adopted the globe as a symbol of world dominion: in allegorical paintings made for Jahāngīr in the 1610s and 1620s, the emperor is shown standing or seated on a globe, sometimes embracing the Safavid Shāh ʿAbbās or shooting an arrow at his enemies. The English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe records that he presented Jahāngīr with an atlas by Mercator, which the emperor later returned because none of his scholars could read it. The episode is often cited to show a lack of interest in European cartography; it may equally show that maps in a foreign script and convention were of little use to a court whose own geographical knowledge was organised in other ways.

Historical Note: Islamic Geographical Learning in India

Indo-Persian scholars inherited the geographical tradition of the Islamic world, with its seven climes (iqlīm), coordinate tables (zīj) and world maps. Al-Bīrūnī’s work on India (Chapter 6) belongs to this tradition, as do the astronomical tables compiled in India from the fourteenth century onward. Mughal geographical knowledge combined this learning with the administrative records of the empire and with Indian knowledge of the land (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 5.5 Rajput, Maratha and Other Regional Maps
5.5.1 Jaipur
docs.text: The largest single collection of pre-colonial Indian maps is in the former royal archive of the Kachhwāhā rulers of Amber and Jaipur. It contains plans of the city of Jaipur, founded by Sawai Jai Singh II in 1727, of Amber, Delhi, Mathurā, Vṛndāvana and other places, and maps of estates and routes, drawn on cloth and paper in the eighteenth century. Jai Singh, the builder of the masonry observatories described in Chapter 3, had a strong interest in the mathematical sciences. Jaipur’s grid plan has often been explained as an application of the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala (see below); Vibhuti Sachdev and Giles Tillotson have argued that this interpretation is a later reading, and that the plan reflects practical choices about site, water and trade as much as any canonical diagram (Sachdev and Tillotson 2002).

docs.title: 5.5.2 Marathas and Others
docs.text: Maratha administration produced maps and plans of forts, routes and territories, especially in the eighteenth century, and much documentation survives in the Peshwa records in Pune; its cartographic content has not been fully studied. Many smaller states and estates had maps of boundaries and landholdings drawn for revenue purposes or disputes. In southern India, temple and village records described land in words, with boundaries defined by streams, trees, tanks and neighbouring fields, as copper-plate land grants had done for centuries; written boundary descriptions of this kind were often preferred to drawn maps (Harley and Woodward 1992).

docs.title: 5.6 Route Maps and Itineraries
docs.text:
Travellers, armies and merchants used itineraries listing stages and distances. Strip maps, which show a road as a straight band with towns, rivers and halting places along it, survive from the eighteenth century and were used by the Mughals and their successors. Such a map is read from one end to the other, like a written itinerary; its scale changes along its length, and turns in the road are straightened out. The roads themselves, with their sarāys and the kos mīnārs that marked the distances, are described in Chapter 8, and the itineraries in Persian in Chapter 7.

Colonial surveyors, beginning with James Rennell, made heavy use of these itineraries and of Indian route surveys, as Matthew Edney and Kapil Raj have shown (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 5.7.1 Directions and Their Guardians
docs.text:
Space in Indian ritual and architecture was oriented by the four cardinal and four intermediate directions, each with a guardian deity (dikpāla; Table 5.1). The scheme is religious and architectural rather than geographical, but it shaped how space was described: maps, temple plans and even the Kūrmavibhāga are organised by direction.

Table 5.1. The eight directions and their guardians (dikpāla) Direction Guardian Direction Guardian East (pūrva) Indra West (paścima) Varuṇa South-east (āgneya) Agni North-west (vāyavya) Vāyu South (dakṣiṇa) Yama North (uttara) Kubera South-west (nairṛta) Nirṛti North-east (aiśānya) Īśāna

docs.title: 5.7.2 The Gnomon and the East–West Line
docs.text: The earliest Indian texts on laying out space are the Śulbasūtras, manuals for constructing Vedic fire altars, composed in the later Vedic period (conventionally c. 800–200 BCE). The Baudhāyana and Kātyāyana Śulbasūtras give a method for finding the east–west line: set up a gnomon, draw a circle round it, mark the two points where the tip of the shadow touches the circle before and after noon, and join them (Plofker 2009). The same method was used in Greek and Roman surveying. Altars were then laid out with cords and pegs using geometrical constructions, including the relation that we call Pythagoras’ theorem.

docs.title: 5.7.3 The Vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala
docs.text: Texts on architecture describe a square grid, the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, of 64 or 81 squares (and other sizes), on which a building or settlement is planned. The grid is identified with the body of a being, the vāstupuruṣa, pinned down by the gods, who occupy its squares: Brahmā at the centre, the directional guardians and other deities round the edges. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (chapter 53) gives an early account (Bhat 1981); later treatises on architecture elaborate it. The diagram is a ritual and design tool. It guided the placement of parts of a temple or house in relation to the directions and could be applied, in principle, to a town.

docs.title: 5.7.4 Village and Town Plans in the Śilpa Texts
docs.text:
Treatises on architecture such as the Mānasāra (date disputed; often placed in the second half of the first millennium CE, though parts may be later) and the Mayamata describe standard plans for villages and towns, including the daṇḍaka, sarvatobhadra, nandyāvarta, padmaka, svastika, prastara, kārmuka and caturmukha, which differ in the arrangement of streets and gates. These are prescriptive types; how far actual towns followed them is a matter for archaeology, and few historical towns match them closely. They show, however, a developed tradition of thinking about settlements in plan.

The Arthaśāstra (2.4) gives an earlier plan for a royal fort-city: three royal roads running east–west and three running north–south, twelve gates, the palace north of the centre, and quarters assigned to different deities, occupations and social groups (Olivelle 2013). Like the town plans of the architectural treatises, it is an ideal. Excavated early historic cities, such as Sisupalgarh in Odisha with its square rampart and regularly placed gateways, show that some cities were planned on regular lines, while others grew more irregularly.

docs.title: 5.8 Ritual Diagrams and Sacred Space
docs.text:
A further family of spatial representations belongs to ritual. In Hindu, Buddhist and Jain worship, diagrams drawn on the ground, painted on cloth or engraved on metal—maṇḍalas and yantras —map the abode of a deity and its retinue. A maṇḍala is typically a square palace with four gates, oriented to the directions and set within concentric circles, with the principal deity at the centre and attendant deities arranged around it; the worshipper enters it in imagination, moving from the outer enclosure to the centre. Tibetan monks construct such maṇḍalas in coloured sand and then destroy them; in South Asian domestic ritual, women draw geometrical designs (kolam, rangolī, alpanā) on thresholds and floors each day or at festivals.

These diagrams are not maps of territory, but they share with cosmographical and temple plans a way of thinking about space: as centred, bounded and oriented, with value increasing towards the centre. The same pattern can be seen in the layout of temple towns, with concentric streets for processions round the central shrine, as at Madurai and Śrīraṅgam, and in the Purāṇic picture of the world itself. Understanding this pattern helps to explain why so many Indian maps are organised around a centre rather than on a uniform grid.

docs.title: 5.9 Nautical Charts
docs.text:
Navigation in the Indian Ocean depended above all on the pilot’s knowledge of winds, stars, coasts and soundings, carried in memory and in written sailing directions (Chapter 11). The Arabic sailing manuals of Aḥmad ibn Mājid (later fifteenth century) and Sulaymān al-Mahrī (early sixteenth) describe routes along the coasts of India in detail (Tibbetts 1971). Indian pilots of Gujarat and other coasts had comparable knowledge, recorded in Gujarati and other languages in later centuries as rahmānīs (books of sailing directions).

Whether pilots also used drawn charts is uncertain. The Portuguese historian João de Barros, writing in the mid-sixteenth century, reports that at Malindi in East Africa in 1498 a pilot from Gujarat showed Vasco da Gama a chart of the whole coast of India, drawn with meridians and parallels. The pilot was later often identified with Ibn Mājid, but there is no good evidence for this. A handful of nautical charts drawn by Indian (mostly Kutchi and Gujarati) navigators survive from the nineteenth century. Schwartzberg concluded that the evidence for earlier Indian nautical charts is real but slight, and that the absence of surviving examples may reflect the practical, perishable and private nature of such charts (Harley and Woodward 1992).

docs.title: 5.10 Maps of India Made Outside India
docs.text:
India also appears on maps made elsewhere, and these show how its shape was imagined by others. The regional maps of the Balkhī school of Islamic geographers in the tenth century included a map of Sind with the Indus (Section 7.1). Al-Idrīsī’s world map and the sectional maps of his geography, completed for Roger II of Sicily in 1154, placed India in the first and second climes and drew its coast from Arabic sailors’ and merchants’ reports; S. Maqbul Ahmad’s edition and study of the Indian sections remains the guide to them (Ahmad 1960). When Ptolemy’s Geography was recovered in fifteenth-century Europe, maps drawn from his coordinates gave India its short, broad peninsula and enormous Taprobane (Section 6.1), until the Portuguese voyages replaced them.

In East Asia, Buddhist world maps placed Jambudvīpa, shaped as the Abhidharmakośa describes it (Figure 2.3b), at the centre of the world and filled it with the countries of India named in Xuanzang’s record. The best known are the Japanese maps of the “Five Indias” (Gotenjiku-zu); the earliest surviving example, kept at the temple of Hōryūji, is dated 1364. Such maps draw the route of the pilgrim through Central Asia and India, with Lake Anavatapta (identified with Mānasarovar) and its four rivers near the centre, and they remained the standard Japanese picture of the world until European maps arrived in the sixteenth century (Harley and Woodward 1994). They are a reminder that India’s own pilgrims’ and cosmographers’ geography travelled, and was mapped, far beyond the subcontinent.

docs.title: 5.11 Measuring the Land
docs.text: Map-making is only one way of recording space. Pre-colonial Indian states measured and recorded land extensively, mostly in registers rather than on maps.

docs.title: 5.11.1 Cōḻa Land Surveys
docs.text: Inscriptions of the Cōḻa kingdom record a general survey of land carried out under Rājarāja I around 1001 CE, and a resurvey under Kulottuṅga I in 1086. The officials responsible bore titles celebrating their work, and the measured holdings, their classification and the revenue due from them were recorded village by village. Later Cōḻa inscriptions refer back to these surveys when describing land. Boundary descriptions in Cōḻa and other South Indian grants are often minutely detailed, tracing a village’s edges from landmark to landmark.

docs.title: 5.11.2 The Mughal Revenue Survey
docs.text:
Under Akbar the revenue minister Todar Mal developed a system (zabṭ) in which cultivated land was measured field by field, crops were recorded, and the revenue was assessed on average yields and prices over a ten-year period (the dahsāla arrangement of 1580). Measurement was made with a standard chain (jarīb) of bamboo pieces joined by iron rings, introduced to replace the rope, which stretched and shrank with the weather, and areas were recorded in a standard bīghā. The resulting records were kept by local officials—the qānūngo at the level of the pargana and the village accountant (patwārī)—and formed the statistical basis of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī’s provincial accounts (Habib 1999). Village accountants’ records, maintained in later periods in many regions, became one of the main sources used by colonial revenue surveyors.

Such surveys show that pre-colonial states had a highly developed capacity to measure and record land. What they generally did not do was to combine their measurements into scaled maps; land was known as a set of measured holdings and named places linked by recorded boundaries and routes.

docs.title: 5.12 Assessing the Record
docs.text:
The surviving record can be summarised by kind of map and by the period from which most examples date (Table 5.2).

Table 5.2. The surviving Indian maps by kind and period Kind of map Main period Notes Jain cosmographies 15th–19th c. cloth and paper; very numerous Hindu and Buddhist cosmographies mostly 18th–19th c. diagrams and a few globes Pilgrimage and sacred-site maps 17th–19th c. pictorial; mainly Rajasthan and Gujarat Town, fort and estate plans 17th–19th c. Jaipur collection; Maratha plans Route maps and strip maps 18th–19th c. Mughal successors; used by surveyors Nautical charts 19th c. very few; earlier use in texts

Geographic Insight: Why Do So Few Early Maps Survive?

Several reasons have been proposed: the perishable materials used (cloth, paper, palm leaf, drawings on the ground); the preference in Indian administrative practice for written descriptions of boundaries and itineraries rather than drawn maps; and the destruction of archives. The first two are well supported; the third applies to all periods and regions. The scarcity of early maps does not mean that Indians lacked spatial knowledge, but neither can the existence of a rich tradition of map-making be inferred from texts that do not mention maps. Each claim has to rest on surviving evidence.

Comparison with Europe should be made carefully. Indian cartography did not develop map projections or a systematic practice of scaled topographic mapping before the colonial period; European cartography did so from the fifteenth century onward, under the influence of the recovered Geography of Ptolemy and the needs of navigation and empire. Indian maps answered other needs—religious instruction, pilgrimage, the management of estates and the display of royal domains—and should be judged by how well they served them.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Harley and Woodward (1992) (Schwartzberg’s chapters on South Asia) and Gole (1989) are fundamental; Schwartzberg (1978) provides the historical maps. On Mughal geography see Habib (1982); on Jaipur, Sachdev and Tillotson (2002); on Indian Ocean navigation, Tibbetts (1971).

docs.title: Chapter 6: India in the Accounts of Foreign Travellers
docs.text:
From the time of the Achaemenid Persian empire onward, visitors to India wrote about what they saw and heard. Greek envoys and merchants, Chinese and Korean Buddhist pilgrims, Arab and Persian geographers, a Central Asian polymath, a Moroccan judge, Italian, Persian and Russian travellers of the fifteenth century, and French physicians and jewellers of the seventeenth left accounts that are among the most important sources for the historical geography of the subcontinent. For some periods and regions they are the only detailed descriptions we have.

These accounts must be read critically. Each traveller had his own purposes, prejudices and sources; many relied on interpreters and hearsay; some repeated the marvels expected of distant lands. Their descriptions of religion and society are often filtered through their own categories. But when they describe routes, distances, cities, ports, products and the places they visited, and when their statements can be checked against inscriptions, archaeology and Indian texts, they are often of great value. This chapter presents the principal travellers in chronological order, with the dates of their journeys and the main editions in which their accounts can be read.

docs.title: 6.1.1 Before Megasthenes
docs.text: Greek knowledge of India began with the Persian empire, which included the Indus region from the late sixth century BCE. Herodotus, in the fifth century, knew of the Indians as the most numerous people of the Persian empire and repeated stories of gold-digging ants. Alexander’s campaign in the north-west (327–325 BCE) produced accounts by his officers, notably the admiral Nearchus, whose voyage down the Indus and along the Makran coast was later summarised by Arrian.

docs.title: 6.1.2 Megasthenes
docs.text:
Megasthenes was sent by Seleucus I as envoy to Candragupta Maurya at Pāṭaliputra around 300 BCE; the exact date and the length of his stay are debated (Bosworth 1996). His Indica is lost, but long passages survive in Diodorus, Strabo and Arrian, and shorter ones in Pliny and others. The fragments were collected by E. A. Schwanbeck in 1846 and translated by J. W. McCrindle in 1877 (McCrindle 1877); McCrindle later collected the shorter notices of India in other Greek and Latin writers (McCrindle 1901). Richard Stoneman’s recent study places them in the context of Greek writing on India (Stoneman 2019).

Megasthenes described India as a quadrilateral bounded by mountains and sea, watered by great rivers and enjoying two rainy seasons and two harvests a year. He described Pāṭaliputra (Palibothra) at the confluence of the Ganges and the Son as a long, narrow city enclosed by a wooden palisade with many gates and towers and a moat. Excavations at Bulandi Bagh and Kumrahar in Patna early in the twentieth century found remains of a massive timber palisade, which agrees with his account in general, though the exact numbers he gave cannot be checked. He also described a division of Indian society into seven classes (philosophers, farmers, herders and hunters, artisans and traders, soldiers, overseers, and councillors); this does not match the Indian varṇa scheme and probably combines observation of occupations with a Greek interest in classifying peoples. Alongside these observations he repeated fabulous stories of mouthless men and men with ears large enough to sleep in, which were standard features of Greek writing about the edges of the world.

docs.title: 6.1.3 Megasthenes on Mauryan Administration
docs.text: Some of the most interesting fragments of Megasthenes, preserved by Strabo, describe officials concerned with the land. Some, he says, supervised the rivers, measured the land as in Egypt, and inspected the sluices by which water was let out from the main channels into branches, so that all might have an equal supply; the same officials looked after the roads and set up pillars at regular intervals to show turnings and distances. Other boards of officials in the city supervised crafts, foreigners, births and deaths, trade, and weights and measures. Historians have compared these descriptions with the officials of the Arthaśāstra; the comparison shows both agreements and differences, and the date of the Arthaśāstra (Chapter 1) means that the two cannot simply be used to confirm each other (Stoneman 2019; Olivelle 2013).

docs.title: 6.1.4 Arrian’s Indica
docs.text: Arrian, a Greek historian of the second century CE, wrote a short Indica as a companion to his history of Alexander. Its first part summarises Megasthenes and Eratosthenes on the size and shape of India, its rivers and its peoples; its second part tells the story of Nearchus’ voyage from the mouth of the Indus along the coast of Makran to the Persian Gulf in 325–324 BCE, with its harbours, landmarks, shortages of water and encounters with the fish-eating peoples of the coast. It is one of the earliest surviving narratives of a coastal voyage in the region (McCrindle 1877).

docs.title: 6.1.5 The Periplus Maris Erythraei
docs.text:
The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is a practical handbook written in Greek by a merchant based in Roman Egypt, probably in the mid-first century CE (Casson 1989). It describes the ports of the Red Sea, Arabia, East Africa and India, with the goods traded at each, the best seasons for sailing and the hazards of the approach. For India it is the most detailed source of its time (Table 6.1 and Figure 6.1).

Table 6.1. Indian places named in the Periplus and their usual identifications Name in the Periplus Usual identification Notes Barbarikon in the Indus delta port for the Indus valley Barygaza Bharuch, on the Narmadā the great port of the north-west coast; difficult approach and strong tides Ozene Ujjain former royal capital; inland source of goods for Barygaza Paithana, Tagara Paithan, Ter inland markets of the Deccan Souppara, Kalliena Sopara, Kalyan ports near modern Mumbai Muziris near Kodungallur (Pattanam), Kerala the leading pepper port Nelkynda, Bakare inland and coastal sites in southern Kerala pepper trade (exact locations debated) Kolchoi Korkai, Tamil Nadu pearl fishery Poduke Arikamedu, near Puducherry trading station on the east coast Figure 6.1. Ports and inland markets of India named in the Periplus Maris Erythraei (mid-first century CE), at the sites with which they are usually identified (Table 6.1). Barbarikon lay somewhere in the Indus delta and Nelkynda inland in southern Kerala; both are shown approximately. Dashed lines join the inland markets to Barygaza, as the Periplus describes, and do not follow actual roads. The coastline is simplified; the delta coast of the Periplus period was not where it is today.

The Periplus says that goods came down to Barygaza from Ozene and from Paithana and Tagara in the Deccan, and it describes the open-sea crossing to southern India with the south-west monsoon, which it associates with a pilot named Hippalus. Its account of the east coast and the lands beyond the Ganges is vaguer.

Archaeology has confirmed the trade it describes. At Arikamedu, excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945 and later by Jean-Marie Casal and Vimala Begley, Roman amphorae and Italian red-gloss pottery were found; at Pattanam in Kerala, excavations since 2007 have produced Mediterranean pottery and are thought by many to locate Muziris. A papyrus now in Vienna records a loan contract for a cargo shipped from Muziris to Egypt in the mid-second century (Tomber 2008; Begley and De Puma 1991).

docs.title: 6.1.6 Ptolemy
docs.text: Claudius Ptolemy’s Geography (c. 150 CE) gives latitude and longitude for many places in India, which he divided into India “within the Ganges” and “beyond the Ganges”. The theoretical chapters are translated by Berggren and Jones; for the Indian coordinates and their identifications McCrindle’s old commentary is still the most convenient guide (Berggren and Jones 2000; McCrindle 1885). His coordinates were derived from merchants’ itineraries rather than from observation, and his map of India is badly distorted: the peninsula is much too short and broad, so that the coast runs roughly east–west instead of turning sharply south, and Taprobane (Sri Lanka) is hugely enlarged. Many of his place-names can nevertheless be identified, and they are an important record of the towns and peoples known to the Roman world. When Ptolemy’s work was translated into Latin in the early fifteenth century, its picture of India shaped European expectations before the Portuguese voyages.

docs.title: 6.1.7 After Ptolemy: Pliny and Cosmas
docs.text:
Roman writers noted the cost of the Indian trade. Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s CE, complained that India drained the Roman empire of at least fifty million sesterces a year, and that India, China and Arabia together took a hundred million, in exchange for luxuries; he also describes the route to India and the sailing seasons. The large number of Roman gold and silver coins found in southern India, especially in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, confirms that the trade was paid for partly in coin (Tomber 2008).

In the sixth century the Alexandrian merchant known as Cosmas Indicopleustes (“who sailed to India”) included in his Christian Topography a description of Taprobane (Sri Lanka) as a great meeting point of ships from India, Persia and Ethiopia, and of the pepper country of “Male” (Malabar), where he reports a Christian community. His book is better known for its attempt to prove that the earth is flat, like the Tabernacle of Moses—a reminder that sound practical knowledge of distant lands and a fanciful cosmology could sit side by side in one author, as they did in many traditions.

docs.title: 6.2.1 Faxian
docs.text:
The monk Faxian left Chang’an in 399 CE to find complete texts of the monastic rules. He crossed Central Asia, entered India from the north-west, and spent several years in the Gangetic plain, studying at Pāṭaliputra and visiting the sites of the Buddha’s life. He then spent two years at Tāmralipti in Bengal and two in Sri Lanka before sailing home by way of the Indonesian archipelago, reaching China in 412. His Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms (Foguo ji) is short but precise about routes and distances (Legge 1886).

Faxian’s India is the India of the Gupta period, though he never names the king. He describes the Middle Country as prosperous and mildly governed, with few corporal punishments. He also records that the caṇḍālas lived apart, and that when they entered a town or market they struck a piece of wood to warn others to avoid contact with them—one of the earliest dated descriptions of the practice of untouchability by an outside observer.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Xuanzang
docs.text:
Xuanzang left China in 629 against an imperial ban and returned in 645.
