In the intervening years he travelled through Central Asia and across much of India, studied for several years at Nālandā under the teacher Śīlabhadra, met King Harṣa of Kanauj and King Bhāskaravarman of Kāmarūpa, and attended Harṣa’s great assembly at Prayāga. His Record of the Western Regions of the Great Tang (Da Tang Xiyu ji, 646), compiled with his disciple Bianji, describes 138 countries, about 110 of which he says he visited himself. For each it gives the size of the country and its capital, the climate, products, customs, language, the state of Buddhism (numbers of monasteries and monks, schools followed) and sacred sites with their legends (Beal 1884; Li 1996). Figure 6.2 traces the order of his journey.

Figure 6.2. Xuanzang’s journey in India, 630s–640s, simplified. Places are joined by straight lines in the order in which his Record of the Western Regions describes them, not along actual roads; the journey through Gandhāra, Taxila and Kashmir lies north of the frame. Between Kanyākubja and Nālandā the route passes, in order, Ayodhyā, Prayāga, Kauśāmbī, Śrāvastī, Kapilavastu, Kuśinagara, Vārāṇasī and Vaiśālī, of which Ayodhyā, Kauśāmbī, Kapilavastu and Vaiśālī are not labelled; the open circle east of Nālandā is Campā. After the circuit he returned to Nālandā (dashed); the visit to Kāmarūpa and the journey to Harṣa at Kanyākubja and Prayāga came at the end of his stay. Countries named by region (open circles) are placed approximately, and several identifications, among them Kapilavastu, Kosala and Karṇasuvarṇa, are debated (Beal 1884; Cunningham 1871). The coastline is simplified.

The account is the single most important source for the historical geography of seventh-century India. In the nineteenth century Alexander Cunningham used Xuanzang’s directions and distances to identify many ancient sites, including Śrāvastī, Kuśinagara and Sāṅkāśya (Cunningham 1871). Xuanzang also records the decline of Buddhism in many regions, with deserted monasteries in places such as Kapilavastu and Śrāvastī, and the strength of non-Buddhist traditions.

docs.title: 6.2.3 How Xuanzang Described a Country
docs.text: Xuanzang’s descriptions follow a regular pattern, which makes them unusually useful for historical geography. For each country he gives its circumference in li, the circumference of its capital, the quality of its soil and crops, its climate, the character and dress of its people, its script and language, the number of Buddhist monasteries and monks and the schools they followed, the number of temples of other traditions, and then the sacred sites with their legends. He often names the ruling king and his caste. He describes, for example, the great city of Kanyākubja (Kanauj) under Harṣa, with its monasteries and temples; the country of Mahārāṣṭra under Pulakeśin II, whose proud and warlike people had resisted Harṣa’s attack; and the decline of once-famous Buddhist sites (Beal 1884; Li 1996). The figures for circumference and distance are approximate and sometimes conventional; it is the order of the countries and the directions between them that made Cunningham’s identifications possible.

docs.title: 6.2.4 Yijing
docs.text:
Yijing (635–713) travelled by sea. He sailed from Guangzhou in 671, studied Sanskrit for six months at Śrīvijaya in Sumatra, and reached Tāmralipti in 673. He spent about ten years at Nālandā and then several years in Śrīvijaya copying and translating texts before returning to China in 695. His Record of the Inner Law Sent Home from the South Seas describes Buddhist monastic practice in India and Southeast Asia (Takakusu 1896); a second work gives brief lives of some sixty Chinese and Korean monks who travelled to India in the seventh century, many by sea and many of whom died on the way. Yijing recommended Śrīvijaya, where he reported more than a thousand monks, as a place for Chinese monks to study before going on to India. His works are a key source for the maritime route between China and India and for the place of Southeast Asian ports in the Buddhist world (Sen 2003).

Historical Note: Nālandā

Nālandā, in Bihar, was founded in the fifth century CE and was the greatest Buddhist monastic centre of learning in India for several centuries. Xuanzang and Yijing both studied there and describe its life. It was sacked during the campaigns of Bakhtiyār Khaljī in Bihar around 1200, and the Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin, who visited in 1234–36, found only a small community living among the ruins (Roerich 1959). Popular claims that its library held “nine million manuscripts” have no basis in the sources.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Merchants and Geographers
docs.text: From the ninth century, Arabic writers described India on the basis of merchants’ reports and their own travels. The Account of China and India attributed to the merchant Sulaymān (851), the route book of Ibn Khurradādhbih (Kitāb al-masālik wa’l-mamālik, ninth century), al-Masʿūdī’s Meadows of Gold (943) and the collection of sailors’ tales The Wonders of India (tenth century) describe the ports of the west coast, the trade in spices, textiles and horses, and the kingdoms of India. They call the greatest king of India the “Balharā”, a title derived from the Rāṣṭrakūṭa kings of the Deccan, and they note the security of trade in Rāṣṭrakūṭa territory (Ahmad 1989).

docs.title: 6.3.2 Al-Bīrūnī
docs.text:
Abū Rayḥān Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Bīrūnī (973–c. 1050), born in Khwarazm, was taken to Ghazni after Maḥmūd of Ghazni conquered his homeland, and spent years in the Ghaznavid-held Punjab. He learned Sanskrit, worked with Indian scholars, and around 1030 completed a book on India, Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind (“Verifying all that the Indians recount”), translated by Eduard Sachau as Alberuni’s India (Sachau 1910).

Al-Bīrūnī set out to describe Indian beliefs and sciences as Indians themselves understood them, quoting Sanskrit texts and comparing them with Greek ideas. His geographical chapters cover the measures of distance; the routes and distances between Kanauj and other cities; the rivers of India; the Purāṇic description of the earth, Meru and the seven continents; the astronomers’ spherical earth; the inhabited world and the position of Laṅkā; and the methods of finding longitude. He is critical of Indian scholars where he finds their statements inconsistent and of the Purāṇic cosmography, but he is also frank about the damage done by Maḥmūd’s raids, which he says destroyed the prosperity of the country and left Hindus with an aversion to all foreigners. His work is the most thorough account of Indian learning by any pre-modern outsider. His measurement of the earth’s radius near Nandana is described in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 6.3.3 Al-Bīrūnī’s Routes
docs.text: Al-Bīrūnī’s chapter on the geography of India gives distances between major cities, measured in farsakhs, along routes radiating from Kanauj and other centres, and lists the provinces and peoples in each direction. He drew this information from Indian informants and texts and from the itineraries of Ghaznavid campaigns, and it is one of the earliest systematic records of the road network of north India (Sachau 1910).

docs.title: 6.4 Later Chinese and Arabic Geographers
docs.text:
After the age of the pilgrims, Chinese knowledge of India came mainly through maritime trade. Zhao Rugua, a customs official at the port of Quanzhou, compiled in 1225 a Description of Foreign Peoples (Zhufan zhi) from the reports of merchants, with entries on Malabar, Gujarat, the Cōḻa country and Sri Lanka and on the goods they traded (Hirth and Rockhill 1911). Two centuries later, Ma Huan, a Muslim interpreter who sailed with the Ming fleets of Zheng He, described Cochin, Calicut and Bengal from personal observation in his Overall Survey of the Ocean’s Shores (Yingya shenglan); his account of Calicut’s markets, weights, currency and customs is one of the best descriptions of the port before the Portuguese (Mills 1970).

In the Arabic tradition, al-Idrīsī’s great geography, completed in 1154 for King Roger II of Sicily, included sections on India compiled from earlier Arabic writers and merchants’ reports, with a world map divided into the seven climes. Later Arabic and Persian geographers and historians, including the historians of the Delhi Sultanate, added detail on the routes and provinces of north India. These works belong to the Islamic tradition of descriptive geography, which organised knowledge by routes (masālik) and kingdoms (mamālik) and which strongly influenced Indo-Persian writing on India (Chapter 7). Al-Idrīsī’s Indian sections have been edited and studied by S. Maqbul Ahmad (Ahmad 1960); his maps are described in Section 5.10.

docs.title: 6.5.1 Marco Polo
docs.text: The Venetian Marco Polo (1254–1324) visited southern India around 1292–93, on the sea voyage from China to Persia on which he and his relatives escorted a Mongol princess. His book, written down in prison in Genoa in 1298 by the romance-writer Rustichello of Pisa, describes the Pāṇḍya kingdom of Maʿbar on the Coromandel coast, with its pearl fishery and the shrine of St Thomas at Mylapore; the kingdom of Mutfili (the Kākatīya kingdom, entered through the port of Motupalli), ruled by a queen who had governed for many years since her husband’s death—evidently Rudramadevī; Kayal, Quilon, Cape Comorin, Mount Eli, Malabar, Gujarat, Thane and Cambay (Yule 1903; Latham 1958). His descriptions mix observation, hearsay and legend (such as the story of diamonds collected by eagles from inaccessible valleys).

docs.title: 6.5.2 Ibn Baṭṭūṭa
docs.text: Ibn Baṭṭūṭa (1304–1368/69 or 1377), a Moroccan jurist, travelled for some three decades across Africa, the Middle East and Asia. He reached the Indus in 1333, went to Delhi, and served Sultan Muḥammad bin Tughluq as a judge (qāḍī) for some eight years. In 1342 the sultan sent him as envoy to China; after the loss of his ships at Calicut he spent time on the Malabar coast, served as judge in the Maldives (Section 11.7), visited Sri Lanka and Maʿbar, and went on through Bengal and Southeast Asia to China. His Riḥla, dictated in Fez to Ibn Juzayy in 1355–56, gives a vivid account of the Tughluq court, Delhi, the roads and the royal post, and the ports of Malabar with their Chinese and Arab shipping. The Indian chapters are best read in the full Hakluyt translation (Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1971); Gibb’s earlier selection (Gibb 1929) and Ross Dunn’s study (Dunn 1986) are convenient introductions. The Riḥla was written from memory years later, and parts of it are confused or borrowed from earlier writers; historians use it with care.

docs.title: 6.5.3 Ibn Baṭṭūṭa’s Delhi
docs.text: Ibn Baṭṭūṭa describes Delhi as the greatest city of the Muslim east, made up of four adjoining cities built by successive rulers, with walls, mosques, reservoirs and markets. He gives a vivid and critical portrait of Sultan Muḥammad bin Tughluq, generous and learned but violent and unpredictable, and of the sultan’s attempt to move the population of Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan, which he says left Delhi almost empty. He describes the roads, the post, the system of grants to officials, and the dangers of travel in a countryside where the sultan’s authority was often contested. Historians check his statements against the Persian chronicles of the period; where they can be checked, his descriptions of places are often accurate, while his accounts of events and numbers need caution (Dunn 1986; Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1971).

docs.title: 6.6 Visitors to Vijayanagara and the Coasts, c. 1420–1540
6.6.1 Niccolò de’ Conti
docs.text: The Venetian merchant Niccolò de’ Conti spent about twenty-five years in the East, from about 1419 to 1444, living in Damascus, Persia, India and Southeast Asia. On his return he recounted his travels to the humanist Poggio Bracciolini, who included them in Book 4 of his De varietate fortunae (c. 1448). He described Vijayanagara, Mylapore, Sri Lanka, Sumatra, Burma and Java (Major 1857).

docs.title: 6.6.2 ʿAbd al-Razzāq Samarqandī
docs.text: ʿAbd al-Razzāq (1413–1482), envoy of the Timurid ruler Shāh Rukh, sailed from Hormuz in 1442 and reached Calicut, where he described the port and its ruler, the Zamorin. In 1443 he travelled to Vijayanagara, where he was received by Devarāya II. His account, in his history Maṭlaʿ al-saʿdayn, describes the city’s concentric fortifications, its markets and the Mahānavamī festival, and is one of the best descriptions of the city at its height (Major 1857).

docs.title: 6.6.3 Afanasy Nikitin
docs.text: The Russian merchant Afanasy Nikitin of Tver travelled through Persia to India in about 1469 and spent some three years in the Bahmani sultanate of the Deccan, including its capital Bidar, before returning by way of Persia and the Black Sea; he died near Smolensk on the journey home, probably in 1472 or 1475. His Journey Beyond Three Seas records Deccan markets, horses and religious life (Major 1857).

docs.title: 6.6.4 Portuguese Accounts
docs.text: After 1498 Portuguese writers produced detailed accounts of the coasts and states of India. The chronicles of Domingos Paes (c. 1520) and Fernão Nunes (c. 1535) describe Vijayanagara under Kṛṣṇadevarāya and Acyutarāya, its walls, markets, festivals and water works; Robert Sewell translated both (Sewell 1900). Two other writers of the early sixteenth century give especially systematic descriptions of the coasts. Duarte Barbosa, who lived for years in Cannanore and Cochin and knew Malayalam, wrote around 1516 an account of the coasts from East Africa to China, describing for each port its ruler, merchants, goods and customs; his description of the castes and customs of Malabar is one of the earliest by a European. Tomé Pires, an apothecary who served in India and Malacca, wrote his Suma Oriental in 1512–15, a survey of the trade of the whole Indian Ocean and the archipelago, with much information on Gujarati, Bengali and Coromandel merchants. Both drew on Indian and Arab informants as well as their own observation, and both wrote with the commercial and political interests of the Portuguese crown in mind.

docs.title: 6.7.1 François Bernier
docs.text: The French physician François Bernier (1620–1688) was in India from about 1658 to 1669. He witnessed the war of succession among Shāh Jahān’s sons, served the Mughal noble Dānishmand Khān, and accompanied Aurangzeb’s court on its journey to Kashmir in the 1660s. His Travels in the Mogul Empire (French 1670–71) describes Delhi, Agra, Kashmir and the workings of the empire (Bernier 1891). A letter to the minister Colbert argued that the Mughal emperor was the owner of all land and that the absence of private property ruined agriculture. This argument was widely influential in European thought on “oriental despotism”; historians of Mughal India, notably Irfan Habib, have shown that it misrepresented the complex system of rights in land (Habib 1999).

docs.title: 6.7.2 Jean-Baptiste Tavernier
docs.text: The French jeweller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier (1605–1689) made six journeys to Persia and India between 1630 and 1668, trading in precious stones. His Six Voyages (1676) gives routes and distances between the main cities, describes the diamond mines of the Golconda region and the trade of Surat, and records the Peacock Throne of Shāh Jahān. He sold to Louis XIV a large blue diamond from India which, recut, is generally identified as the ancestor of the Hope diamond (Tavernier 1889).

docs.title: 6.7.3 Bābur’s Description of Hindustan
docs.text: Ẓahīr al-Dīn Muḥammad Bābur (1483–1530), the Timurid prince from Ferghana who founded the Mughal dynasty after his victory at Pānīpat in 1526, was a newcomer to India when he wrote the section of his Turkic memoirs, the Bāburnāma, that describes Hindustan. He describes its boundaries and mountains, its rivers and the absence of running water in its towns and gardens, its rains, its animals, birds, fruits and flowers, its peoples and its systems of counting, weights and measures, often in comparison with his homeland in Central Asia (Thackston 1996). The description is that of an observant outsider with strong likes and dislikes—Bābur complains that Hindustan has few pleasures, while admiring its wealth, its craftsmen and its rains—and it is one of the most vivid pieces of natural description of the period.

docs.title: 6.7.4 Others
docs.text: Many other Europeans wrote about Mughal India: the English ambassador Sir Thomas Roe (1615–19), the merchant Peter Mundy, the Venetian Niccolao Manucci, and missionaries. Their accounts are rich in detail, and also show the beginnings of the comparisons between Europe and India that later shaped colonial thinking.

docs.title: 6.8 Foreign Eyes and the Image of India
docs.text:
The accounts surveyed in this chapter helped to form the image of India in the wider world. Greek writers presented India as a land of marvels and of philosophers at the edge of the earth; Chinese pilgrims saw it as the holy land of Buddhism; Arab and Persian writers described a land of great wealth and learning but of religious error; Europeans of the Mughal age described its riches and its “despotism”. Each image said as much about the observer as about India.

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, colonial scholarship drew on these accounts and added its own generalisations—that India was unchanging, other-worldly, without history or without a sense of geography. Critics such as Edward Said, and historians of India such as Ronald Inden, have analysed how such images served colonial power and shaped even the categories through which Indians came to see themselves (Inden 1990). The same accounts remain indispensable for ports, prices and routes; the frame affects their judgements more than their observations.

docs.title: 6.9 Reading Foreign Accounts Critically
docs.text:
Table 6.2 summarises the travellers discussed in this chapter.

Table 6.2. Foreign accounts of India: dates and main geographical value Traveller Dates in India Main geographical value Megasthenes c. 300 BCE Mauryan India; Pāṭaliputra; rivers Periplus author mid-1st c. CE ports and trade of the western and southern coasts Ptolemy (did not travel) c. 150 CE coordinates and place-names Faxian c. 402–409 Buddhist sites; Gangetic plain; sea route Xuanzang c. 630–643 systematic description of most of India Yijing 673–685 monastic life; the sea route via Śrīvijaya Al-Bīrūnī c. 1017–1030 in the Punjab; Indian sciences; cosmography; routes and distances Marco Polo c. 1292–93 Coromandel and Malabar coasts Ibn Baṭṭūṭa 1333–c. 1346 Delhi Sultanate; Malabar; Maldives Niccolò de’ Conti c. 1420s–1440s Vijayanagara; coasts ʿAbd al-Razzāq 1442–43 Calicut; Vijayanagara Afanasy Nikitin c. 1469–72 Bahmani Deccan Domingos Paes, Fernão Nunes c. 1520, c. 1535 Vijayanagara François Bernier c. 1658–69 Mughal empire; Kashmir Jean-Baptiste Tavernier 1640s–1660s several visits; routes; Golconda; Surat

Using Foreign Accounts

  • Distinguish what the traveller saw from what he was told and what he copied from earlier writers.

  • Check routes, distances and identifications against inscriptions, archaeology and Indian sources.

  • Note the traveller’s purpose (diplomacy, trade, pilgrimage, scholarship) and his categories: Buddhist pilgrims saw a Buddhist India, Muslim travellers judged by Islamic norms, Europeans compared India with Europe.

  • Use them especially where Indian sources are thin: ports and trade, urban life, routes, and the views of outsiders on social practices such as untouchability and satī.

Taken together, the foreign accounts show how India appeared to its neighbours and trading partners over two thousand years: as a land of great rivers and cities, of wealth and learning, and also as a land of unfamiliar customs that outsiders often misunderstood. Their value is greatest when they are read alongside Indian sources. Where a traveller drew on Indian informants, as al-Bīrūnī and Xuanzang did, agreement between his account and an Indian text is not independent confirmation of either.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Translations: McCrindle (1877), Casson (1989), Legge (1886), Beal (1884), Li (1996), Takakusu (1896), Sachau (1910), Latham (1958), Gibb (1929), Major (1857), Sewell (1900), Bernier (1891) and Tavernier (1889). Studies: Stoneman (2019), Dunn (1986), Sen (2003) and Ahmad (1989).

docs.title: Chapter 7: Geography in Persian: From the Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam to the Mughal Gazetteers
docs.text:
From the thirteenth century to the early nineteenth, Persian was the language of government, diplomacy and much of the learning of northern and central India, and of the Deccan courts as well. A great deal of the geographical knowledge produced in India in those six centuries was written in it: descriptions of provinces, lists of roads and stages, statistical returns of districts and villages, tables of latitudes and longitudes, encyclopaedias arranged by the climes of the earth, and accounts of journeys. Most of this writing was done in India by people who lived there, many of them Hindus of the scribal communities who had learned Persian for service in the revenue and chancery offices. It is therefore part of the Indian geographical tradition, not a foreign view of it, and it deserves to be read beside the Sanskrit and regional-language sources of the earlier chapters (Alam and Subrahmanyam 2007; Kinra 2015).

This chapter traces that tradition: the Islamic geographical learning that Persian writers inherited, the geography of the Delhi Sultanate, the Āʾīn-i Akbarī and its statistical description of the Mughal provinces, the road books and itineraries, and the regional and late Persian geographies on which the first British surveyors drew. Al-Bīrūnī’s book on India, which belongs to this story but was written in Arabic by a visitor, is treated with the other foreign accounts in Chapter 6; Mughal maps and globes are described in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 7.1 The Inheritance: Climes, Routes and Realms
docs.text:
Persian geographical writing in India drew on a tradition that had taken shape in Arabic in Baghdad and the eastern Islamic lands between the ninth and eleventh centuries. That tradition had two main branches (Harley and Woodward 1992).

The first was mathematical. From Ptolemy’s Geography and from Indian and Persian astronomy, Islamic astronomers took the idea of locating places by latitude and longitude, and they compiled tables of coordinates in their astronomical handbooks (zīj). They also took over the Greek division of the inhabited quarter of the earth into seven “climes” (iqlīm, from Greek klima), east–west bands defined by the length of the longest day. In this scheme most of the Indian peninsula fell in the first and second climes and the Panjab and the upper Gaṅgā plain in the second and third, while Kashmir lay further north. The climes were a convenient frame for arranging knowledge as much as a physical description, and Persian encyclopaedias written in India used them to order their entries centuries later.

The second branch was descriptive. Writers of the genre called “routes and realms” (al-masālik wa’l-mamālik), beginning with Ibn Khurradādhbih in the ninth century (Chapter 6), described the lands of the world by their roads, stages and distances, their towns and products, and the taxes they yielded. A group of tenth-century geographers often called the Balkhī school, among them al-Iṣṭakhrī and Ibn Ḥawqal, produced a standard set of regional maps of the Islamic world, one of which showed Sind with the Indus, Multan and Manṣūra. These maps were schematic: rivers were drawn as straight or evenly curved bands, towns as circles, and coasts as geometrical arcs, so that they show the order of places along routes rather than their measured positions (Harley and Woodward 1992).

docs.title: 7.1.1 The Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam
docs.text: The oldest surviving geography in New Persian, the anonymous Ḥudūd al-ʿĀlam (“The Limits of the World”), was written in 982–83 for the Farīghūnid ruler of Gūzgānān in what is now northern Afghanistan. It describes the known world region by region, beginning with seas, islands, mountains and rivers and then taking each country in turn, with its towns, rulers, products and peculiarities. Its section on Hindūstān draws on earlier Arabic geographers and on merchants’ reports: it names Indian kings and towns, notes the goods for which places were known, and records the Muslim communities of Sind and Multan. Its knowledge of the interior of India is thin and in places garbled, as one would expect of a work compiled far from the country, but it established in Persian the pattern of country-by-country description that later writers in India would fill with far more detail. The text survives in a single manuscript, which Vladimir Minorsky translated with an extensive commentary (Minorsky 1937).

docs.title: 7.1.2 Coordinates and the Problem of the Qibla
docs.text: The mathematical branch reached its peak with al-Bīrūnī. His Taḥdīd nihāyāt al-amākin (“Determination of the coordinates of places”), completed at Ghazni in 1025, set out methods for determining the latitudes and longitudes of cities from astronomical observations and from measured distances along roads, with the practical aim of finding the direction of Mecca (qibla) from Ghazni (al-Bīrūnī 1967). His later handbook, the al-Qānūn al-Masʿūdī, dedicated to Sultan Masʿūd of Ghazni in the 1030s, includes a table of the coordinates of several hundred places. Several Indian towns appear in it, some probably located from Indian sources whose longitudes were counted from the meridian of Ujjain (Chapter 3) and converted to the Islamic reckoning from the western edge of the inhabited world. The practice of listing places by coordinates passed into the later Persian handbooks used in India, and lists of latitudes and longitudes of Indian towns appear in Mughal works, including the Āʾīn-i Akbarī.

docs.title: 7.2 The Geography of the Delhi Sultanate
docs.text: The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) produced no single geographical treatise, but its histories contain a great deal of geography, because their subject was campaigns, conquests and the assignment of revenue from territory.

docs.title: 7.2.1 The Chronicles
docs.text: Minhāj-i Sirāj Juzjānī’s Ṭabaqāt-i Nāṣirī, completed around 1260, is the main narrative source for the first half-century of the Sultanate. In describing the conquest of Bengal it divides the territory of Lakhnautī into two “wings” on either side of the Gaṅgā: Rāl to the west and Barind to the east, that is, the old regions of Rāḍha and Varendra of the Sanskrit inscriptions (Chapter 12). It also describes Bakhtiyār Khaljī’s disastrous expedition, around 1205–06, into the hills north of Bengal, which Juzjānī reconstructed from the accounts of survivors and which is one of the earliest Persian descriptions of the approaches to the eastern Himālaya. Later chroniclers, from Baranī in the fourteenth century to the historians of the Afghan dynasties, record the marches of armies stage by stage, the rivers crossed and the forts besieged, so that the historical geography of the period can be reconstructed from them in considerable detail.

docs.title: 7.2.2 An Arabic View of the Tughluq Empire
docs.text: The fullest description of the Sultanate at its greatest extent was written not in Delhi but in Damascus and Cairo. Shihāb al-Dīn al-ʿUmarī (1301–1349), a secretary in the Mamluk chancery, devoted part of his encyclopaedia Masālik al-abṣār to India under Muḥammad ibn Tughluq (r. 1325–51), using the reports of travellers, merchants and scholars who had been at the sultan’s court. He gives the number of the sultan’s provinces as twenty-three and names them, from Lahore and Multan in the west to Lakhnautī in the east and Maʿbar and Dvārasamudra in the far south, and he describes Delhi, the roads and the system of couriers. Read with Ibn Baṭṭūṭa’s account (Chapter 6), it shows how the Tughluq empire was imagined as a set of provinces held from Delhi, and briefly from Daulatābād, the Deccan capital to which Muḥammad ibn Tughluq moved much of the Delhi élite in 1327.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Praise of Hindustan
docs.text:
Persian poets writing in India gave their land a literary geography of its own. In his poem Nuh Sipihr (“Nine Heavens”, 1318), Amīr Khusrau of Delhi argued that Hindustan was superior to other lands in its climate, its learning and its many languages, which he listed by region—among them the speech of Sindh, Lahore, Kashmir, Bengal, Gujarat and the Telugu country. Later Persian writers in India often opened their histories with a similar description of the land and its excellences, and a list of its regions became a standard part of the description.

A word about names. Persian writers used Hindūstān in two senses: for the whole subcontinent, and more narrowly for the north, the plains of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as distinct from the Deccan (Dakhan, from Prakrit dakkhiṇa, “south”), Bengal (Bangāla) and Gujarat. The narrower usage survives in the Hindi and Urdu of the Gangetic plain and in the name of Hindustani music, whose northern tradition is distinguished from the southern (Karnatak) one. The ambiguity has to be kept in mind whenever a Persian source says that something is true “of Hindustan”.

docs.title: 7.3 The Āʾīn-i Akbarī as a Work of Geography
docs.text: The Āʾīn-i Akbarī, the third part of Abū’l-Faẓl’s history of Akbar’s reign, completed in the late 1590s, is the greatest geographical description of India produced in the pre-colonial period (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873, 1891–1894). It is also an administrative manual, a statistical return and an encyclopaedia, and its geography cannot be separated from these other purposes.

docs.title: 7.3.1 The Account of the Provinces
docs.text:
In 1580 Akbar divided the empire into twelve provinces (ṣūba): Kabul, Lahore, Multan, Delhi, Agra, Awadh, Allahabad, Bihar, Bengal, Ajmer, Gujarat (Ahmadabad) and Malwa. The Deccan conquests of 1596–1601 added Berar, Khandesh and Ahmadnagar. Each province was divided into districts (sarkār), and each district into sub-districts (pargana, also called maḥal), which were made up of villages (mauẓaʿ). Figure 7.1 shows the seats of the provinces. The Āʾīn’s “account of the twelve provinces” takes them in turn, beginning with Bengal in the east, and describes each in two parts.

Figure 7.1. The provinces (ṣūba) of Akbar’s empire, shown by their seats, with the main imperial roads of the Persian road lists drawn as straight lines between their termini. Kabul, the twelfth province of 1580, lies beyond the frame. Bengal and Malwa, whose seats moved, are named by region, as is Berar. Provincial boundaries are not drawn; for them, and for the districts, see Habib’s Atlas (Habib 1982). The coastline is simplified.

The first part is descriptive. It gives the province’s length and breadth in kos, its boundaries, its climate and seasons, its rivers and mountains, its crops, fruits, flowers and animals, its crafts and markets, its places of pilgrimage and its “wonders”, and often a history of its earlier rulers. Some entries contain observations of real value: on the flooding of the Bengal rivers, on the snow and saffron of Kashmir, and on the mines, crafts and markets of particular districts. Abū’l-Faẓl explains the name Bangāla, for example, as the old name Bang with the addition of āl, the earthen embankments that the people raised in their fields against the floods; whatever its value as etymology, the explanation reflects an exact observation of the deltaic landscape.

The second part is statistical. For each sarkār and pargana the Āʾīn gives a set of figures and notes, summarised in Table 7.1. They were drawn from the records of the revenue administration and were not collected for the book; Abū’l-Faẓl edited and arranged figures that already existed in the imperial offices (Habib 1999).

Table 7.1. What the Āʾīn-i Akbarī records for each district and sub-district of a province Entry Content Measured area (ārāẓī) Land measured under the zabṭ system, in bīghās; given only where measurement had been carried out Assessed revenue (jamʿ) The revenue expected from the unit, in dāms (copper coins, forty to the rupee) Revenue grants (suyūrghāl) Revenue assigned to scholars, religious men and institutions Castes of the zamīndārs The communities holding superior rights in the land, such as Rajputs, Jats, Brahmins or Afghans Troops Cavalry and infantry (and sometimes elephants) that the local zamīndārs were expected to furnish Forts and notes Brick or stone forts; occasionally markets, mines or other features

These tables make the Āʾīn something rare among pre-modern descriptions of any country: a systematic statistical geography, arranged by territorial units, for an empire covering most of northern and central India. Shireen Moosvi has used them to estimate the area under cultivation, the size of the revenue and the distribution of resources around 1595, and Irfan Habib plotted the sarkārs and parganas, with their revenue and other data, on the sheets of his Atlas of the Mughal Empire (Moosvi 1987; Habib 1982). Both have also shown the limits of the material. The measured area was recorded only in the provinces where the zabṭ system of measurement had been introduced; for some provinces, Bengal among them, the land had not been measured and the figures come from other systems of assessment; the units of land and money varied; and a number recorded in a revenue office was a target and a claim, not necessarily what was collected. The survey on which the measured figures rested is described in Section 5.11.

docs.title: 7.3.2 Hindu Learning and the Coordinates of Places
docs.text: The Āʾīn also contains a long account of Hindu learning, written with the help of Brahmin informants at Akbar’s court. Among much else it summarises the Purāṇic division of the earth into continents and oceans, the astronomers’ spherical earth and the reckoning of longitude from the meridian of Laṅkā and Ujjain (Chapters 2 and 3), and it sets these beside the climes and coordinates of the Islamic tradition, with a table of the latitudes and longitudes of places. Abū’l-Faẓl did not try to reconcile the two systems; he reported both, with the respect for Indian learning that was part of Akbar’s court culture.

docs.title: 7.4 Roads, Stages and Itineraries
docs.text:
Persian writers measured travel in manzils, a day’s stage, and in kos (Chapter 8). The Mughal court was itself an itinerant capital for much of the year, and the chronicles record the emperor’s marches stage by stage. Jahāngīr’s memoirs are the richest example. On his journeys to Gujarat and Kashmir he noted the halting places, the distances in kos, the passes and rivers, and the birds, animals, flowers and trees that he saw, often with the precision of a naturalist; his descriptions of the route over the Pīr Panjāl and of the spring in Kashmir are among the most detailed pieces of landscape description in Persian (Jahāngīr 1999).

Below the level of the court, itineraries listing the stages and distances on the main roads circulated among officials, soldiers and merchants. Two works of the late seventeenth and mid-eighteenth centuries gathered such information into descriptions of the empire, the second with something like a road book.

  • The Khulāṣat al-Tawārīkh (1695–96) of Sujān Rāy Bhandārī, a Hindu secretary (munshī) from Batala in the Panjab, is a history of India that opens with an account of the provinces of the empire under Aurangzeb, their rivers, towns, products, shrines and revenue.

  • The Chahār Gulshan of Rāy Chaturman, a Kāyastha, written in the mid-eighteenth century, adds lists of the stages and distances on the main imperial roads radiating from Delhi to the provinces, as well as provincial statistics.

Jadunath Sarkar translated the topographical parts of both works and used them to reconstruct the roads and provinces of Aurangzeb’s empire and to compare them with Akbar’s (Sarkar 1901). The road lists show a network of trunk routes—Delhi to Lahore and Kabul, Agra to Ajmer and Ahmadabad, Agra to Burhanpur and the Deccan, Agra to Allahabad, Patna and Bengal—lined with sarāys and, on the northern roads, with kos mīnārs (Section 8.1).

docs.title: 7.4.1 News, Couriers and the Information Order
docs.text: Geographical knowledge in the Mughal empire moved through people as much as through books. The empire posted news-writers (wāqiʿa-nawīs) in the provinces and districts, and runners and horsemen carried their reports along the roads to the court. Local officials, bankers and merchants kept their own correspondence. When the East India Company began to govern in Bengal it inherited this system and its personnel; C. A. Bayly has described how the Company depended on Indian news-writers, runners (harkāras) and munshīs for its knowledge of the country, and how its failures of information could be costly (Bayly 1996). The itineraries and route lists used by the first British mapmakers came, in large part, out of this Persianate information order (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 7.5.1 Geographical Encyclopaedias
docs.text:
The Haft Iqlīm (“Seven Climes”, 1594) of Amīn Aḥmad Rāzī, an Iranian who wrote in Mughal India, arranges its notices of countries and cities, and above all of their famous men and poets, according to the seven climes of Islamic geography, with a long section on the cities of Hindustan. It is more a biographical dictionary set in a geographical frame than a geography, but the frame itself shows how the climes still organised knowledge in the age of Akbar.

The Shāhid-i Ṣādiq of Muḥammad Ṣādiq Iṣfahānī, completed at Jaunpur in 1647, is an encyclopaedia of history, ethics and the sciences. Its geographical part includes a gazetteer of places with their coordinates, and some manuscripts contain a set of sectional maps drawn on a grid of latitude and longitude, which Schwartzberg discusses as one of the very few Indo-Persian atlases (Harley and Woodward 1992). The maps use the coordinates of the tables rather than any new survey; their interest lies in the attempt to present the known world, India included, on a consistent grid.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Regional Descriptions
docs.text:
From the late seventeenth century, as the empire weakened and provincial courts grew stronger, Persian writers produced histories and descriptions of particular regions.

  • The Mirʾāt-i Aḥmadī (completed 1761) of ʿAlī Muḥammad Khān, an imperial revenue official (dīwān) in Gujarat, ends with a supplement describing the province: its towns and ports, its shrines and gardens, its administrative divisions and revenue. It is one of the fullest descriptions of any Indian province before the colonial gazetteers.

  • The Riyāẓ al-Salāṭīn (1788) of Ghulām Ḥusain Salīm, a history of Bengal written at the request of an English official at Malda, opens with a description of the province’s boundaries, rivers and towns before turning to its rulers.

  • Histories of Kashmir in Persian continued the tradition of Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (Chapter 10) and described the valley’s parganas, springs and shrines.

This literature was written mostly by officials and secretaries, many of them Hindus of the scribal castes—Kāyasthas, Khatrīs and Brahmins—and it combines the conventions of Islamic geography with detailed knowledge of the land gained in administration. Rajeev Kinra’s study of Chandar Bhān Brahman, a Brahmin secretary of Shāh Jahān’s reign, shows how such men understood their Persian learning as part of their own culture, not as something borrowed (Kinra 2015).

docs.title: 7.6 Persian Geography in the Service of the Company
docs.text:
The East India Company governed in Persian for its first seventy years in Bengal. Its revenue records, correspondence with Indian rulers and court proceedings were in Persian until 1837, when English and the regional languages replaced Persian as the language of the courts and revenue offices. During that period Persian geographical knowledge flowed into the Company’s own.

  • The Āʾīn as a source. Francis Gladwin published an English translation of parts of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī in Calcutta in 1783–86. James Rennell drew on the Āʾīn’s lists of provinces and distances for his Map of Hindoostan and its Memoir (Chapter 14).

  • Itineraries and informants. Company officers collected route lists and descriptions from munshīs, news-writers and merchants, and surveyors used them where they could not measure (Raj 2007).

  • Commissioned journeys. The veterinary surgeon and explorer William Moorcroft sent his Persian secretary, Mīr ʿIzzatullāh, ahead of him in 1812–13 on a journey from Kashmir through Ladakh, Yarkand and Kashgar to Bukhara. ʿIzzatullāh’s Persian account of the route, its stages, passes, towns and rulers was later translated into English, and it anticipated by half a century the journeys of the pundits (Chapter 14).

The Persian administrative vocabulary outlived Persian itself. The units and records of the Mughal revenue system—the pargana, the district (ḍilaʿ, Hindi zilā), the tahsīl (from taḥṣīl, “collection”) and the taʿalluqa (tāluk), the village (mauẓaʿ, mauzā), and the patwārī’s field book (khasra) and record of rights (jamābandī)—passed into British administration and remain in use in the land records of much of India today. The Hindi and Urdu word for a province or state, sūbā, is the Mughal ṣūba; it gave its name to the “Punjabi Suba” movement for a Punjabi-speaking state (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 7.7 The Place of Persian Geography
docs.text: Indo-Persian geographical writing was neither a branch of Arabic geography transplanted to India nor a precursor of colonial science. It was a tradition of its own, which used the frames of Islamic learning—the climes, the coordinate tables, the description of realms and routes—to organise a vast store of knowledge about the land that came from the practice of government in India. Its strength lay in description and enumeration: of provinces and their products, of roads and their stages, of districts and their revenue. Its weakness, from the point of view of later cartography, was the same as that of the Sanskrit and regional sources: it seldom turned this knowledge into scaled maps (Chapter 5). When British surveyors did so, they relied heavily on what the Persian records contained.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On Islamic geography and cartography, Harley and Woodward (1992); on the Āʾīn-i Akbarī, Abū’l-Faẓl (1891–1894), Habib (1999) and Moosvi (1987); for maps of Mughal India, Habib (1982); on roads and provinces under Aurangzeb, Sarkar (1901); on Indo-Persian travel and the Persian secretaries, Alam and Subrahmanyam (2007) and Kinra (2015); on the information order of late Mughal and Company India, Bayly (1996).

docs.title: Chapter 8: Routes, Passes and Merchants
docs.text: The geography that mattered most to many people in pre-modern India was the geography of routes: which roads were safe, where rivers could be crossed and in which season, where water and fodder could be found, which passes were open, and where goods could be bought and sold. This knowledge belonged above all to merchants, caravan leaders, boatmen, carriers and the officials who taxed them. It was rarely written down as such, but it can be reconstructed from texts, inscriptions, the distribution of coins and monuments, and the accounts of travellers (Neelis 2011; Ray 1986). This chapter follows the land and river routes; the sea routes and their monsoon calendar are described with the coasts in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 8.1 The Great Routes of the North and South
8.1.1 Uttarāpatha
docs.text:
In early Buddhist and Sanskrit texts, Uttarāpatha, “the northern road”, means both the north-west of the subcontinent (Gandhāra and the Punjab, the country of horses) and the route that led there from the Gangetic plain. That route ran from Takṣaśilā (Taxila) across the Punjab rivers to the Yamunā and then down the Gaṅgā valley through cities such as Mathurā, Kauśāmbī and Vārāṇasī to Pāṭaliputra and on to the port of Tāmralipti in Bengal (Figure 8.1). Branches led north-west through Puruṣapura (Peshawar) and the Kabul valley to Bactria and Central Asia, and north through the upper Indus valley.

The Mauryan state maintained this road. Greek writers drawing on Megasthenes describe a royal road from the north-west to Pāṭaliputra and officials who set up markers at regular intervals showing turnings and distances. Aśoka’s inscriptions are found at many points along major routes, and his Pillar Edict 7 says that he had banyan trees and mango groves planted, wells dug and drinking-places set up along the roads. Later rulers rebuilt and extended the road. Sher Shāh Sūr (r. 1540–45) rebuilt a long trunk road from Bengal to the Punjab with sarāys at regular intervals (Section 8.9). The Mughals maintained it and marked their roads with kos mīnārs, solid masonry pillars set at intervals of one kos, many of which still stand along the old road between Agra, Delhi and Lahore. The British, after rebuilding the road in the nineteenth century, called it the Grand Trunk Road. The name is colonial; the route is much older.

Figure 8.1. Early routes and some passes. The northern road (Uttarāpatha) is drawn through the cities named in the text; the southern road follows the stages of the journey of Bāvarī’s disciples in the Sutta Nipāta, from Patiṭṭhāna to Sāvatthī (the site of Māhissatī is debated). Lines join places and do not follow actual roads. Near the Western Ghats the ports of Sopara and Kalyan and the cave sites of Kanheri, Nashik, Nāṇeghāṭ, Junnar, Kārle and Bhājā lie too close together to be labelled separately. The Bolan pass is shown approximately; the Khyber, Zoji La, Karakoram and Rohtang passes lie north of the frame. The coastline is simplified.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Dakṣiṇāpatha
docs.text:
Dakṣiṇāpatha, “the southern road”, came to mean the Deccan itself. A route list in the Pārāyanavagga of the Pali Sutta Nipāta follows the disciples of the teacher Bāvarī from Patiṭṭhāna (Paithan) on the Godāvarī northward through Māhissatī, Ujjenī (Ujjain), Vedisa (Vidiśā), Kosambī, Sāketa and Sāvatthī to the Buddha’s country—an early itinerary of the road between the Deccan and the Gangetic plain, drawn in Figure 8.1. Vidiśā and Ujjain, at the northern end of this road, were among the richest cities of early India, and the great stūpas of Sāñcī near Vidiśā were paid for in part by donations from merchants, guild members and lay families recorded in hundreds of short inscriptions.

Which Route Is Better? Kauṭilya’s Answer

The Arthaśāstra (7.12) records a debate about trade routes. Earlier teachers preferred the route towards the Himālaya, which brought elephants, horses, perfumes, ivory, skins, silver and gold. Kauṭilya disagrees: the southern route is better, because, apart from blankets, skins and horses, it yields more goods—conch shells, diamonds, gems, pearls and gold—and it passes through many mines and populous regions. He also compares land and water routes and prefers coastal shipping to the open sea as safer (Olivelle 2013). The passage shows that routes were compared by what they carried, not merely by distance.

docs.title: 8.2 Passes of the Western Ghats and the Deccan Caves
docs.text: The Deccan plateau is separated from the western coast by the steep scarp of the Western Ghats. In the centuries around the beginning of the common era, under the Sātavāhanas and the Western Kṣatrapas, trade between the coastal ports (Sopara, Kalyan, Chaul) and the inland markets (Paithan, Ter, Junnar, Nashik) went up and down a small number of passes. Buddhist monastic caves were cut at the heads of these passes and along the routes: Kārle and Bhājā near the Bor Ghāṭ, Junnar near the Nāṇeghāṭ, Nashik, Kanheri near Sopara and Kalyan. Their inscriptions record gifts from merchants, guilds, bankers and foreign donors (Yavanas), showing that monasteries were part of the network of trade (Ray 1986). At the Nāṇeghāṭ pass, a cave contains the long inscription of the Sātavāhana queen Nāyanikā, recording Vedic sacrifices and gifts—a royal monument on a trade route.

docs.title: 8.3.1 The North-West
docs.text: The mountain wall of the north-west is crossed by several passes. The Khyber (about 1,070 m) links the Peshawar valley with the Kabul river; the Bolan (roughly 1,800 m at its head) links the Kachhi plain of the lower Indus with Quetta and Kandahar; the Gomal and Kurram passes lie between them. These were the main routes between the subcontinent and Afghanistan, Iran and Central Asia for traders, pilgrims and armies. Horses, which did not breed well in most of India, were imported through them in large numbers throughout history, as well as by sea from Arabia and the Gulf.

docs.title: 8.3.2 The Upper Indus and the Karakoram
docs.text: A more difficult route led from Gandhāra up the Indus gorge through Gilgit and over the Karakoram to the Tarim basin. Along the upper Indus near Chilas and Shatial, thousands of rock carvings and inscriptions in Kharoṣṭhī, Brāhmī, Sogdian, Chinese and Tibetan record the passage of merchants and pilgrims between the first and eighth centuries CE, including Sogdian traders from Central Asia (Neelis 2011). Faxian travelled this way in about 400 CE. Later, the route from Kashmir and Ladakh over the Karakoram Pass (Table 8.1) to Yarkand was used by caravans until the mid-twentieth century.

docs.title: 8.3.3 The Himalayan Passes
docs.text:
Further east, trade between India and Tibet crossed the Himalaya by passes that are open only in summer. Tibetan salt, wool and borax were exchanged for grain, sugar, cloth and metal goods, often by specialised trading communities of the high valleys such as the Bhotiyas of Kumaon and Garhwal, who moved with their flocks and goods between Tibetan marts and the foothills. Table 8.1 lists the principal passes.

Table 8.1. Some Himalayan and trans-Himalayan passes (heights rounded; published figures differ slightly) Pass Approx. height Route Zoji La about 3,500 m Kashmir valley to Ladakh Karakoram Pass about 5,500 m Ladakh to Yarkand (Xinjiang) Shipki La over 4,500 m Kinnaur along the Sutlej to western Tibet Rohtang about 4,000 m Kullu to Lahaul (bypassed by the Atal Tunnel since 2020) Lipu Lekh over 5,000 m Kumaon to western Tibet (Kailāsa route) Nathu La about 4,300 m Sikkim to the Chumbi valley; reopened for border trade in 2006 Jelep La about 4,300 m Sikkim/Kalimpong to the Chumbi valley; main India–Lhasa trade route c. 1900

docs.title: 8.4 Rivers as Highways
docs.text:
The rivers of the Gangetic plain were the cheapest way of moving bulk goods. Boats carried grain, salt, cotton, stone and timber, and the large cities of the plain—Pāṭaliputra, Vārāṇasī, Prayāga, Kauśāmbī—stood on navigable rivers. The Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of shipping (nāvadhyakṣa, 2.28) supervises ferries, river and sea traffic and port towns, collects fees, and is responsible for the safety of travellers (Olivelle 2013). The Jātaka stories and the Mahābhārata describe merchants travelling by boat, and Faxian and Xuanzang both travelled on the Ganges.

At the mouth of the river system, Tāmralipti (Tamluk) in Bengal was the principal port for the sea routes to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia from at least the Mauryan period: Faxian sailed from there to Sri Lanka, and Yijing landed there from Śrīvijaya. As the Ganges delta shifted eastward, the main ports moved too: to Saptagrām (Satgaon) in the later medieval period and then to Hugli and, in the colonial period, Calcutta.

docs.title: 8.5 The Desert Routes
docs.text:
The Thar desert separated Sindh from the Gangetic plain and Gujarat, but caravan routes crossed it, linking Multan, Jaisalmer, Bikaner, Jodhpur and the ports of Gujarat. Desert towns grew rich on the caravan trade, as the merchants’ mansions (havelīs) of Jaisalmer still show. Travel depended on knowledge of wells and on travelling at night.

The first story in the Pali Jātaka collection, the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, tells of two caravans crossing a desert: one is deceived by demons into throwing away its water and perishes; the other, led by the future Buddha, keeps its water and survives. The second, the Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka, tells of a caravan crossing a sandy waste by night, guided by a “land pilot” (thalaniyyāmaka) who steers by the stars. Whatever their date, these stories reflect real techniques of desert travel.

Stepwells (vāv, bāolī) and tanks in Gujarat and Rajasthan provided water for towns and travellers. The Rani ki Vav at Patan, built in the eleventh century under the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) dynasty and now a World Heritage Site, is the most elaborate.

docs.title: 8.6.1 The Caravan
docs.text:
The sārtha (caravan) and its leader, the sārthavāha, are familiar figures in Buddhist and Jain literature. The caravan leader decided routes and halting places, negotiated with rulers and tolls, and was responsible for the safety of those who travelled with him. Jain narrative literature describes merchants who invite all who wish to travel to join their caravan, providing food and protection.

In Mughal India much of the overland carrying trade was in the hands of the Banjārās, communities of carriers who moved grain, salt and other bulk goods on huge herds of pack-oxen, numbering in the tens of thousands for a single camp. Armies relied on them for supplies, and contemporaries described their movements as a kind of moving town. Irfan Habib has shown their central place in the economy of Mughal India (Habib 1990).

docs.title: 8.6.2 Guilds and Merchant Networks
docs.text:
Merchants were organised in guilds (śreṇī, nigama) from the early historical period; inscriptions at Sāñcī, Nashik and elsewhere record guild donations and endowments. In South India from the ninth century, merchant bodies such as the “Five Hundred of Ayyāvoḷe” (Aihole) and the Maṇigrāmam operated across the peninsula and overseas; a Tamil inscription of the Ayyāvoḷe body dated 1088 has been found at Barus in Sumatra. Jewish, Christian and Muslim merchants on the Malabar coast received privileges recorded in copper-plate grants, such as the Kollam plates of 849.

In later centuries Indian merchants worked across Asia. Multani and Punjabi Khatri merchants and bankers were established in Iran, Central Asia and as far as Astrakhan on the Volga in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Levi 2002); Gujarati merchants traded throughout the western Indian Ocean; Chettiar bankers from Tamil Nadu financed trade and agriculture in Burma, Malaya and Ceylon in the colonial period. These networks were held together by kinship, caste and credit, and by bills of exchange (huṇḍī) that could be cashed in distant cities.

Scholarly Note: Merchants as Holders of Geographical Knowledge

Merchants needed to know prices, routes, seasons, the safety of roads and the policies of distant rulers. That knowledge circulated in letters, account books and conversation. Little of it survives in written form from before the seventeenth century, but its existence is evident from the way trade networks functioned. When European companies arrived, they depended on Indian brokers, bankers and pilots for exactly this kind of knowledge.

docs.title: 8.7 Salt, Horses and Grain
docs.text:
Three commodities show how the geography of production shaped routes.

Salt was produced in only a few places: by evaporation of sea water along the coasts, especially in Gujarat, Odisha and the Coromandel; from the salt lake of Sambhar in Rajasthan; and from the rock-salt deposits of the Salt Range in the Punjab. Every inland village needed it, so salt moved along almost every route, carried by specialised carriers such as the Banjārās. Its universal necessity also made it an object of taxation, from the Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of salt to the colonial salt monopoly against which Gandhi marched to Dandi in 1930.

Horses of good quality did not breed well in most of India and were imported, overland from Central Asia and Afghanistan through the north-western passes and by sea from Arabia and the Gulf to the ports of the west coast and the Coromandel. Marco Polo describes the great sums spent by the kings of Maʿbar on horses brought by sea; the Vijayanagara kings and the Deccan sultans competed for them; and the horse trade was a major source of revenue for the ports that handled it.

Grain moved over shorter distances by land, but in great quantities along the rivers and the coasts. Rice from Bengal and the Kāverī delta and wheat from the Punjab were shipped to deficit regions, and in times of famine the movement of grain became a matter of life and death, in which carriers, merchants and states all played a part.

docs.title: 8.8 Monks on the Road
docs.text: Merchants were not the only regular travellers. Buddhist and Jain monks and nuns were enjoined to wander from place to place outside the rainy season, and their rules show careful attention to the conditions of travel. The Jain Ācārāṅga Sūtra regulates how a monk should walk (looking ahead so as not to harm living beings), when he may cross a river by boat or wade through shallow water, how he should behave on roads frequented by thieves or through the territories of hostile kings, and where he may stay. The Buddhist monastic code contains similar rules. Monasteries and caves along the trade routes—Sāñcī, the Western Ghats caves, the monasteries of Gandhāra and the upper Indus—served as halting places for monks and lay travellers alike, and monks often travelled with merchant caravans for safety (Neelis 2011; Ray 1986). Brahmin scholars, wandering ascetics of many orders, bards and performers also moved along the roads, carrying texts, ideas and news.

docs.title: 8.9.1 Rest-Houses and Wells
docs.text: Travel on the great routes depended on places to stop, and Aśoka’s shade trees, wells and rest-houses (Section 8.1) had many successors. Hindu, Jain and Buddhist donors built dharmaśālās at pilgrimage places and on routes; Muslim rulers and nobles built sarāys, walled enclosures with rooms round a courtyard, a mosque and a well, where caravans could spend the night in safety. Sher Shāh Sūr is credited with building sarāys at regular intervals along his road, and Mughal nobles built many more; the Nurmahal Sarai in the Punjab, built in the time of Jahāngīr and his queen Nūr Jahān, still stands. Stepwells in western India served the same purpose for water.

docs.title: 8.9.2 Ferries and Tolls
docs.text: Rivers were crossed by ferries at recognised ghāṭs, where tolls were collected. The Arthaśāstra lays down ferry charges and penalties for crossing elsewhere, and inscriptions record grants of ferry revenues. Tolls and customs at frontiers, ferries and town gates were a constant subject of complaint by merchants and of negotiation with rulers; the Kākatīya inscription at Motupalli and Mughal orders remitting transit duties are examples of rulers trying to attract trade by lowering or fixing them.

docs.title: 8.9.3 The Royal Post
docs.text: States kept systems of couriers for official news. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa describes the post of the Delhi Sultanate in the fourteenth century, with relays of horsemen and of runners stationed at short intervals along the roads, by which letters, and even water from the Ganges for the sultan to drink, were carried with remarkable speed (Gibb 1929). The Mughals maintained a similar system of news-writers and couriers (ḍāk), which the East India Company later adapted for its own postal service.

docs.title: 8.9.4 Speed and Season
docs.text: Travel was slow and seasonal. Caravans of pack-oxen covered only a few kos a day; travellers on horseback or in carts moved faster but rarely travelled in the rains, when roads became impassable and rivers flooded. The travel accounts of Tavernier and Bernier give the stages and times of journeys between the main cities of the Mughal empire and are a valuable source for reconstructing them (Tavernier 1889; Bernier 1891).

docs.title: 8.9.5 Itineraries
docs.text: Travellers and administrators recorded routes as lists of stages. Persian writers of the Mughal period used the manzil (a day’s stage) as the unit of travel, and itineraries listing the stages between cities, with distances in kos, circulated among officials, merchants and soldiers. Tavernier’s Six Voyages gives such itineraries for the roads from Surat to Agra, from Agra to Bengal and from Surat to Golconda (Tavernier 1889). Later, in the eighteenth century, itineraries collected from Indian informants were among the main sources for the first British maps of India (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 8.10 Coins as Evidence of Routes
docs.text: Coins are among the best evidence for the geography of trade, because they are durable, often datable and found where they were lost or buried. The silver punch-marked coins of the early historical period are found across north India and the Deccan, showing the spread of a common monetary system along the routes. Hoards of Roman gold and silver coins of the first centuries CE, concentrated in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Andhra, mark the ports and inland routes of the trade described in the Periplus. Coins of the Kuṣāṇas and of the Western Kṣatrapas, Sātavāhana lead and copper coins, and later the gold coins of the Guptas and the issues of medieval dynasties allow historians to trace the extent of political control and of commercial circulation. Finds of Chinese coins on the Coromandel coast and of Indian coins in Southeast Asia point to the reach of the eastern sea routes (Tomber 2008; Ray 2003).

docs.title: 8.11 The Trade of Bengal
docs.text: In the Mughal period Bengal was one of the richest provinces of the empire, and its trade depended on its rivers. Rice, sugar, raw silk and above all cotton textiles—including the fine muslins of Dhaka—were carried by boat to river ports such as Patna, Murshidabad, Dhaka and Hugli, and thence to the coast and overseas. Saltpetre from Bihar, used for gunpowder, was a major export to Europe. European companies set up factories along the Hugli in the seventeenth century, and Calcutta, founded by the English company in 1690, grew into the capital of British India. Travellers of the period—Bernier and Tavernier among them—describe the density of boats on the rivers and the wealth of the province. Popular stories about the destruction of the Dhaka muslin industry, such as the claim that weavers’ thumbs were cut off, are not supported by the evidence; the industry declined mainly because of competition from machine-made British cloth and changes in markets in the early nineteenth century.

docs.title: 8.12 Railways and the New Geography of Trade
docs.text:
The first passenger railway in India ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853. Within half a century tens of thousands of kilometres of track linked the interior to the great ports of Bombay, Calcutta, Madras and Karachi. The railways reshaped the geography of trade that this chapter has described. Bulk goods that had moved slowly by river, pack-ox and cart now moved quickly by rail, mostly towards the ports, which handled the export of raw cotton, jute, wheat, oilseeds, tea and other produce and the import of manufactured goods. River traffic on the Gaṅgā declined; old inland trading towns that the lines bypassed declined with it, and new railway junctions grew. The Banjārās lost much of their carrying trade.

The railways also changed the movement of people—labourers, soldiers, pilgrims and migrants—and the response to famine, since grain could now be moved quickly to distressed regions, although in the great famines of the late nineteenth century it was often moved out of them by the market as well. The route network that the railways created largely followed the alignments of the older roads along the Gangetic plain and through the passes of the Western Ghats, but it reoriented the whole system towards the colonial ports and the world market.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Neelis (2011) on the routes of the north-west; Ray (1986) on the Deccan; Habib (1990) and Levi (2002) on merchants in Mughal and later India. The economic history of trade, guilds and coinage is the subject of Volume 19 of this series, Vāṇijya and Samudra.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Rivers: Hymns, Goddesses and Water Management
docs.text:
gaṅge ca yamune caiva godāvari sarasvati narmade sindhu kāveri jale ’smin saṃnidhiṃ kuru “O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu and Kāverī, be present in this water.”

— A verse widely recited before ritual bathing

The rivers of the Indian subcontinent are at once the basis of its agriculture, its main highways before the railway, and some of its most important deities. The verse quoted above, recited by many Hindus while bathing, calls seven great rivers from the north, the Deccan and the far south into a single vessel of water: a small act of sacred geography that unites the subcontinent through its rivers. This chapter looks at the rivers in the Vedic hymns, the problem of the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā and the rivers of the peninsula, and the long history of water management.

docs.title: 9.1 Rivers in the Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda speaks often of “the seven rivers” (sapta sindhavaḥ); the Avesta similarly knows a land of the “seven rivers” (hapta hindu). Which seven are meant is not stated and was probably not fixed. The geography of the hymns is centred on the Indus (Sindhu) and its Punjab tributaries, with the Sarasvatī to the east.

The Nadīstuti hymn (Ṛgveda 10.75), one of the later hymns of the collection, praises the Sindhu as the greatest of rivers and names others in two groups. The first runs from east to west, beginning with the Gaṅgā, which appears here for one of the very few times in the Ṛgveda.

Ṛgveda 10.75.5

imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri stomaṃ sacatā paruṣṇy ā asiknyā marudvṛdhe vitastayārjīkīye śṛṇuhy ā suṣomayā

“O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, with the Paruṣṇī attend to this praise of mine; O Marudvṛdhā with the Asiknī, O Ārjīkīyā with the Vitastā and the Suṣomā, hear me.”

The Śutudrī is the Sutlej, the Paruṣṇī the Ravi, the Asiknī the Chenab and the Vitastā the Jhelum; the Marudvṛdhā, Ārjīkīyā and Suṣomā are smaller streams whose identification is less certain. The next verse names western tributaries of the Indus, among them the Kubhā (Kabul), Krumu (Kurram) and Gomatī (Gomal). The ordering reflects real knowledge of the river system of the north-west. Michael Witzel and others have used the distribution of river names in Vedic texts of different periods to trace the movement of the centre of Vedic culture from the Punjab and the Sarasvatī region eastward into the Gaṅgā–Yamunā Doab (Witzel 1995).

docs.title: 9.2.1 In the Texts
docs.text: In the Ṛgveda the Sarasvatī is a great river and goddess, “best of mothers, best of rivers, best of goddesses” (ambitame nadītame devitame sarasvati, 2.41.16). One hymn (7.95.2) describes her as flowing pure “from the mountains to the samudra”; whether samudra here means the sea or another great body of water is debated. In later Vedic texts the river is described as disappearing in the sands at a place called Vinaśana (“the disappearing”), and rites were performed along its course. In the Mahābhārata, Balarāma makes a pilgrimage along the Sarasvatī, and in later tradition the river is said to flow underground to join the Gaṅgā and Yamunā invisibly at Prayāga.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Identification
docs.text: Since the nineteenth century most scholars have identified the Sarasvatī of the later Vedic texts with the Ghaggar–Hakra, a now seasonal river system that flows from the Siwalik hills through Haryana and Rajasthan and into Cholistan in Pakistan, where its dry bed continues towards the Indus. Many sites of the Harappan civilisation lie along this system. Its small modern tributary, the Sarsuti, preserves the name. Some scholars have instead identified the Ṛgvedic Sarasvatī, at least in its oldest hymns, with the Helmand in Afghanistan, whose Avestan name Haraxvaitī corresponds to Sarasvatī.

docs.title: 9.2.3 What the Geological Evidence Shows
docs.text:
Satellite images and field surveys have mapped a broad palaeochannel along the Ghaggar–Hakra, showing that a large river once flowed there. The crucial question is when, and from what source. Recent studies of the sediments have given a clearer answer than was available a generation ago.

  • Dating of sand grains in the palaeochannel indicates that it carried sediment from the high Himalaya during the late Pleistocene, when it was probably fed by the Sutlej or the Yamunā, and that this connection had been lost well before the Harappan period (Clift et al. 2012).

  • A study of the landscape of the Harappan period concluded that the Ghaggar–Hakra was then fed by the monsoon, not by glaciers, and that the Harappans settled along a river whose seasonal floods made agriculture possible (Giosan et al. 2012).

  • A later study found that the Sutlej abandoned this course around eight thousand years ago, so that the Harappan towns grew up along a former river valley that still held monsoon-fed flows and groundwater rather than a great glacier-fed river (Singh et al. 2017).

Some Indian geologists, notably K. S. Valdiya, have argued for a larger, Himalayan-fed river persisting into the Holocene (Valdiya 2002), and the debate is not closed. The most widely read statement of that view, Michel Danino’s The Lost River, combines the palaeochannels seen from satellites, the distribution of Harappan sites and the Vedic descriptions into a single story of a great river that dried in stages, its last waters failing near the end of the mature Harappan period (Danino 2010). The book explains why the popular view persists: each line of evidence seems to confirm the others. It parts from the sediment studies on the decisive point of timing, since those studies date the loss of the Himalayan supply thousands of years before the Harappan cities. But the popular claim that a mighty, glacier-fed Sarasvatī flowed until about 1900 BCE and that its drying caused the end of the Harappan cities is not supported by the recent sediment studies. The decline of the Harappan cities had several causes, of which changing rainfall and river behaviour were probably important ones (Wright 2010).

The Sarasvatī Debate in Summary

  • Textual: the Vedic Sarasvatī is a great river in the Ṛgveda and a disappearing one in later texts.

  • Identification: usually with the Ghaggar–Hakra; some scholars propose the Helmand for the oldest hymns.

  • Geology: a Himalayan-fed river flowed in the Ghaggar–Hakra valley in the late Pleistocene; by the Harappan period the river was monsoon-fed.

  • Open questions: the exact timing of river shifts, the meaning of the Ṛgvedic descriptions, and the relation between the hymns and the Harappan landscape.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Physical Geography
docs.text: The Gaṅgā rises at Gaumukh, the snout of the Gangotri glacier in the Garhwal Himalaya, at nearly 4,000 m; this headstream is called the Bhāgīrathī. At Devaprayāg it is joined by the Alakanandā, which has gathered the waters of several tributaries at a series of confluences (Vishnuprayag, Nandaprayag, Karnaprayag and Rudraprayag) on the way. The combined river leaves the mountains at Haridvār and flows some 2,500 km in all across the plains, joined by the Yamunā at Prayāga and by the Ghaghara, Gandak, Son and Kosi further east, before dividing into the distributaries of the Bengal delta: the Hugli to the west and the Padmā, which joins the Brahmaputra, to the east. Its delta, with the Sundarbans mangrove forests, is the largest in the world.

docs.title: 9.3.2 The River Goddess
docs.text: The descent of the Gaṅgā is told in the Rāmāyaṇa (Bālakāṇḍa) and the Mahābhārata: King Bhagīratha brings her down from heaven to purify the ashes of his ancestors, and Śiva breaks her fall in his matted hair. The name Bhāgīrathī preserves the story, as Jāhnavī recalls the sage Jahnu who swallowed and released the river. Every city on the river’s course has sacred bathing places, and the confluences of the upper river are tīrthas in their own right (Eck 2012).

docs.title: 9.3.3 River Goddesses at the Temple Door
docs.text: From the Gupta period onward, many temple doorways in north and central India carry figures of the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Gaṅgā standing on a makara (a crocodile-like water creature) and Yamunā on a tortoise. Placed at the threshold of the sanctum, they purify those who enter, as bathing in the rivers purifies the pilgrim. Gupta and post-Gupta examples survive at Udayagiri near Vidiśā and at Deogarh, and the motif became a standard part of temple architecture. Through it the sacred geography of the two great rivers of the Middle Country was carried into temples throughout the land (Eck 2012).

docs.title: 9.4.1 The Indus
docs.text: The Indus (Sanskrit Sindhu) rises in western Tibet, not far from Mānasarovar, flows north-west through Ladakh and Gilgit, turns south through the mountains and enters the plains of the Punjab, where it is joined by the five rivers of the Punjab (the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej) before flowing through Sindh to the Arabian Sea. It is some 3,000 km long. The first cities of the subcontinent grew up in its basin, and the hymns of the Ṛgveda were composed there. From its name come the words Hindu, India and Hindustan (Chapter 1). Since 1947 most of its course has lain in Pakistan, and the sharing of its waters between India and Pakistan has been governed by the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960.

docs.title: 9.4.2 The Brahmaputra
docs.text:
The Brahmaputra rises as the Yarlung Tsangpo in south-western Tibet, flows east for more than 1,000 km along the northern side of the Himālaya, turns south through a deep gorge round the eastern end of the range, and enters Assam as the Siang (Dihang). It flows west through the Assam valley and then south into Bangladesh, where it joins the Gaṅgā. Whether the Tsangpo and the Brahmaputra were the same river was one of the great geographical questions of the nineteenth century, and the explorer Kinthup was sent to answer it (Chapter 14).

The Brahmaputra, “son of Brahmā”, is one of the few rivers in Indian tradition regarded as male. Its valley was the ancient kingdom of Prāgjyotiṣa or Kāmarūpa; the temple of Kāmākhyā stands on a hill above the river at Guwahati (Chapter 4), and the Paraśurāma Kuṇḍa on the Lohit in Arunachal Pradesh draws pilgrims for a winter bathing festival. Majuli, an island in the river, is the centre of the Vaiṣṇava monasteries (satra) founded in the tradition of Śaṅkaradeva (traditionally 1449–1568), the Assamese saint who also wrote and staged devotional dramas. The river’s floods and shifting channels make its valley one of the most dynamic landscapes of the subcontinent.

docs.title: 9.5 The Rivers of the Peninsula
docs.text:
Six of the major rivers of the peninsula are summarised in Table 9.1. Their lengths are rounded, and published figures differ by several per cent according to the point taken as the source and the channel measured through the delta.

Table 9.1. Six major rivers of the peninsula (approximate lengths) River Source Length Notes Narmadā Amarkantak 1,310 km flows west through a rift valley between the Vindhya and Satpura to the Gulf of Khambhat Tāpī Satpura hills 720 km also west-flowing, to the sea near Surat Mahānadī Sihawa hills, Chhattisgarh 860 km flows east through Chhattisgarh and Odisha to the Bay of Bengal Godāvarī Tryambakeshwar, near Nashik 1,465 km largest peninsular river; called the “southern Gaṅgā” Kṛṣṇā near Mahabaleshwar 1,400 km with the Tuṅgabhadrā, waters the Deccan Kāverī Talakaveri, Kodagu 800 km delta in Tamil Nadu; the heart of the Cōḻa country

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Narmadā
docs.text: The Narmadā is unusual among large Indian rivers in flowing west. In religious tradition it is one of the holiest of rivers. A verse quoted in the Purāṇic praises of the river says that the Sarasvatī purifies in three days, the Yamunā in seven, the Gaṅgā at once, and the Narmadā at the mere sight of it. Stones from its bed, smoothed by the current, are worshipped as liṅgas (bāṇaliṅga). The Narmadā parikramā, in which pilgrims walk from the source to the sea along one bank and back along the other, is described in Chapter 4. In recent decades the river has also been the scene of the conflict over the Sardar Sarovar dam and the displacement of villages, much of it Adivasi land, that it caused.

docs.title: 9.5.2 The Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇā
docs.text: The Godāvarī rises at Tryambakeshwar near Nashik, at one of the twelve jyotirliṅgas, and flows east across the Deccan to the Bay of Bengal. Nashik is one of the four sites of the Kumbh Melā, and the river’s bathing festival (puṣkaram) is held every twelve years when Jupiter enters Leo. The Kṛṣṇā and its tributary the Tuṅgabhadrā water the central Deccan; the capital of Vijayanagara stood on the Tuṅgabhadrā.

docs.title: 9.5.3 The Kāverī
docs.text: The Kāverī rises in the hills of Kodagu and flows through Karnataka into the plains of Tamil Nadu, where its delta was the agricultural heartland of the Cōḻa kingdom. The Tamil epic Cilappatikāram opens in Pukār (Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam), the port at the river’s mouth, and celebrates the river. The sharing of its water has been the subject of a long dispute between the states of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, settled by a tribunal award in 2007 and a Supreme Court judgment in 2018.

docs.title: 9.5.4 The Vaikai and the Tamil Rivers
docs.text: Tamil poetry has its own rivers. The Paripāṭal, one of the Caṅkam anthologies, contains songs in praise of the river Vaikai at Madurai, describing the people of the city going out to bathe and play in the floodwaters, with music, ornaments and quarrels between lovers. The Kāverī, the Tāmraparṇī of the Pāṇḍya country and the Periyār of Kerala appear in poems, inscriptions and later māhātmyas. In Tamil tradition the Kāverī flood festival (āṭipperukku), celebrated in the month of Āṭi (July–August) when the river rises, honours the river as the source of the delta’s prosperity.

docs.title: 9.6 Moving Rivers
docs.text:
The rivers of the northern plains do not stay in one place. Carrying huge loads of sediment from the Himālaya, they build up their beds and periodically break out into new courses. The Kosi in Bihar has moved westward by more than a hundred kilometres over the last few centuries and broke its embankment disastrously in 2008. The Gaṅgā and the Brahmaputra have shifted their lower courses many times; in the late eighteenth century the Brahmaputra moved into a new channel (the Jamuna) in Bengal, and the main flow of the Gaṅgā shifted from the Bhāgīrathī–Hugli eastward towards the Padmā, which contributed to the silting of western Bengal’s ports. The Indus delta, too, has moved and changed.

These movements explain many features of the historical geography of the plains: abandoned river beds and oxbow lakes, towns that once stood on a river and now stand inland, ports that silted up, and the frequent changes in the course of the boundary-rivers of kingdoms and districts. They also explain why the identification of ancient river names and courses—the Sarasvatī is the best-known case, but by no means the only one—requires the help of geology as well as of texts.

docs.title: 9.7 Rivers as Boundaries
docs.text:
Rivers have often marked political frontiers. In the seventh century the Narmadā became the boundary between the kingdom of Harṣa in the north and that of the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II in the Deccan, after Harṣa’s attempt to cross it failed.
