In the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries the fertile land between the Kṛṣṇā and the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Raichur Doab, was fought over again and again by the kings of Vijayanagara and the Bahmani and later Deccan sultans. In 1809 the Treaty of Amritsar fixed the Sutlej as the boundary between the Sikh kingdom of Ranjit Singh and the territories under British protection. In 1947 the boundary drawn by the Radcliffe commission between India and Pakistan cut across the rivers of the Punjab and the deltas of Bengal, dividing irrigation systems and leaving questions of water sharing that were addressed, for the Indus basin, in the treaty of 1960.

Rivers make awkward boundaries, because they move (see above) and because the people on both banks usually belong to a single economy and culture. Ferry towns, bridges and fords were places of exchange as well as of control. In Indian tradition, too, the crossing of a great river often marks a change of region, and the names of many regions—Antarvedī (the land between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā), Pañcanada or Punjab (“five rivers”), Doāb itself (Persian, “two waters”)—are drawn from rivers.

docs.title: 9.8.1 Texts
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra encourages the king to build water works (setu), distinguishing those that use naturally available water from those to which water is brought, and sets out rules for irrigation charges and for penalties for damaging embankments and channels (Olivelle 2013). The lexicographers distinguish lands watered by rivers (nadīmātṛka, “having a river for mother”) from lands that depend on rain (devamātṛka, “having the god for mother”).

The Arthaśāstra also describes a rain gauge (varṣamāna), a vessel placed in front of the royal storehouse, and gives the expected amount of rain for different kinds of land and regions in units of droṇa, so that the superintendent of agriculture could decide which crops to sow (Arthaśāstra 2.5 and 2.24; (Olivelle 2013)). It is one of the earliest known prescriptions for measuring rainfall; how far it was ever put into practice is not known. Varāhamihira later describes the measurement of rain in an āḍhaka vessel (Section 3.4).

docs.title: 9.8.2 The Sudarśana Lake
docs.text: One of the best documented water works of ancient India is the Sudarśana reservoir near Girnar in Gujarat. The rock inscription of the Western Kṣatrapa ruler Rudradāman at Junagadh (150 CE) records that the lake had been made by Puṣyagupta, provincial governor under Candragupta Maurya, provided with conduits under Aśoka, burst in a great storm, and been rebuilt by Rudradāman’s minister. A later inscription of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta on the same rock records a further breach and repair in 455–56. Together they give a history of a single reservoir over more than seven centuries.

docs.title: 9.8.3 Tanks and Anicuts in South India
docs.text:
In much of peninsular India, where rivers are seasonal, agriculture depended on tanks (ēri in Tamil): earthen embankments across shallow valleys that stored the monsoon rains, often in chains in which the overflow from one tank fed the next. Pallava and Cōḻa inscriptions record gifts for building and repairing tanks and the work of village committees responsible for them; the inscriptions of Uttaramērūr from the reign of the Cōḻa king Parāntaka I (early tenth century) describe a committee for tanks among others.

The Kallaṇai or “Grand Anicut” on the Kāverī, traditionally attributed to the early Cōḻa king Karikāla, is a masonry weir that diverts water into the channels of the delta. The tradition of its ancient origin is strong, though the structure has been repaired and rebuilt many times; in the 1830s the British engineer Arthur Cotton studied it and used its principles when he built new works on the Kāverī system and later on the Godāvarī.

docs.title: 9.8.4 Reservoirs and Channels of the Deccan Kingdoms
docs.text: The kingdoms of the Deccan built large water works. The rulers of Vijayanagara (fourteenth to sixteenth centuries) built weirs across the Tuṅgabhadrā and long channels to irrigate the land round their capital, some of which are still in use, as well as tanks and aqueducts within the city. In Telangana, tank systems built under the Kākatīyas, such as the great lakes at Ramappa and Pakhal, stored monsoon water for irrigation; and the Qutb Shāhī rulers of Golconda built the Hussain Sagar lake at Hyderabad (1562). Such works show the continuity of hydraulic expertise across dynasties of different religions and regions.

docs.title: 9.8.5 Water in the Desert
docs.text:
In the arid west, where rivers are few and rainfall scanty and uncertain, communities developed ways of harvesting and storing every drop: village ponds (nāḍī, talāb), covered underground cisterns (kuṇḍ or ṭāṅkā) fed by carefully prepared catchment surfaces, earthen check-dams (johaḍ), and stepwells (Chapter 8). The town of Jaisalmer depended on the Gaḍīsar lake, an artificial reservoir built in the fourteenth century and surrounded by shrines and steps. Such systems required collective maintenance and rules for use, and their decay in the twentieth century, and their revival by voluntary organisations in parts of Rajasthan, have been much discussed in debates on water policy.

Modern Relevance: Rivers Today

Many of India’s sacred rivers are now heavily polluted and over-extracted, and the reverence in which they are held has not by itself protected them. Government programmes such as the National Mission for Clean Ganga (Namami Gange, launched in 2014) appeal to that reverence. Disputes over water between states, dams and the displacement they cause, and the effects of climate change on Himalayan glaciers and monsoon rainfall all show that the management of rivers remains one of the central geographical questions of the subcontinent.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On Vedic river geography see Witzel (1995); on the Sarasvatī problem, Giosan et al. (2012), Clift et al. (2012), Singh et al. (2017) and Valdiya (2002); on rivers in religion, Eck (2012) and Feldhaus (1995).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Mountains: Himālaya, Vindhya and the Ghats
docs.text:
asty uttarasyāṃ diśi devatātmā himālayo nāma nagādhirājaḥ pūrvāparau toyanidhī vigāhya sthitaḥ pṛthivyā iva mānadaṇḍaḥ “In the north there is a king of mountains named Himālaya, whose soul is divine; plunging into the eastern and western oceans, he stands like a measuring-rod of the earth.”

— Kālidāsa, Kumārasambhava 1.1

The opening of Kālidāsa’s Kumārasambhava, probably of the fourth or fifth century CE (the poem itself is discussed in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā), is a geographer’s image as much as a poet’s. The range is laid across the north like a surveyor’s rod (mānadaṇḍa), long enough to touch the eastern and the western sea, and it is at the same time a being with a divine soul. Extent and sanctity together run through Indian thinking about mountains. The Himālaya bounds the subcontinent to the north, shapes the monsoon, feeds the great rivers, and is the home of gods. The Vindhya divides north from south. The Western Ghats separate the Deccan from the western coast and catch the monsoon rains. Many individual peaks are sacred. And the people who live in the mountains hold a practical knowledge of them that the texts of the plains rarely record.

docs.title: 10.1 The Himālaya in Texts and Tradition
docs.text:
The Himālaya (“abode of snow”) or Himavat (“snowy”) stretches some 2,400 km from the Indus gorge in the west to the Brahmaputra in the east, in several parallel ranges rising from the foothills to the high peaks. In the Purāṇic cosmography it is the range that separates Bhāratavarṣa from Kimpuruṣavarṣa (Chapter 2); in the epics it is the region of sages’ hermitages, of the sources of the Gaṅgā, and of the journey towards heaven. In the Mahābhārata’s Mahāprasthānikaparvan the Pāṇḍavas, at the end of their lives, walk north into the mountains, falling one by one until only Yudhiṣṭhira remains. In the Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa, Sugrīva’s instructions to the search party sent north describe the Himālaya, Kailāsa and the land of the Uttarakurus beyond, in a mixture of real and mythical geography.

The texts also show practical familiarity with the mountains’ resources. The deodar cedar (devadāru, “tree of the gods”) and the birch, whose bark (bhūrja) was a common writing material in Kashmir and the north-west, appear frequently; musk, medicinal plants, yak-tail fans and gold were among the products brought down from the hills, and are listed among the tribute brought to Yudhiṣṭhira in the Sabhāparvan.

docs.title: 10.1.1 Sacred Places of the Himālaya
docs.text:
The upper valleys of the Gaṅgā in Garhwal contain some of the most important Hindu pilgrimage places: the sources of the Yamunā and Bhāgīrathī at Yamunotrī and Gaṅgotrī, the Śiva shrine of Kedārnāth and the Viṣṇu shrine of Badrīnāth (Chapter 4). Further west lie the cave of Amarnāth in Kashmir, with its ice liṅga, and the shrine of Vaiṣṇo Devī in the Trikuta hills; further east, Buddhist monasteries and sacred lakes in Sikkim, Bhutan and Arunachal Pradesh. Kailāsa and Mānasarovar lie beyond the main range in Tibet.

Kedārnāth (Table 4.1) is snowbound for half the year. In June 2013 heavy rain and the breaching of a glacial lake above the shrine caused a flood that killed several thousand pilgrims and residents in the Kedārnāth valley and across Uttarakhand; the exact number is not known. The temple survived, but the disaster drew attention to the risks of unregulated building and mass pilgrimage in fragile mountain valleys.

docs.title: 10.1.2 Hidden Lands and Pilgrimage Guides of the Buddhist Himālaya
docs.text: In the Buddhist Himālaya, sacred geography took distinctive forms. Tibetan pilgrimage guides (gnas yig) describe the sacred sites of a mountain, lake or valley, the deities that dwell there and the merits of visiting them. A tradition associated with Padmasambhava speaks of “hidden lands” (sbas yul), valleys concealed by the master for refuge in times of trouble and revealed later by visionary lamas; Sikkim, called in Tibetan the hidden land of Demojong, and valleys in Nepal and Arunachal Pradesh were identified as such and settled by migrants who believed they were entering a sacred refuge. Monasteries and pilgrimage routes in Ladakh, Spiti, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh thus form part of a Himalayan sacred geography that links India with Tibet, Bhutan and Nepal.

docs.title: 10.1.3 The Goddess of the Mountains: Nandā Devī
docs.text: In Garhwal and Kumaon the goddess Nandā is identified with the mountain Nandā Devī (7,816 m), the highest peak wholly within India. About once every twelve years a great procession, the Nandā Devī Rāj Jāt, escorts the goddess from the village of Nauti near Karnaprayag towards the high mountains, a journey of some three weeks on foot through villages, forests and high pastures to the lake of Rūpkuṇḍ and beyond, led by a four-horned ram that is released at the end of the journey. The procession, organised by local royal and priestly families, unites the villages of the region in a ritual of the mountain goddess’s return to her husband’s home on Kailāsa. It is a striking example of a regional sacred geography centred on mountains rather than on rivers or temples.

docs.title: 10.2 Passes and Routes
docs.text:
The passes of the north-west and the Himālaya, and the trade that crossed them, are described in Chapter 8. Here it is enough to note that most Himalayan passes are open only from about June to October, that they were crossed by traders and pilgrims on foot with yaks, sheep, goats and ponies as pack animals, and that their names often record their dangers: Rohtang, between Kullu and Lahaul, is popularly explained as Tibetan for “plain of corpses”. Until roads were built in the twentieth century, the passes were the domain of the specialised trading communities of the high valleys, such as the Bhotiyas of Kumaon and Garhwal, and of the guides who knew them.

The Arthaśāstra discusses forts in mountains (pārvata durga) among its types of fortification, and its book on war discusses fighting in different kinds of terrain (Olivelle 2013). Control of passes and frontier forts was a recurring concern of states from the Mauryas to the Mughals, whose campaigns in the north-west depended on the Khyber and the routes through Kabul and Kandahar.

docs.title: 10.3 Ladakh and the Trans-Himalayan Trade
docs.text:
Ladakh, in the upper Indus valley, was for centuries a crossroads of trans-Himalayan trade. Leh, its capital, was a meeting place for caravans from Kashmir and the Punjab, from Yarkand and Kashgar over the Karakoram, and from western Tibet. The fine goat wool (pashm) of the high Changthang plateau was brought through Ladakh to Kashmir, where it was woven into the famous shawls; salt, borax and brick tea came from Tibet; textiles, spices, sugar and metal goods went north. After a war between Ladakh and Tibet in the 1680s, a treaty regulated this trade and established periodic missions between Leh and Lhasa, which continued, with interruptions, until the mid-twentieth century.

The traders who conducted this commerce—Ladakhi, Kashmiri, Tibetan, Central Asian and Punjabi—knew the seasons of the passes, the pastures and halting places of the high plateaus and the politics of the regions they crossed. Their routes were among those later traced by the pundit explorers of the Survey of India (Chapter 14), and the closing of the Tibetan and Chinese borders after 1950 ended a trade that had lasted for many centuries.

docs.title: 10.4 Kashmir: A Valley and Its Chroniclers
docs.text:
The valley of Kashmir, enclosed by the Pir Panjal and the Great Himalaya and drained by the Vitastā (Jhelum), has an unusually rich literature about its own geography. The Nīlamata Purāṇa, a local Purāṇa, describes the origin of the valley from a lake drained by the gods and lists its sacred springs, rivers and festivals. Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī (“River of Kings”, 1148–49), a verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir, is full of precise topographical information: towns, temples, streams, passes and the courses of rivers (Stein 1900).

Kalhaṇa records one of the best-known water-management projects of early medieval India. Under King Avantivarman (r. 855–883), an engineer named Suyya is said to have cleared the bed of the Vitastā of the rocks that had blocked it below the Wular lake, regulated the course of the river and its confluence with the Sindh, built embankments, and reclaimed marshy land for cultivation, so that the price of rice fell sharply. Whatever exaggeration the account may contain, it shows a ruler and his expert reshaping the hydrology of an entire valley. Around 1900 Aurel Stein used Kalhaṇa’s chronicle, together with his own surveys, to reconstruct the ancient geography of Kashmir in one of the classic studies of Indian historical geography.

docs.title: 10.5 The Vindhya: A Cultural Boundary
docs.text:
The Vindhya hills run east–west across central India, north of the Narmadā. They are not high—most of the range is below 700 m, and the higher Satpura hills to the south of the Narmadā reach about 1,350 m at Dhupgarh near Pachmarhi—but they were long regarded as the boundary between north and south. The Manusmṛti defines the Middle Country and Āryāvarta as lying between the Himālaya and the Vindhya (Chapter 1), and Dakṣiṇāpatha began beyond them.

A well-known story, told in the Mahābhārata (Book 3) and the Purāṇas, explains why the Vindhya is low. Jealous of Meru, around which the sun circles, the Vindhya began to grow until it blocked the sun’s path. The sage Agastya, the Vindhya’s teacher, asked the mountain to bow down to let him pass southward and to stay low until he returned; Agastya never returned, and the Vindhya remains bowed. In Tamil tradition Agastya (Akattiyar) is the sage who brought learning to the south and is credited with the first Tamil grammar. The story expresses, in mythical form, the idea of the Vindhya as a barrier between two cultural worlds, and of northern Brahmanical culture moving south. Tamil literature, it should be remembered, had its own long and independent history, and the southward movement of Sanskrit culture was an exchange rather than a one-way transmission.

docs.title: 10.6 The Western Ghats
docs.text:
The Western Ghats, or Sahyādri, run some 1,600 km parallel to the western coast from near the Tāpī river to the southern tip of the peninsula. Their steep western scarp faces the Arabian Sea; to the east they slope gently into the Deccan, so that most of the peninsula’s great rivers rise within a few dozen kilometres of the western sea and flow east to the Bay of Bengal. The range catches the full force of the south-west monsoon, and parts of it receive several metres of rain a year. Together with Sri Lanka it forms one of the world’s recognised biodiversity hotspots, and parts of the range were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

Movement across the Ghats was concentrated at a few passes (ghāṭ) and gaps: the Thal Ghāṭ and Bhor Ghāṭ behind Mumbai, used by the first railways into the Deccan in the 1860s; the Nāṇeghāṭ and other passes of the Sātavāhana period (Chapter 8); and in the south the Palakkad (Palghat) Gap, a broad, low break in the range between the Nilgiri and Anaimalai hills, which carried trade between the Kerala coast and the Kāverī plains and still carries the main road and railway between Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

The southern Western Ghats are the Malaya mountains of Sanskrit literature, famous for sandalwood and pepper, and the scene of many poetic conventions: the Malaya breeze, cooled by the sandal forests, is the wind of spring in classical poetry.

docs.title: 10.6.1 The Hill Forts of the Sahyādri
docs.text: The steep, flat-topped hills of the northern Western Ghats made natural fortresses, and from the medieval period onward they were crowned with forts. In the seventeenth century Śivājī (1630–1680) built his power on control of these hill forts—Torna, Rajgad, Raigad, Pratapgad, Sinhagad and many others—and of the passes between the Deccan and the Konkan, together with sea forts on the coast such as Sindhudurg. Maratha military strategy depended on intimate knowledge of this terrain: of paths, water sources, monsoon conditions and the movement of armies through narrow valleys. The forts, with their rock-cut cisterns and walls following the edges of the cliffs, remain a striking example of the use of mountain geography for defence, and in 2025 a group of them was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the “Maratha Military Landscapes of India”.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Śabarimala
docs.text: The shrine of Ayyappan at Śabarimala, in the forests of the Western Ghats in Kerala, draws very large numbers of male pilgrims each winter, who observe a period of vows and walk the last stretch through the forest. The temple’s custom of excluding women of menstruating age led to a Supreme Court judgment in 2018 declaring the exclusion unconstitutional, protests in Kerala, and, in 2019, a reference of the wider questions of religious practice and equality to a larger bench of the Court.

docs.title: 10.7 The Forests and Hills of Central India
docs.text:
Between the Gangetic plain and the Deccan lies a broad belt of hills, plateaus and forests: the Vindhya and Satpura ranges, the Chhotanagpur plateau, the hills of Bastar and the Eastern Ghats. In Sanskrit literature this was the great forest of the south, the Daṇḍakāraṇya through which Rāma travels in the Rāmāyaṇa, and the home of peoples described from outside as “forest dwellers” (āṭavika) or by tribal names such as Śabara and Pulinda. Aśoka’s edicts warn the forest peoples of his power; Samudragupta’s Allahabad inscription claims to have made the kings of the forest tracts his servants.

The forest belt was not empty or unknown. It was home to many communities—Gonds, Bhils, Baigas, Santals, Mundas, Oraons, Khonds and others—with their own knowledge of its plants, animals, water and seasons, and their own sacred places, often hills, groves and springs. It was crossed by routes that linked north and south and by networks of exchange in forest products such as lac, honey, resins, hides and timber, on which the economies of the plains depended, and from the medieval period it had kingdoms of its own, such as those of the Gonds (Section 12.9).

Colonial forest policy from the 1860s reserved large areas of these forests for the state, restricting the rights of their inhabitants to cultivate, graze and gather, and provoking repeated resistance. Since independence, mining, dams and industry have brought further displacement. The geography of the central Indian forests is therefore also a history of contested rights, and its knowledge-holders are the Adivasi communities themselves, whose traditions are discussed in Volume 23 of this series, Jana–Jāti: Tribal and Folk Knowledge.

docs.title: 10.8 Sacred Hills of the South and Beyond
10.8.1 Aruṇācala
docs.text: The hill of Aruṇācala at Tiruvannamalai in Tamil Nadu is worshipped as a form of Śiva himself, the column of fire in which he appeared to Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Pilgrims walk round it (giripradakṣiṇa, about 14 km), above all at the festival of Kārttikai Dīpam, when a great fire is lit on the summit. The twentieth-century sage Ramaṇa Maharṣi (1879–1950) lived on and below the hill for more than fifty years and composed hymns to it, which made Aruṇācala widely known outside India.

docs.title: 10.8.2 Tirumala and Other Hills
docs.text: The temple of Veṅkaṭeśvara on the Tirumala hills in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh is among the most visited pilgrimage places in the world. In Sri Lanka, Adam’s Peak (Śrī Pāda) bears a footprint venerated by Buddhists as the Buddha’s, by Hindus as Śiva’s and by Muslims and Christians as Adam’s; Ibn Baṭṭūṭa climbed it in 1344. Jain sacred hills—Śatruñjaya, Girnār, Sammeta Śikhara and Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa—are described in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 10.9 A Poet’s Itinerary: The Meghadūta
docs.text:
Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta (“The Cloud Messenger”) is a love poem, but its first half is also one of the most famous pieces of geographical writing in Sanskrit. A yakṣa, exiled for a year to the hill of Rāmagiri in central India, asks a monsoon cloud to carry a message to his wife in the city of Alakā, on the slopes of Kailāsa. He then describes the route the cloud should take northward: over the mountain Āmrakūṭa; past the Revā (Narmadā) spreading among the rocks at the foot of the Vindhya; through the country of the Daśārṇas to Vidiśā on the Vetravatī (Betwa); with a detour west to Ujjayinī, the city of Mahākāla; over the Gambhīrā and Carmaṇvatī (Chambal) rivers; past Daśapura (Mandsaur), Brahmāvarta and the battlefield of Kurukṣetra; to Kanakhala where the Gaṅgā leaves the mountains; and up into the Himālaya, through the Krauñca pass, to Kailāsa and Alakā.

Figure 10.1. The route of the cloud in Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta, drawn through the places of the poem that can be located: from Rāmagiri (traditionally Ramtek near Nagpur; other sites have been proposed) past Āmrakūṭa and the Revā (Narmadā) to Vidiśā, west to Ujjayinī, north through Daśapura, Brahmāvarta and Kurukṣetra to Kanakhala, where the Gaṅgā leaves the mountains, and over the Himālaya to Kailāsa and the mythical city of Alakā. Straight lines join the places; the poem’s rivers and lesser stations are omitted. The coastline is simplified.

The route (Figure 10.1) follows the path of the monsoon clouds as they move north-west across central India in the rainy season, and it names real rivers, towns and shrines in a plausible order. The poem shows how geographical knowledge was woven into literature: an educated audience was expected to know these places and to enjoy the poet’s evocation of each. Later poets imitated the form in many “messenger poems” (sandeśakāvya), which send a cloud, a goose or a cuckoo along routes through their own regions and so preserve something of the regional geography of their time.

docs.title: 10.10 Hill Stations
docs.text: The British created a new kind of mountain place: the hill station. From the 1820s, officials and their families began to spend the hot season in the hills, and towns grew up at Shimla, Mussoorie, Nainital and Darjeeling in the Himālaya, at Ootacamund (Udhagamandalam) in the Nilgiris, and at Mahabaleshwar and Matheran in the Western Ghats. From 1864 Shimla became the summer capital of the Government of India, so that for half of every year the empire was governed from a Himalayan ridge. Hill stations were built on land often taken from local communities such as the Todas of the Nilgiris, and they depended on the labour of porters and servants from the hills and the plains. Tea and coffee plantations in Darjeeling, Assam and the Nilgiris transformed the hill landscapes and their economies, and brought migrant labourers from central India and Nepal. The hill stations are a reminder that the colonial period produced its own geography of the mountains, quite different from the sacred geography of the pilgrim or the working geography of the herder.

docs.title: 10.11 Mountain Peoples and Mountain Knowledge
docs.text:
The most detailed knowledge of the mountains has always belonged to the people who live in them, and very little of it was recorded in classical texts. Some examples:

  • Transhumant herders, such as the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh, the Bakarwals and Van Gujjars, and the Bhotiyas of Kumaon and Garhwal, move their flocks and households between winter grazing in the foothills and summer pastures (bugyāl in Garhwal) in the high mountains, following routes and rights that have been negotiated over generations.

  • Traders of the high valleys conducted the trans-Himalayan trade, timing their journeys to the opening and closing of passes and the fairs of Tibetan market towns.

  • Farmers of the north-east, such as the Apatani of Arunachal Pradesh, developed intensive wet-rice systems in mountain valleys, while many communities practised shifting cultivation (jhūm) on hill slopes; Khasi and Jaintia villages in Meghalaya trained the roots of rubber fig trees into living bridges across streams.

  • Hill communities in the peninsula, such as the Todas of the Nilgiris, the Soligas of the Biligiri Rangan hills and many others, have their own knowledge of forest, pasture and water.

This knowledge was not static or always benign, and it was reshaped by colonial forest laws, which restricted access to forests in the name of conservation and revenue. Resistance to those restrictions runs through the modern history of the Himālaya. The Chipko movement of the 1970s in Garhwal, in which villagers, many of them women, embraced trees to prevent commercial felling, drew on older traditions of peasant protest and became a symbol of environmental movements in India (Guha 1989).

Modern Relevance: Mountains and Change

The Himalayan glaciers are retreating, and changes in snowfall and monsoon rainfall affect the rivers of the plains. Road building, dams and mass tourism and pilgrimage have increased landslide and flood risks, as the Kedārnāth disaster of 2013 showed. The local knowledge of mountain communities—of snow, slopes, streams and seasons—can contribute to understanding and coping with these changes, alongside scientific monitoring, provided that it is recorded carefully and its holders have a voice in decisions.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On sacred mountains and pilgrimage see Eck (2012) and McKay (2015); on Himalayan history and environment, Guha (1989).

docs.title: Chapter 11: Coasts, Ports and Islands
docs.text:
samudravasane devi parvatastanamaṇḍale viṣṇupatni namas tubhyaṃ pādasparśaṃ kṣamasva me “O Goddess whose garment is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountains, consort of Viṣṇu, I bow to you; forgive me for touching you with my feet.”

— Recited by many Hindus on waking, before touching the ground

The coastline of the Indian mainland and its islands was long given officially as about 7,500 km; a remeasurement by the National Hydrographic Office and the Survey of India, reported in 2024–25, gives about 11,100 km. The coast has not grown. The new figure was measured on more detailed maps and follows more of the creeks, estuaries and islands, and an indented coastline always comes out longer the more finely it is measured. It runs from the salt marshes of Kutch past the gulfs of Khambhat and the Konkan, the lagoons of Kerala and the sandy, surf-beaten shore of the Coromandel to the deltas of the Godāvarī, Kṛṣṇā, Mahānadī and Gaṅgā. Offshore lie Sri Lanka, the coral atolls of Lakshadweep and the Maldives, and, far out in the Bay of Bengal, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. For two thousand years and more, this coast connected India with Africa, Arabia, the Mediterranean, Southeast Asia and China. Much of the knowledge needed to use it—of winds, currents, tides, shoals and landmarks—belonged to fishermen, boat-builders, pilots and sailors, and is known to us only indirectly (Ray 2003; Chaudhuri 1985).

docs.title: 11.1.1 Gujarat and the Konkan
docs.text:
The coast of Gujarat, with its two great gulfs of Kutch and Khambhat, has been a centre of seafaring from Harappan times. Lothal, at the head of the Gulf of Khambhat, was a Harappan town and a centre of bead-making and trade, with a large brick-lined basin whose function is debated.

Scholarly Note: The “Dockyard” at Lothal

The basin at Lothal was interpreted by its excavator, S. R. Rao, as a tidal dockyard, and is often described as the world’s earliest dock. This interpretation has been seriously questioned: L. S. Leshnik argued that the basin was more probably a water reservoir for irrigation and drinking water (Leshnik 1968), and the evidence for its connection to a tidal channel is disputed. The dockyard claim should be treated as one interpretation among several, not as established fact.

In the early historical period the great port was Barygaza (Bharuch) on the Narmadā, whose difficult approach through tidal mudflats is described in the Periplus, which says that local pilots in boats met incoming ships to guide them in (Casson 1989). Later the leading ports were Khambhat (Cambay), from about the tenth to the sixteenth century, and Surat, from the sixteenth to the eighteenth. Gujarati merchants and ships were active from the Red Sea to Malacca.

South of Gujarat the Konkan coast is a narrow strip between the Western Ghats and the sea, cut by many creeks and estuaries. Its ports—Sopara, Kalyan, Chaul, Dabhol and later Goa and Bombay—linked the Deccan, through the passes, to the sea. At Chaul in 1508 a Portuguese squadron was defeated by a Mamluk fleet allied with the Gujarat sultanate; the next year the Portuguese destroyed that fleet off Diu, and in 1510 they took Goa.

docs.title: 11.1.2 Malabar
docs.text:
The coast of Kerala is characterised by lagoons and backwaters (kāyal) behind the shore, which allowed sheltered inland navigation, and by the pepper and other spices of its hinterland. Its ports attracted merchants from the Mediterranean, the Middle East and China, and its Muslim communities, studied by Sebastian Prange, grew out of the trade that linked Malabar with Arabia and the Gulf (Prange 2018).

  • Muziris (Muciṟi in Tamil), near modern Kodungallur, was the great pepper port of the Roman period, described in the Periplus and in Tamil Caṅkam poems; excavations at Pattanam have revealed much Mediterranean pottery and are thought by many to locate it (Tomber 2008). Tradition holds that the harbour silted up after a great flood in 1341, which opened the harbour at Kochi.

  • Kollam (Quilon) was a major port of the ninth to fourteenth centuries, visited by Arab and Chinese ships.

  • Calicut (Kozhikode), ruled by the Zamorin (Sāmūtiri), was the leading port of Malabar in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Ibn Baṭṭūṭa saw Chinese junks there; the Ming admiral Zheng He’s fleets called there between 1405 and 1433; and Vasco da Gama arrived there in 1498.

docs.title: 11.1.3 The Coromandel and the East Coast
docs.text:
The east coast south of the Kṛṣṇā is mostly open, sandy and exposed to surf, with few natural harbours. Ships anchored offshore and cargo and passengers were carried through the surf in flexible sewn-plank boats (the masula boats of the Coromandel) or on log rafts.

  • Pukār (Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam), at the mouth of the Kāverī, was the port of the early Cōḻas. The Caṅkam poem Paṭṭiṉappālai describes horses arriving by sea, pepper brought by land, and goods from Īḻam (Sri Lanka) and Kāḻakam (in Southeast Asia) in its markets. A later Tamil epic, the Maṇimēkalai, tells that the city was swallowed by the sea; underwater and coastal archaeology has found remains of early historic structures in the area.

  • Arikamedu, near Puducherry, was a trading station with Mediterranean contacts in the early centuries CE (Chapter 6).

  • Māmallapuram was the port of the Pallava kings in the seventh and eighth centuries.

  • Nāgapaṭṭiṉam was the main Cōḻa port. Copper plates of the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I record his grant of a village to a Buddhist monastery there built by the Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya—a sign of the close and complicated relations across the Bay of Bengal (Chapter 13).

  • Motupalli, in Andhra, was the port of the Kākatīya kingdom; an inscription of Gaṇapatideva (1244/45) guarantees merchants’ safety and fixes the duties they paid, and Marco Polo landed in the kingdom (Chapter 6). In the seventeenth century Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) was the great port of the Golconda sultanate.

  • Further north, the ports of Kaliṅga (Odisha) and Bengal—Tāmralipti in early times, Saptagrām, Hugli and Chittagong later—linked the Gangetic plain to the Bay of Bengal (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 11.2 Surat and the Merchants of Gujarat
docs.text:
In the seventeenth century Surat, on the Tāpī, was the greatest port of the Mughal empire. Through it passed the textiles of Gujarat and the north, indigo, saltpetre and other goods to the Red Sea, the Gulf, Southeast Asia and, increasingly, to Europe through the English and Dutch companies, which had their main Indian factories there. It was also the principal port for the Hajj (Chapter 4). Its merchants included Hindu and Jain vāṇiyās, Muslim Bohras and other Muslim traders, Parsis, Armenians and Arabs. The greatest of them, Mullā ʿAbd al-Ghafūr (d. 1718), a Bohra merchant, owned a fleet of ocean-going ships trading to the Red Sea and the Gulf.

Ashin Das Gupta’s study of Surat in the early eighteenth century shows how the port’s prosperity depended on the security of the routes to the Red Sea and on the stability of the Mughal, Safavid and Ottoman empires; when all three declined, and as the English company’s power grew, Surat’s Indian shipping declined and Bombay rose in its place (Das Gupta 1979). The story of Surat is a reminder that the geography of ports was shaped by politics as much as by harbours and winds.

docs.title: 11.2.1 The Backwaters of Kerala
docs.text: Behind the coast of central Kerala lies a network of lagoons, lakes, rivers and canals, of which Vembanad is the largest. For centuries this network carried much of the region’s traffic in boats: rice from the low-lying fields of Kuttanad, pepper and other spices from the hills, coir, coconuts and passengers moved between the inland towns and the ports of Kochi and Kollam. Large cargo boats of planks sewn with coir (keṭṭuvaḷḷam) were the typical craft. The fields of Kuttanad, partly below sea level and protected by bunds, are an example of land reclaimed and managed by local communities over generations.

docs.title: 11.3.1 The Monsoon
docs.text:
The word “monsoon” comes, through Portuguese, from the Arabic mawsim, “season”. Over the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal the winds blow from the south-west from about June to September and from the north-east from about November to February, with variable winds in between. The pattern governed sailing (Table 11.1) and shaped a calendar of trade for the whole Indian Ocean until the coming of steam (Chaudhuri 1985).

Table 11.1. The monsoon calendar of sailing in the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal Season Effect on sailing Early south-west monsoon (May–June) and its end (late August–September) ships from the Red Sea and Arabia sail to India; Indian ships cross the Bay of Bengal eastward Height of the south-west monsoon (June–August) storms and heavy seas; west-coast ports largely closed North-east monsoon (about November–February) ships sail from India to Arabia, the Red Sea and East Africa, and from Southeast Asia back to India Transitions (March–May, October) variable winds; coastal sailing; cyclones in the Bay of Bengal in October–November

Indian, Arab and Persian sailors knew these winds long before Greek and Roman merchants learned to use them for the open-sea crossing to India in the late first century BCE or early first century CE. The Periplus associates the crossing with a pilot named Hippalus, after whom the south-west wind was sometimes called; but Hippalus learned what local sailors already knew (Casson 1989).

docs.title: 11.3.2 Pilots and Their Knowledge
docs.text:
Indian Ocean pilots navigated by the stars, by soundings and by coastal landmarks. They measured the altitude of the Pole Star and other stars with a simple device, the kamāl—a small board held at arm’s length on a knotted string—in units of “fingers”, which gave a measure of latitude. They knew the colour of the water and the kinds of sea-bottom brought up by the sounding lead, the birds and sea-snakes that indicated nearness to land, and the profiles of mountains and headlands seen from the sea. Aḥmad ibn Mājid’s Kitāb al-Fawāʾid (c. 1490) and the works of Sulaymān al-Mahrī record this knowledge in Arabic for the western Indian Ocean, including the coasts of India (Tibbetts 1971). Gujarati and other Indian pilots shared in it; the pilot who guided Vasco da Gama from Malindi to Calicut in 1498 was, according to the Portuguese chroniclers, a Gujarati (Chapter 5).

Scholarly Note: What the Texts Do and Do Not Tell Us

Sanskrit texts mention ships, sea voyages and shipwrecks—the Jātaka stories, for instance, tell of merchants sailing to Suvarṇabhūmi and of a blind master mariner of Suppāraka (Sopara) who could tell where a ship was from the water. A Sanskrit compendium, the Yuktikalpataru, traditionally attributed to King Bhoja but of uncertain date, classifies ships by size and timber. But no Sanskrit manual of navigation comparable to the Arabic pilot books survives. The navigational knowledge of Indian sailors was transmitted largely by practice and oral instruction, and much of what is said about it rests on later sources and on inference.

docs.title: 11.3.3 Boats
docs.text: Boat-building responded to local conditions. On the west coast, ocean-going ships were traditionally built of planks sewn together with coir rope rather than nailed, a technique noted by Marco Polo and other medieval travellers and used in the western Indian Ocean until recent times. On the surf-beaten Coromandel coast, the masula boat, with planks sewn with coir and no frame, was flexible enough to survive landing through the breakers, and the kaṭṭumaram (Tamil, “tied logs”), a raft of logs lashed together, could be launched and landed through heavy surf; the English word “catamaran” is derived from it, though modern catamarans are twin-hulled boats of a different kind.

docs.title: 11.4 Seafaring Memories of the East Coast
docs.text:
The seafaring traditions of Kaliṅga (Odisha) and Bengal are remembered in festivals and stories. In Odisha, the festival of Bāli Jātrā at Cuttack, held at the full moon of Kārttika (October–November), when the north-east monsoon allowed ships to sail south-east, recalls the voyages of the sādhabas, merchant-mariners who traded with “Bāli”, Java and Sumatra; on the same day people float small boats on rivers and tanks. In Bengal, medieval narrative poems (maṅgalkāvya) tell of merchants such as Cānd Saudāgar and Dhanapati who sailed down the rivers to the sea and across to Laṅkā and beyond, naming river ports and landmarks along the way. These memories are literary and ritual, not logs of voyages, but they show how deeply sea trade entered the culture of the eastern coast.

On the west coast, the ports of Kutch and Saurashtra, such as Mandvi, kept alive the building of large wooden sailing ships (vahāṇ) and the knowledge of the routes to Arabia and East Africa well into the twentieth century; Kutchi pilots and sailors were among the last practitioners of traditional Indian Ocean navigation, and some of their pilot books and charts survive (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 11.5 Sri Lanka
docs.text:
Sri Lanka is separated from India by the Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar. Between Rāmeśvaram and Mannar island stretches a chain of sand-banks and limestone shoals, some 30 km long, known as Adam’s Bridge or Rāma Setu. During the low sea levels of the last ice age, when the sea was more than 100 m lower than today, India and Sri Lanka were joined by land; the connection was finally submerged in the early Holocene.

In Hindu tradition the shoals are the bridge built by Rāma’s army to reach Laṅkā. Satellite photographs published by NASA in 2002 were widely reported as showing a man-made structure; NASA itself stated that the images said nothing about the origin of the shoals, which geologists regard as natural. The proposed Sethusamudram shipping canal through the shoals became a subject of political and legal controversy from 2005. The identification of the Laṅkā of the Rāmāyaṇa with Sri Lanka is traditional and very old, though some scholars have argued that the epic’s Laṅkā was originally imagined elsewhere.

Sri Lanka’s historical connections with India are documented independently of the epic. The Pali chronicles of the island, the Dīpavaṃsa and Mahāvaṃsa, tell of settlers from northern India led by Vijaya and of the arrival of Buddhism with Aśoka’s son Mahinda. Tamil Caṅkam poetry knows the island as Īḻam and mentions goods from it in the markets of Pukār. Gems, pearls from the Gulf of Mannar and cinnamon were among its famous products, and its ports were stations on the routes between the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.

docs.title: 11.6 The Andaman and Nicobar Islands
docs.text:
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands form an arc in the eastern Bay of Bengal, more than 1,000 km from the Indian mainland and much closer to Myanmar and Sumatra. Ships on the route between India and Southeast Asia passed them, and travellers reported them, often with fear of their inhabitants. Yijing in the seventh century describes a “country of naked people”, probably the Nicobars, on his voyage from Kedah on the Malay peninsula to Tāmralipti. The great inscription of the Cōḻa king Rājendra I at Tanjavur, listing the places taken in his expedition against Śrīvijaya around 1025, includes Mānakkavāram, usually identified with the Nicobars. Marco Polo mentions both island groups under the names Necuveram and Angamanain, repeating stories of cannibals that later writers copied.

The Andamans were inhabited by peoples—the Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese—whose ancestors appear from genetic studies to have lived in the islands for a very long time, and whose languages are unrelated to those of the mainland. The Nicobars are home to the Nicobarese and the Shompen. The British established a penal settlement at Port Blair in 1858, after the revolt of 1857, and built the Cellular Jail there between 1896 and 1906. Colonial settlement, disease and later development reduced the Great Andamanese to a few dozen people; the Sentinelese continue to refuse contact. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami devastated the islands, especially the Nicobars. Any account of the “geographical knowledge” of the islanders must start from respect for their autonomy and from the recognition that most of what has been written about them was written by outsiders.

docs.title: 11.7 Lakshadweep and the Maldives
docs.text:
The coral atolls of Lakshadweep lie some 200–400 km off the coast of Kerala; the much larger Maldive archipelago lies further south. They were landmarks and hazards on the routes across the Arabian Sea, and their inhabitants were skilled sailors. Most of the people of Lakshadweep speak a form of Malayalam; on Minicoy, the southernmost island, the language is Mahl, a form of Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives. The islanders are Muslim, with matrilineal customs like those of parts of the Malabar coast; tradition dates their conversion to Islam to the early centuries of Islam, though the details are legendary. The islands were later controlled for a time by the Ali Rajas of Kannur and then by the British.

The Maldives converted to Islam in the twelfth century (traditionally in 1153). Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who served as a judge there in 1343–44 and married into the islands’ ruling families, described an island economy based on coconut fibre (coir), dried fish and cowrie shells, and a society in which he found the women’s freedom of dress and movement remarkable (Gibb 1929; Dunn 1986). Maldivian cowries were exported in great quantities to Bengal and, later, to West Africa, where they served as currency.

docs.title: 11.8 The Coasts and the European Companies
docs.text:
From 1498 the coasts of India became the arena of European commercial and naval competition. The Portuguese established fortified trading posts and their capital at Goa (1510), tried to control the spice trade of Malabar, and required Asian ships to buy passes (cartaz). In the seventeenth century the Dutch and English East India Companies, followed by the French and Danes, set up factories on both coasts: the English at Surat (1613), Madras (1639), Bombay (1668) and Calcutta (1690); the Dutch at Pulicat, Cochin and Nāgapaṭṭiṉam; the French at Pondicherry; the Danes at Tranquebar.

The geography of the ports changed with them. Some old ports declined as trade was redirected or harbours silted up; new ones grew around company forts, which became the great colonial port cities of Bombay, Madras and Calcutta. European pilots and hydrographers charted the coasts in detail, relying at first on Indian and Arab pilots and their knowledge. The charts of the coasts made by the English company’s marine surveyors in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, like the land surveys described in Chapter 14, drew on and gradually replaced the knowledge held by local mariners (Chaudhuri 1985; Pearson 2003).

docs.title: 11.9 The Sacred Coast
docs.text: The coasts of India are lined with sacred places of many religions. Hindu shrines stand at the extremities and landmarks of the coast: Somanātha and Dvārakā in Saurashtra, Gokarṇa on the Karnataka coast, Kanyākumārī at the southern tip, where the goddess is said to wait for her divine bridegroom, Rāmeśvaram, Purī and Gaṅgāsāgar at the mouth of the Hugli, where pilgrims bathe each January. Sailors and fishermen worship their own deities of the sea and of safe return. Muslim shrines include the dargāh of the saint Shāhul Hamīd at Nagore on the Coromandel coast, visited by fishermen and sailors of all religions; Christian shrines include the basilica of Our Lady of Good Health at Velankanni nearby, associated in tradition with the rescue of Portuguese sailors from a storm, and the church of St Thomas at Mylapore. The mosques of the Malabar coast, some of them among the oldest in South Asia, and the synagogues of Kochi record the communities that the sea brought to India. The coast is thus a sacred landscape as plural as the communities that lived and traded along it.

docs.title: 11.10 Underwater Archaeology and Its Claims
docs.text: Marine archaeology in India began in the 1980s, when the National Institute of Oceanography undertook underwater surveys off Dvārakā and Bet Dwarka in Gujarat under the direction of S. R. Rao. Stone structures, anchors and other finds were reported and were interpreted by some as the remains of the city of Kṛṣṇa described in the Mahābhārata, submerged by the sea. The dating and interpretation of these finds are disputed: many of the stone anchors are of types used over long periods, and the structures have not been securely dated to the second millennium BCE. Similar claims have been made about a “submerged city” in the Gulf of Khambhat, based on sonar images and dredged objects, which most archaeologists reject. Marine archaeology has produced valuable results on ancient ports and shipwrecks, but claims that it has confirmed the literal history of the epics are not established (Ray 2003).

docs.title: 11.11 The Pearl Fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar
docs.text:
The shallow banks of the Gulf of Mannar, between southern Tamil Nadu and north-western Sri Lanka, were for two thousand years among the world’s most famous sources of pearls. Greek and Roman writers knew of them, the Periplus names Kolchoi (Korkai) as the centre of the fishery under the Pāṇḍyas, and Caṅkam poems mention the pearls of Korkai. Marco Polo described the divers of the Coromandel coast and the charms used to protect them from sharks; later the Portuguese, then the Dutch and finally the British controlled the fisheries on both sides of the gulf, leasing them out and taxing the catch (Casson 1989; Yule 1903).

The fishery depended on detailed local knowledge: of the position and condition of the oyster banks, which were inspected before each season; of the brief calm season in spring when diving was possible; and of the skills of the divers, most of them from the Parava and other fishing communities, who dived without apparatus, using stones to descend. The banks were exhausted by over-exploitation and changing conditions in the twentieth century, and the great fisheries came to an end. Their history illustrates both the richness of coastal knowledge and the way in which states and companies appropriated its profits.

docs.title: 11.12 Cyclones and Storm Surges
docs.text:
The east coast of India and the coasts of Bangladesh and Myanmar are exposed to tropical cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal, chiefly in the transitional seasons before and after the south-west monsoon. The funnel shape and shallow waters of the northern Bay amplify the storm surges that accompany them, and some of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history have struck the deltas of the Gaṅgā, Brahmaputra, Mahānadī and Godāvarī. Seafarers knew the dangerous months and avoided them; Indian Ocean sailing calendars in Arabic and Indian sources mark the closing of the seas.

Coastal communities developed their own knowledge of storm signs—changes in the swell, the colour of the sky, the behaviour of birds—and built in ways that took floods into account, while temples and other strong buildings served as refuges. Modern meteorology, satellite tracking and organised evacuation have greatly reduced the loss of life from cyclones on the Indian coast since the Odisha cyclone of 1999, which killed thousands. How much local knowledge contributed to that improvement has not been measured; that the two kinds of knowledge could work together in warning and evacuation is a reasonable hope rather than a demonstrated result.

docs.title: 11.13 Fishing Communities
docs.text:
The fishing communities of the Indian coasts—the Kolīs of Gujarat and the Konkan, the Mukkuvar of Kerala and southern Tamil Nadu, the Paravar of the pearl-fishing coast, the Pattanavar and others of the Coromandel, and many more—hold detailed knowledge of the sea: the seasons and movements of fish, the local winds, currents and tides, the location of reefs and fishing grounds, and the signs of approaching storms. They were also, historically, among the people most exposed to the power of states and companies: the Paravar of the pearl coast converted to Catholicism in large numbers in the 1530s under Portuguese protection, and fishing communities have often been socially marginalised.

Modern Relevance: Coastal Knowledge Today

Marine scientists and fisheries managers increasingly recognise the value of fishers’ knowledge, alongside scientific surveys, for understanding fish stocks, coastal change and the effects of climate change. The 2004 tsunami and later cyclones showed both the vulnerability of coastal communities and the importance of local knowledge in warning and recovery.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Ray (2003) on early seafaring; Chaudhuri (1985) and Pearson (2003) on the Indian Ocean; Casson (1989) and Tomber (2008) on the Roman trade; Tibbetts (1971) on navigation. Ships, ports and seafaring are treated more fully in Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Regions, Realms and Boundaries: From Janapada to State
docs.text: The map of modern India is divided into states whose names are mostly old: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Bengal, Odisha, Kerala, Punjab, Kashmir. Behind each name lies a long history of peoples, kingdoms and administrative units, and of shifting boundaries between them. Earlier chapters described the land’s physical regions—its rivers, mountains and coasts. This chapter turns to political and administrative geography: the janapadas and the normative regions of the early texts, how kingdoms and empires described and divided the territory they ruled, how the historical regions of the subcontinent took shape and got their names, how place-names record the history of settlement, how boundaries were marked, and how the provinces of British India became the linguistic states of the Republic. Its principal guides are D. C. Sircar’s studies of the geography of the inscriptions and Joseph Schwartzberg’s Historical Atlas of South Asia (Sircar 1971; Schwartzberg 1978).

docs.title: 12.1 What Is a Region?
docs.text:
Geographers and historians have approached the regions of South Asia in two ways. One starts from the land. O. H. K. Spate’s India and Pakistan (1954), the classic regional geography of the subcontinent, divided it into regions defined by relief, climate, soils and drainage, and then showed how each had shaped, and been shaped by, its history (Spate 1954). The archaeologist Bendapudi Subbarao proposed in The Personality of India a simple and influential scheme: the great alluvial plains and deltas were “areas of attraction”, where population, agriculture and states concentrated; the forested hills of middle India and the north-east were “areas of isolation”, where older ways of life persisted; and between them lay “areas of relative isolation”, open to influence but able to keep their own character (Subbarao 1958).

The other approach starts from people. Bernard Cohn distinguished “objective” regions, drawn by an observer on the basis of chosen criteria, from “subjective” regions, those that their own inhabitants recognise and name, through a shared language, literature, cult centres, marriage networks and memories of a kingdom (Cohn 1967). The two do not always coincide. A region such as Bengal or the Tamil country is both: a physical unit and a cultural one with its own name and literature. Others, such as the Deccan, are clear on a physical map but have been divided among several linguistic and political regions for most of their history.

Maps of the states of South Asia over time, of which Schwartzberg’s Atlas is the fullest set, show a further pattern. Power repeatedly formed in a small number of “nuclear” areas—the middle Gaṅgā valley around Magadha, the Gaṅgā–Yamunā Doab, Gujarat, the Kāverī delta, the Krishna–Godāvarī deltas, the upper Indus plains—while certain zones between them were contested again and again: the Raichur Doab between the Krishna and the Tuṅgabhadrā, fought over by Cālukyas and Cōḻas and later by Vijayanagara and the Bahmanī sultans, is the classic example (Chapter 9; (Schwartzberg 1978)). Historians of early medieval India have shown how regional kingdoms grew up in such areas from the sixth century onward, by the extension of agriculture, the settlement of Brahmins on granted land, the building of temples and the incorporation of local chiefs and cults (Chattopadhyaya 1994; Kulke 1995). Many of the regions of modern India took their lasting form in that period.

docs.title: 12.2.1 Janapadas
docs.text:
The word janapada, “the foothold of a people (jana)”, refers to a territory named after the people who lived in it and, in the period from c. 600 BCE, to the states that formed there. Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE) gives grammatical rules for forming the names of peoples and their countries, and Buddhist and Jain texts list the “great janapadas” (mahājanapada). The best-known list, in the Pali Aṅguttara Nikāya, gives sixteen (Table 12.1); the Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra gives a different sixteen. The Pali list reflects the political map of north India around the fifth century BCE as remembered by the compilers of the canon (Thapar 2002).

Table 12.1. The sixteen mahājanapadas of the Aṅguttara Nikāya Mahājanapada Capital Approximate region Aṅga Campā eastern Bihar (near Bhagalpur) Magadha Rājagṛha (Rājgir) southern Bihar Kāśī Vārāṇasī eastern Uttar Pradesh Kosala Śrāvastī eastern Uttar Pradesh Vajji (Vṛji) Vaiśālī northern Bihar Malla Kuśinārā, Pāvā eastern Uttar Pradesh Ceti (Cedi) Sotthivatī Bundelkhand Vaṃsa (Vatsa) Kauśāmbī near Prayagraj Kuru Indapatta (Indraprastha) Delhi–Haryana region Pañcāla Ahicchatra, Kāmpilya western Uttar Pradesh Maccha (Matsya) Virāṭanagara north-eastern Rajasthan Śūrasena Mathurā the Mathurā region Assaka (Aśmaka) Potana on the Godāvarī, Deccan Avanti Ujjayinī western Madhya Pradesh (Malwa) Gandhāra Takṣaśilā north-western Pakistan Kamboja uncertain eastern Afghanistan

The list is not a survey of the whole subcontinent: it says nothing of the far south, the east beyond Aṅga or the north-east. In the Buddha’s lifetime Kosala had already absorbed Kāśī and Magadha absorbed Aṅga, and Magadha went on to become the core of the Nanda and Maurya empires.

docs.title: 12.2.2 The Middle Country and Āryāvarta
docs.text:
Classical writers divided the subcontinent into a small number of large regions. The Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE) defines the Madhyadeśa, the “Middle Country”, as the land between the Himālaya and the Vindhya, east of Vinaśana (where the Sarasvatī disappears) and west of Prayāga (2.21), and Āryāvarta as the land between the same mountains from the eastern to the western sea (2.22). These are normative definitions of the land in which Brahmanical norms were held to apply, not neutral descriptions, and the boundary of Āryāvarta shifted from text to text (Olivelle 2005).

Buddhist texts have their own Middle Country (Pali Majjhimadesa). The monastic code (Vinaya, Mahāvagga 5) defines it by boundary markers: the town of Kajaṅgala in the east, the river Salalavatī in the south-east, the town of Setakaṇṇika in the south, the brahmin village of Thūṇa in the west and the mountain Usīraddhaja in the north. Monks living outside this region, in the “border countries”, were allowed relaxations of certain rules—for instance, ordination by a smaller number of monks, and the use of sandals and leather mats. The Buddhist Middle Country lay further east than the Brahmanical Madhyadeśa, centred on Magadha and Kosala rather than the Gaṅgā–Yamunā Doab: each tradition placed the normative centre in its own heartland.

docs.title: 12.2.3 The Five Divisions and Rājaśekhara’s Geography for Poets
docs.text:
The Purāṇas describe a five-fold division: the Middle Country, and the eastern (Prācya or Pūrvadeśa), southern (Dakṣiṇāpatha), western (Aparānta or Paścāddeśa) and northern (Udīcya or Uttarāpatha) regions. Varāhamihira’s Kūrmavibhāga instead uses nine divisions, the Middle Country and the eight directions, laid out as if on the body of a tortoise (Section 3.4).

The fullest statement of the five-fold scheme is by Rājaśekhara, a poet and dramatist at the court of the Gurjara-Pratīhāra kings of Kanauj in the early tenth century, in the chapter on the division of places (deśavibhāga) of his Kāvyamīmāṃsā, a manual for poets. He fixes the divisions by boundary points: the eastern country lies beyond Vārāṇasī, the southern road beyond Māhiṣmatī on the Narmadā, the western country beyond Devasabhā (whose site is uncertain), and the northern road beyond Pṛthūdaka (Pehowa, near Kurukṣetra). Between them lies the Middle Country, and at its heart the Antarvedī, the land between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā from Vinaśana to Prayāga. For each division he then names its countries, mountains, rivers and products. The purpose is literary: a poet’s descriptions must be true to place and season, and a companion chapter treats the seasons in the same way. But the result is a compact regional geography of India as seen from Kanauj, and historians have used its lists in identifying the names of early medieval regions (Sircar 1971; Law 1954).

Such schemes organised the peoples and places of India around a centre in the Gaṅgā–Yamunā region, and they tell us as much about the viewpoint of their authors as about the land. The regions that later took shape on the ground, and the names they acquired, are the subject of the rest of this chapter.

docs.title: 12.3 The Geography of Empire in the Inscriptions
docs.text: The earliest documents that describe the territory of an Indian state as a whole are inscriptions.

docs.title: 12.3.1 Aśoka
docs.text:
The edicts of Aśoka (c. 268–232 BCE) are themselves a map of his empire. Versions of the Major Rock Edicts were engraved at the edges of the realm: at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra in the north-west, in the Kharoṣṭhī script; at Kalsi in the Himalayan foothills; at Girnar in Saurashtra; at Sopara on the Konkan coast; at Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha; at Erragudi in Andhra and Sannati in Karnataka; and, in Greek and Aramaic, at Kandahar in Afghanistan. The Minor Rock Edicts are found from Bairat and Sasaram in the north to Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, where they are most numerous. Most call the king only by his titles, devānaṃpiya and piyadasi; at least four of them—at Maski, Nittur and Udegolam in Karnataka and Gujarra in Madhya Pradesh—also give his personal name, Aśoka, and it was the discovery of the Maski inscription in 1915 that confirmed the identification of Piyadasi with the Aśoka of the Buddhist chronicles. Their distribution shows an empire that reached from Afghanistan to the borders of the Tamil country and was held together by roads that carried officials and royal messages to its frontiers.

The edicts also reveal its provincial structure. Princes (kumāra, āryaputra) governed from Takṣaśilā in the north-west, Ujjayinī in the west, Suvarṇagiri in the south and Tosalī in conquered Kaliṅga, and officials (mahāmātra) were posted at Tosalī and Samāpā; the Separate Rock Edicts of Dhauli and Jaugada are addressed to them. The location of Suvarṇagiri is uncertain. The Rock Edicts name the officials who toured the districts (rājūka, prādeśika), and they distinguish three kinds of people at or beyond the edges of the realm: the forest peoples (aṭavī) within it, whom Aśoka warns as well as conciliates in the thirteenth Rock Edict; the peoples of the borderlands within the realm, among them Yonas, Kambojas, Andhras and Pulindas; and the independent neighbours, the Coḍas, Paṇḍiyas, Satiyaputas and Keralaputas of the south, Tambapaṃṇi (Sri Lanka), and the Hellenistic kings of the west, whom the second and thirteenth Rock Edicts name (Thapar 2002).

docs.title: 12.3.2 Samudragupta
docs.text: The praise-poem (praśasti) of the Gupta king Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE), composed by his minister Hariṣeṇa and engraved on an Aśokan pillar now at Prayagraj (the “Allahabad pillar”), describes the king’s conquests as a set of concentric zones. In Āryāvarta, the northern plain, nine kings were violently uprooted and their lands annexed. In Dakṣiṇāpatha twelve kings, among them the rulers of Kosala, Mahākāntāra, Piṣṭapura, Kāñcī and Veṅgī, were captured and then released and reinstated. All the kings of the forest country (āṭavika) were made servants. The frontier kingdoms (pratyanta) of Samataṭa, Ḍavāka, Kāmarūpa, Nepāla and Kartṛpura paid tribute and homage, as did a series of peoples of the west and north-west, among them the Mālavas, Yaudheyas, Mādrakas and Ābhīras. Beyond them were distant rulers, including the Kuṣāṇa “son of god”, the Śakas and the people of Siṃhala, who sent embassies and gifts. Whatever its exaggerations, the inscription is a political geography of the fourth-century subcontinent: a core of directly ruled territory, a ring of tributaries, a forest zone and a frontier of independent peoples (Thapar 2002; Sircar 1971).

docs.title: 12.3.3 Rudradāman
docs.text: A third inscription gives the territory of a western Indian king. On the rock at Girnar that already bore Aśoka’s edicts, the Western Kṣatrapa (Śaka) ruler Rudradāman recorded in 150 CE the repair of the Sudarśana lake (Chapter 9), and listed the lands he ruled: eastern and western Ākara and Avanti, Anūpa, Ānarta, Surāṣṭra, Śvabhra, Maru, Kaccha, Sindhu–Sauvīra, Kukura, Aparānta and Niṣāda—that is, roughly Malwa, the Narmadā valley, northern Gujarat, Saurashtra, the Sabarmatī country, the desert, Kutch, the lower Indus, the Konkan and the forest country of the Niṣādas, together with Kukura, whose location is uncertain. Several of these names were still in use a thousand years later.

docs.title: 12.3.4 The Conquest of the Quarters
docs.text:
What the inscriptions claim for real kings, literature claimed for ideal ones. The digvijaya, the “conquest of the quarters”, is a literary form in which a king marches in turn to each direction and receives the submission of its peoples, so that the narrative becomes a tour of the known world. In the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata, Yudhiṣṭhira’s brothers march in the four directions and receive tribute from long lists of peoples. In the fourth canto of Kālidāsa’s Raghuvaṃśa, King Raghu marches east to the Suhmas and Vaṅgas of Bengal, crosses the Kapiśā into Utkala and Kaliṅga, goes south to the Kāverī, the Pāṇḍyas, the Malaya and Kerala, turns west to the Aparānta coast, goes by land against the Pārasīkas, fights the Hūṇas on the banks of the Vaṅkṣu (the Oxus; some manuscripts read Sindhu), subdues the Kambojas and the mountain peoples of the Himālaya, and returns through Prāgjyotiṣa and Kāmarūpa. The canto is a poetic survey of the world as seen from the Gupta court, organised, like Samudragupta’s inscription, as a centre and its circuit.

The same lists show how the lands beyond the subcontinent were known: mainly by the names of their peoples. The Yavanas (originally Ionian Greeks, later westerners in general), Śakas (Scythians), Pahlavas (Parthians), Pārasīkas (Persians), Hūṇas, Cīnas (Chinese), the Romaka (Rome or Byzantium) and the people of Suvarṇabhūmi appear in epics, law books, astronomical texts and inscriptions. Some names reflect real knowledge of distant states; others had become stock lists of outsiders (mleccha).

docs.title: 12.4 Divisions of the Kingdom
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra gives an ideal scheme. Its chapter on settling the countryside (2.1) tells the king to found villages of between one hundred and five hundred families, their boundaries marked by rivers, hills, forests, ravines, embankments and trees, and to arrange a hierarchy of administrative centres: a sthānīya for every eight hundred villages, a droṇamukha for four hundred, a khārvaṭika for two hundred and a saṃgrahaṇa for every ten (Olivelle 2013). The scheme is symmetrical, like much of the text, but it shows how a theorist of the state thought about organising territory: by counting settlements, fixing boundaries and placing centres at regular levels. The records of actual kingdoms are less tidy.

From the Gupta period onward, thousands of copper-plate grants record gifts of land to Brahmins, temples and monasteries. Because a grant had to identify the land precisely, it located the village within the administrative divisions of the kingdom, and these formulas are the main evidence for how territory was organised. Sircar’s Indian Epigraphical Glossary and his studies of the geography of the inscriptions collect the terms (Sircar 1966, 1971). Table 12.2 gives the main hierarchies.

Table 12.2. Territorial divisions in Indian inscriptions and records (largest unit first) State and period Units Officials and notes Maurya (3rd c. BCE) provinces under princes; districts; villages kumāra, mahāmātra, rājūka, prādeśika Gupta, north India and Bengal (4th–6th c.) deśa or bhukti \(\rightarrow\) viṣaya \(\rightarrow\) vīthī \(\rightarrow\) grāma uparika over a bhukti; viṣayapati with a district council (adhikaraṇa) Pāla and Sena, Bengal (8th–12th c.) bhukti \(\rightarrow\) maṇḍala \(\rightarrow\) viṣaya \(\rightarrow\) grāma the relative order of maṇḍala and viṣaya varies between grants; old units such as Puṇḍravardhana-bhukti persist for centuries Rāṣṭrakūṭa, Deccan (8th–10th c.) rāṣṭra \(\rightarrow\) viṣaya \(\rightarrow\) bhukti \(\rightarrow\) grāma rāṣṭrapati, viṣayapati; here the bhukti is a small unit Cālukya and Hoysaḷa, Karnataka (10th–13th c.) divisions bearing conventional numbers: Gaṅgavāḍi 96,000, Nolambavāḍi 32,000, Banavāsi 12,000; smaller units of 300 or 70 the meaning of the numbers is debated Cōḻa, Tamil country (10th–13th c.) maṇḍalam \(\rightarrow\) vaḷanāḍu \(\rightarrow\) nāḍu \(\rightarrow\) ūr vaḷanāḍus created under Rājarāja I; assemblies of the nāḍu (nāṭṭār) and the village Delhi Sultanate (13th–15th c.) iqṭāʿ or wilāyat \(\rightarrow\) shiqq \(\rightarrow\) pargana \(\rightarrow\) village muqṭiʿ holding an assignment; terms varied over time Mughal (from 1580) ṣūba \(\rightarrow\) sarkār \(\rightarrow\) pargana (maḥal) \(\rightarrow\) mauẓaʿ governor and dīwān; faujdār; qānūngo and chaudhurī (Chapter 7) Maratha (17th–18th c.) prānt \(\rightarrow\) sarkār \(\rightarrow\) pargaṇā or tarf \(\rightarrow\) mauje units largely inherited from the Deccan sultanates British India presidency or province \(\rightarrow\) division \(\rightarrow\) district \(\rightarrow\) tahsīl or tāluk \(\rightarrow\) village collector and commissioner; many districts follow Mughal sarkārs

Three features of this vocabulary are worth noting. First, the same word could mean different things in different kingdoms: the bhukti was a province in Gupta Bengal but a small unit in the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Deccan. Secondly, units were often named after their chief town or an old people, and such names outlived the states that created them; the Puṇḍravardhana-bhukti of the Gupta plates is still named in Sena grants some seven centuries later. Thirdly, in many regions the smaller units were older than the kingdoms that listed them. The Tamil nāḍu, a cluster of villages forming a natural agrarian locality with its own assembly, appears to have existed before the Cōḻas and to have persisted under them; Y. Subbarayalu mapped the nāḍus of the Cōḻa country from inscriptions, and Burton Stein argued that they, rather than the royal centre, were the basic units of medieval South Indian society (Subbarayalu 1973; Stein 1980). Stein’s wider model of a “segmentary state” has been much criticised, but the importance of the nāḍu is generally accepted.

The numbered divisions of medieval Karnataka are a puzzle of their own. Inscriptions speak of “Gaṅgavāḍi Ninety-six Thousand” or “Banavāsi Twelve Thousand” as standing names. The figures are too round, and too stable over centuries, to be counts of villages at the time of writing; they may have begun as notional revenue or village figures attached to a territory and then become part of its name (Sircar 1971). Something similar may lie behind the Aihole inscription of 634, which credits the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II with lordship over “the three Mahārāṣṭrakas” containing ninety-nine thousand villages.

docs.title: 12.5 How the Regions Got Their Names
docs.text:
The historical regions of the subcontinent took their names from peoples, from dynasties, from landforms, and in a few cases from foreign usage. Figure 12.1 places the principal older names approximately on a map.

Figure 12.1. Historical regions of the subcontinent and their older names. The names belong to different periods, from the janapadas of the first millennium BCE to the regional kingdoms of the first millennium CE, and are placed only approximately at the centre of each region; regions had no fixed boundaries, and none are drawn. Gandhāra and Kaśmīra lie north of the frame (about 34° N). The graticule is in degrees; the coastline is simplified, as on the other maps in this volume, and islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted.

docs.title: 12.5.1 The North and North-West
docs.text: Gandhāra, the Peshawar valley and the country east of the Indus around Takṣaśilā, and Kaśmīra are among the oldest regional names that are still in use, the first in the Vedic and Achaemenid record, the second in Pāṇini and the epics. The land of the five rivers was Pañcanada in Sanskrit; its modern name, Panjab or Punjab, is the Persian panj āb, “five waters”, which first became common in the Mughal period; other river names of regions, such as Antarvedī and the Persian doāb, are discussed in Chapter 9. Sindh preserves the name of the river, Sindhu, which also gave the world the words “Hindu” and “India” (Chapter 1).

docs.title: 12.5.2 The East
docs.text: Bihar takes its name from the Buddhist monasteries (vihāra) of the region, through the town of Bihar Sharif, whose name became that of the Mughal ṣūba. The older names—Magadha in the south of the province, Videha or Mithilā in the north—survive in literature, in the Maithili language and in cultural identity. The early regions of Bengal were several: Puṇḍra or Varendra north of the Gaṅgā, Rāḍha to the west, Vaṅga in the centre and east, and Samataṭa and Harikela in the south-east. The name of one of them, Vaṅga, came to stand for the whole: the Persian Bangāla became the name of the sultanate that Shams al-Dīn Ilyās Shāh united in the mid-fourteenth century, and then of the Mughal province (Chapter 7). Odisha keeps the name of the Oḍra people, beside the older Kaliṅga of Aśoka’s conquest and Utkala; Assam is usually derived from the name of the Ahom dynasty that ruled the Brahmaputra valley from the thirteenth century, while its classical names were Prāgjyotiṣa and Kāmarūpa.

docs.title: 12.5.3 The West and the Deccan
docs.text:
Gujarat is named after the Gurjaras, who ruled parts of western India from the sixth century; the Sanskrit Gurjaratrā, “the land protected by the Gurjaras”, became Gujarāt. Its older sub-regions, Ānarta in the north, Lāṭa in the south and Surāṣṭra (Saurashtra) in the peninsula, appear in Rudradāman’s inscription and survive as regional names. Rajasthan is a modern name. The colonial term “Rajputana”, the land of the Rajput states, was used from about 1800, and James Tod’s Annals and Antiquities of Rajast’han (1829–32) popularised the form that the new state adopted when the Rajput states were united after 1947; older names, Maru (the desert, as in Marwar), Mewāṛ and others, named its parts. Avanti, the country of Ujjayinī, became Mālava, Malwa, after the Mālava people who are thought to have moved there from the north-west in the last centuries BCE.

Maharashtra appears in the Aihole inscription of 634 and in the name of the Prakrit of the region, Mahārāṣṭrī; its sub-regions included Vidarbha in the east and Aparānta, the Konkan coast. The word Deccan itself is the Prakrit dakkhiṇa, Sanskrit dakṣiṇa, “south”.

docs.title: 12.5.4 The South
docs.text: The Andhras are named in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa among peoples beyond the Brahmanical pale, and Āndhra is the name of the Telugu country in Sanskrit. A second name, Tiliṅga or Teliṅgāṇa, is attested in inscriptions and in Persian chronicles of the Delhi Sultanate (Tilang) and survives in Telangana; Cynthia Talbot has shown how a sense of a Telugu region took shape under the Kākatīyas of Warangal in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries (Talbot 2001). Karṇāṭa, of uncertain etymology, named the Kannada country. The Tamil land, Tamiḻakam, was defined in the preface to the Tolkāppiyam as the region between Vēṅkaṭam (the Tirupati hills) in the north and Kumari in the south, and was divided among the three ancient kingdoms of the Cēras, Cōḻas and Pāṇḍyas. Their names appear already in Aśoka’s edicts, and the Cōḻamaṇḍalam, “the realm of the Cōḻas”, gave Europeans the name of the whole south-eastern coast, Coromandel. Kerala is the Keralaputa of Aśoka; the Arabic and Persian name of its coast was Malabar.

docs.title: 12.6 Homelands in the Regional Literatures
docs.text:
Names given by kings and grammarians are only half the story. From the late first millennium onward, the literatures of the regional languages began to describe their own lands as homelands, defined by the language spoken in them, by their rivers and shrines, and by stories of their origin. These are Cohn’s “subjective” regions in the making, and Sheldon Pollock has placed them within a wider shift, between about the ninth and the fourteenth centuries, in which regional languages became languages of literature and of political expression alongside Sanskrit (Pollock 2006).

  • Kannada. The Kavirājamārga (“The Royal Road of Poets”), a work on poetics written at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court in the mid-ninth century, describes the land in which Kannada is spoken as stretching from the Kāverī to the Godāvarī, and praises the skill of its people in speech. The definition is literary, not administrative, and it reached further north than the Kannada-speaking area of later centuries; but it is one of the earliest statements in any Indian language that a land is defined by its language.

  • Tamil. The Cilappatikāram, the Tamil epic of Kaṇṇaki and Kōvalaṉ, is divided into three books named after the capitals of the three Tamil kingdoms—Pukār of the Cōḻas, Madurai of the Pāṇḍyas and Vañci of the Cēras—so that the story travels across the whole Tamil land. Together with the Tolkāppiyam’s definition of Tamiḻakam, it presents the Tamil country as a single cultural world divided among several kingdoms. This idea was taken up with new force in the Tamil movements of the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

  • Telugu. A popular tradition derives the name of the Telugu country from Trilinga, “three liṅgas”, and describes it as the land bounded by the Śaiva shrines of Śrīśailam, Kāleśvaram and Drākṣārāmam. The etymology is doubtful, but the tradition defines a region by the sacred places at its corners, much as Hindu sacred geography defined the whole of India by the four dhāms (Chapter 4).

  • Marathi. The Mahānubhāva texts of the thirteenth century, beginning with the Līḷācaritra (Chapter 1), give special value to Maharashtra as the land in which Cakradhara lived and taught. Anne Feldhaus has shown how, in later centuries, river goddesses, pilgrimages and festival processions connected places across the Marathi-speaking country and gave its people a sense of belonging to a common region (Feldhaus 2003).

  • Kerala and the Konkan. The Malayalam Kēraḷōlpatti (“The Origin of Kerala”), a traditional history compiled in the early modern period, tells how Paraśurāma threw his axe into the sea and raised the land of Kerala from the water, and how he settled it with Brahmins in sixty-four villages. A similar story is told of the Konkan coast in the Sahyādrikhaṇḍa. Such origin stories explained the narrow coastal strip between the mountains and the sea, and they also served to justify the privileges of the Brahmin landholders who told them.

  • Kashmir and Odisha. The Nīlamata Purāṇa gives Kashmir an origin story of its own, the draining of a primeval lake (Chapter 10).
