In Odisha the cult of Jagannātha at Purī, whose great temple was built in the twelfth century, became the centre of a regional identity; from the thirteenth century the Gaṅga kings presented the god as the true ruler of the land and themselves as his deputies (Chapter 4).

These literary and religious definitions did not draw lines on a map, and they overlapped and competed. But they are the deeper background of the linguistic states described at the end of this chapter: when the language movements of the twentieth century demanded states for Telugu, Kannada, Marathi or Malayalam speakers, they could appeal to homelands that their literatures had been describing for centuries.

docs.title: 12.7 Place-Names as Historical Geography
docs.text:
Place-names are among the most durable records of settlement. Nundo Lal Dey’s dictionary identified the ancient names of thousands of places, and H. D. Sankalia showed for Gujarat how the place-names and personal names of inscriptions could be used to reconstruct the history of settlement and the movement of peoples (Dey 1927; Sankalia 1949). Many names contain an element describing the kind of place, and these elements form layers that correspond to languages and periods (Table 12.3).

Table 12.3. Some common elements in Indian place-names Element Language Meaning Examples -pura, -pur Sanskrit town, stronghold Jaipur, Nagpur, Kanpur -nagara, -nagar Sanskrit city Srinagar, Ahmadnagar -grāma, -gaon, -gām Sanskrit and its descendants village Goregaon, Jalgaon -kheṭa, -kheḍ Sanskrit and its descendants village, small town Mānyakheṭa (Malkhed), Kheda -ūr, -ūru Tamil, Kannada, Telugu settlement Tañcāvūr, Nellore, Bengaluru -paṭṭaṇam, -patnam Dravidian, from Sanskrit pattana town, often a port Visakhapatnam, Nāgapaṭṭiṉam -pāḷaiyam, -palayam Tamil camp, fortified settlement Mettupalayam -kōṭṭai, -kot Tamil; Indo-Aryan fort Pudukkottai, Sialkot -ābād Persian settled, founded place Ahmadabad, Hyderabad, Aurangabad -ganj Persian market, granary Daryaganj, Hazratganj -sarāy Persian caravan inn Sarai Rohilla, Mughalsarai -bandar Persian port Porbandar

The layers can be read like strata. In the Tamil country, names in -ūr and -kuppam (a hamlet, often of fishers) are older and more local than the Sanskritised temple-town names that accompanied Brahmin settlement and royal patronage. Elsewhere the Persian names of the Sultanate and Mughal periods record the foundation of new towns by rulers and nobles: Ahmadabad by the Gujarat sultan Aḥmad Shāh in 1411, Hyderabad by the Quṭb Shāhīs in 1591, Aurangabad and Farrukhabad in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, and Ilāhābās, later Ilāhābād (Allahabad), by Akbar at Prayāga. Colonial rule added cantonments, civil lines and hill stations named after officials (Dalhousie, Lansdowne, Abbottabad, Jacobabad), and market towns with the Persian suffix attached to English names (Daltonganj, McCluskieganj). Since 1947 many of these names have been replaced and older or local forms restored (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 12.8 Provinces of the Sultans, Mughals, Marathas and Nāyakas
docs.text:
The Delhi sultans governed through assignments (iqṭāʿ) of the revenue of territories to military commanders, who were moved from one assignment to another (Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra); the assignment was a unit of revenue and command before it was a province with fixed boundaries. Under Muḥammad ibn Tughluq the sultanate was described as a set of twenty-three provinces (Chapter 7), and below them the pargana, a cluster of villages around a small market town (qaṣba), emerged as the basic local unit. The pargana proved the most durable of all Indian administrative units. It passed through the Sūr and Mughal administrations, was used by the Marathas and other successor states, and survived into British India, where many tahsīls and tāluks corresponded to one or more old parganas. The name of the West Bengal districts of North and South Twenty-Four Parganas recalls the zamīndārī of twenty-four parganas south of Calcutta granted to the East India Company in 1757.

Akbar’s division of the empire into ṣūbas in 1580 created provinces with fixed seats and boundaries, many of which corresponded to older regions: Bengal, Bihar, Gujarat, Malwa, Awadh, and Kashmir, conquered in 1586 and attached to the province of Kabul. The Mughal ṣūbas in turn became the starting point of the eighteenth-century successor states—Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad—and so of several British provinces.

In the Deccan the Marathas distinguished their home territory, svarājya, from the lands of others from which they claimed a quarter of the revenue (chauth) and an additional tenth (sardeśmukhī). Their administration took over the units of the Deccan sultanates and the Mughals, and their expansion in the eighteenth century produced a patchwork of directly ruled districts, shares of revenue in others’ territory and semi-independent houses at Baroda, Indore, Gwalior and Nagpur (Gordon 1993). In the south, the Vijayanagara kings assigned territories to commanders (nāyakas) who held them in return for military service; after the empire’s decline the nāyakas of Madurai, Thanjavur and Gingee became kings, and the Madurai nāyakas divided their country among pāḷaiyakkārars (“poligars”), chiefs of fortified camps (pāḷaiyam), whose territories became the zamīndārīs of the colonial period.

docs.title: 12.9 Boundaries and Frontiers
docs.text:
Indian law and administration knew the village boundary (sīmā) in great detail. A copper-plate grant described the land it conveyed by its four boundaries (catuḥsīmā), naming the neighbouring villages, streams, tanks, trees and hillocks on each side. The Manusmṛti, in its title on boundary disputes (8.245 ff.), tells the king to fix boundaries by visible markers such as large trees, ponds, wells, streams and shrines, and also by hidden markers buried in the ground—stones, bones, ashes, potsherds, charcoal, bricks—so that a boundary could be proved when the visible signs were lost; disputes were to be settled by the testimony of neighbours and elders (Olivelle 2005). The Tamil and Kannada inscriptions that record boundary walks by village elders, and the Cōḻa surveys (Chapter 5), show such rules in practice.

The edges of kingdoms were different. Between the core lands of states lay zones of forest, hill and desert, inhabited by peoples who were often outside the control of any king. The Arthaśāstra prescribes fortified posts at the frontiers, under frontier commanders (antapāla), and the settlement of forest peoples in the borderlands (Olivelle 2013), and both Aśoka and Samudragupta distinguished the forest peoples from their subjects and their neighbours. A pre-modern frontier was usually a zone, and the allegiance of the chiefs within it shifted with the power of the states on either side.

docs.title: 12.9.1 The Maṇḍala of States
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra’s theory of the “circle” (maṇḍala) of states is a spatial theory of foreign relations. The king who seeks to conquer (vijigīṣu) is imagined at the centre; the state on his border is his natural enemy (ari), the state beyond that is the enemy’s enemy and therefore his natural friend (mitra), and so on outward through the enemy’s friend (arimitra) and the friend’s friend (mitramitra). Behind the would-be conqueror lie his rear enemy (pārṣṇigrāha) and his rear ally (ākranda); beyond the circle stand the “middle” king (madhyama), bordering both the conqueror and his enemy, and the “neutral” king (udāsīna), more powerful than either (Arthaśāstra 6.2; (Olivelle 2013)). The scheme is abstract. Real states were not arranged in neat rings, and the text itself treats the circle as a model for reasoning about alliances. It is sometimes compared with modern geopolitical theories; such comparisons are analogies, not evidence of priority.

docs.title: 12.9.2 Moving Frontiers of Settlement
docs.text:
Many of the most important frontiers were internal: the edges between cultivated plain and forest, between settled villages and the hill and forest peoples. Sumit Guha has argued that for most of the second millennium the relation across these edges was one of exchange as well as conflict. Forest peoples supplied states and markets with elephants, timber, lac, honey, hides and soldiers; kings recruited them, married into their leading families and recognised their chiefs; and forest polities such as the Gond kingdoms of Garha-Mandla, Deogarh and Chanda in central India grew up within the forest zone itself (Guha 1999). The line between “tribe” and “caste”, and between forest and field, moved in both directions as land was cleared, abandoned and cleared again.

The clearest case of a frontier moving in one direction is the Bengal delta. As the main flow of the Gaṅgā shifted eastward towards the Padmā (Chapter 9), the active part of the delta, with its fresh silt and annual flooding, moved east as well. From the late sixteenth century the Mughal administration encouraged the clearing of the forested eastern delta for wet-rice cultivation by granting land to pioneers, many of them associated with mosques and shrines. Richard Eaton has shown how this agrarian frontier, rather than conquest, shaped both the settlement map and the religious map of eastern Bengal (Eaton 1993); the religious side of the story is told in Volume 24, Samanvaya.

Colonial rule hardened these internal frontiers into lines. The Indian Forest Acts of 1865 and 1878 allowed the government to declare large areas reserved or protected forest, with boundaries surveyed and marked on the ground, and to restrict or forbid cultivation, grazing and the collection of forest produce within them. Shifting cultivators, herders and forest peoples who had used the land under customary arrangements found themselves on the wrong side of a mapped boundary. The consequences, including the long struggle for forest rights that led to the Forest Rights Act of 2006, are treated in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

The linear boundary drawn on a map was largely a colonial creation. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries British India fixed its external limits by survey and treaty: the Durand Line with Afghanistan (1893), and in the east the McMahon Line proposed at the Simla Conference of 1913–14, which China did not accept. Lord Curzon, viceroy from 1899 to 1905, made the distinction between frontier zones and boundary lines the theme of a lecture on “Frontiers” in 1907. The partition of 1947 drew the most consequential lines of all. The Boundary Commissions for the Punjab and Bengal, chaired by Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India before, divided provinces, districts and irrigation systems within a few weeks; the award was published two days after independence, and the partition was accompanied by violence and by the displacement of a population usually estimated at between ten and fifteen million people (Chester 2009). The disputes over several of the boundaries drawn or proposed in this period have continued since.

docs.title: 12.10 From Presidencies to Linguistic States
docs.text:
British India grew out of the three presidencies of Bengal, Madras and Bombay, centred on the Company’s fortified settlements at Calcutta, Madras and Bombay. As its territory expanded, new provinces were formed from conquered or annexed lands: the North-Western Provinces (1836), the Punjab (annexed 1849), the Central Provinces (1861), Assam (separated from Bengal in 1874) and others. Their boundaries followed the accidents of conquest and administrative convenience rather than language or culture: the Madras Presidency included speakers of Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada, and the Bombay Presidency those of Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada and Sindhi. Interspersed with the provinces were some five hundred and sixty princely states (the total depends on how the smallest estates are counted; (Menon 1956)), from Hyderabad, as large as a European kingdom, to estates of a few villages in Kathiawar, which covered about two-fifths of the subcontinent and were ruled under British paramountcy.

The first partition of Bengal (1905), which created a province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, provoked the Swadeshi movement and was reversed in 1911, when the capital was moved from Calcutta to Delhi and Bihar and Orissa became a separate province (1912). In 1936 Orissa became the first province formed on the basis of language, and Sind was separated from Bombay in the same year. The Indian National Congress had reorganised its own provincial committees on linguistic lines in 1920, and the demand for linguistic provinces became part of the national movement.

After independence the princely states were integrated, most of them by accession in 1947 and by mergers into new unions in 1948–49, a process directed by Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon (Menon 1956). The government was at first reluctant to redraw boundaries by language. The death of Potti Sriramulu after a fast in December 1952, in support of a Telugu-speaking state, led to the creation of Andhra State in 1953, and a States Reorganisation Commission was appointed. Its report (1955) accepted language as the main, though not the only, basis for states, and the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew the map of southern and western India (States Reorganisation Commission 1955; King 1997). Table 12.4 summarises the main changes since then.

Table 12.4. The main reorganisations of Indian states since independence Year Change 1947–50 Integration of the princely states; the Constitution (1950) groups states into Parts A–D 1953 Andhra State formed from the Telugu-speaking districts of Madras State 1956 States Reorganisation Act: fourteen states and six union territories; Andhra Pradesh and Kerala formed, Mysore and Bombay enlarged, and Hyderabad State divided 1960 Bombay State divided into Maharashtra and Gujarat 1963 Nagaland becomes a state 1966 Punjab divided: Haryana formed, hill districts transferred to Himachal Pradesh, Chandigarh a union territory 1971–72 Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya become states 1975 Sikkim joins India as a state 1987 Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa become states 2000 Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand (then Uttaranchal) and Jharkhand formed 2014 Telangana separated from Andhra Pradesh 2019–20 Jammu and Kashmir reorganised as two union territories (Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh); Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu merged

The linguistic states rest on a map of languages that was itself a product of colonial survey, Grierson’s Linguistic Survey of India and the census (Chapter 14), and on a century of movements for the dignity of the regional languages; Lisa Mitchell has traced how Telugu came to be imagined as a “mother tongue” requiring a territory of its own (Mitchell 2009). Language was never the only principle. Bombay was kept bilingual until the Samyukta Maharashtra movement forced its division in 1960; the Punjabi Suba movement for a Punjabi-speaking state combined language with religious identity; the north-eastern states were created to recognise the distinct identities of their peoples; and the states formed in 2000 were justified less by language than by Adivasi identity, regional neglect and the distinct character of hill and forest regions. Several states have also restored older names: Madras State became Tamil Nadu (1969), Mysore became Karnataka (1973) and Orissa was renamed Odisha (2011).

The result is a map in which many of the historical regions described in this chapter—Gujarat, Maharashtra, Bengal, Odisha, Kerala, the Tamil and Telugu countries—have, for the first time, become political units with fixed boundaries. It is a modern creation built on old foundations.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On historical regions and their names, Sircar (1971), Law (1954) and Schwartzberg (1978); on regional geography, Spate (1954) and Subbarao (1958); on the making of regions, Cohn (1967), Chattopadhyaya (1994), Kulke (1995) and Talbot (2001); on regional homelands in literature and pilgrimage, Pollock (2006) and Feldhaus (2003); on South Indian localities, Subbarayalu (1973) and Stein (1980); on the Marathas, Gordon (1993); on partition boundaries, Chester (2009); on the integration and reorganisation of states, Menon (1956), States Reorganisation Commission (1955) and King (1997).

docs.title: Chapter 13: Indians Abroad: Merchants, Monks, Sailors and Travellers
docs.text: Indian geographical horizons were never limited to the subcontinent. Merchants and sailors from India traded across the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea from at least the last centuries BCE; Buddhist monks carried texts and teachings to Central Asia, China and Tibet; Indian pilgrims went to Mecca; and from the eighteenth century Indians travelled to Europe and wrote about what they saw. This chapter follows these journeys. It also addresses some exaggerated claims: that Indian “colonies” were planted across Southeast Asia, or that Indian sailors reached the Americas.

docs.title: 13.1.1 Early Contacts
docs.text: Archaeology shows that the Bay of Bengal was crossed regularly by the late first millennium BCE. At sites such as Khao Sam Kaeo in peninsular Thailand, Indian-style pottery, beads of carnelian and agate made with Indian techniques, and other objects date from the fourth to second centuries BCE; at Óc Eo in the Mekong delta, a port of the kingdom the Chinese called Funan, Indian, Roman and Chinese objects were found together. The Pali Mahāniddesa, a canonical commentary of the early centuries CE, lists among the places that merchants visited in search of wealth Suvaṇṇabhūmi (“Land of Gold”), Takkola, Java and Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka). Sanskrit sources speak also of Suvarṇadvīpa (“Island of Gold”). These names refer broadly to mainland and island Southeast Asia; their exact application varied and is still debated. A Sri Lankan Buddhist tradition holds that Aśoka sent the monks Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, which Burmese and Thai tradition each identify with their own land. Himanshu Prabha Ray has shown how closely the early sea routes were bound up with the spread of Buddhist monasteries and their lay patrons (Ray 1994).

docs.title: 13.1.2 Sanskrit, Kingship and Temples
docs.text:
From about the fourth and fifth centuries CE, Sanskrit inscriptions appear in Southeast Asia: the sacrificial-post inscriptions of King Mūlavarman at Kutai in Borneo, the inscriptions of Pūrṇavarman of Tārumānagara in western Java, and others in Champa and Cambodia. Rulers took Sanskrit names, patronised Brahmins and Buddhist monks, and built temples to Śiva, Viṣṇu and the Buddha. Over the following centuries this tradition produced Angkor, Borobudur, Prambanan and My Son.

George Coedès called this process “Indianisation” and attributed it largely to Indian merchants and Brahmins (Coedès 1968). Later scholars have emphasised the initiative of Southeast Asian rulers, who selected and adapted Indian ideas to their own purposes, and the two-way nature of the exchange; the terms “localisation” and “convergence” are sometimes preferred. There is no evidence of Indian conquest or colonisation in Southeast Asia before the Cōḻa expedition of the eleventh century, and the older idea of “Indian colonies” has been abandoned (Kulke et al. 2009).

docs.title: 13.1.3 Śrīvijaya and the Cōḻas
docs.text:
Śrīvijaya, centred on Palembang in Sumatra, controlled the Straits of Malacca from the late seventh century and was a major Buddhist centre where, as Yijing reported, monks studied Sanskrit (Chapter 6). Its rulers had close ties with India: a copper-plate grant of the Pāla king Devapāla (ninth century) records the endowment of a monastery at Nālandā built by Bālaputradeva, king of Suvarṇadvīpa, and the Larger Leiden plates record the grant of a village by the Cōḻa king Rājarāja I to the Buddhist monastery that the Śailendra king of Śrīvijaya had built at Nāgapaṭṭiṉam.

Relations changed under Rājarāja’s son Rājendra I (r. 1012–1044). Around 1025 a Cōḻa naval expedition attacked Śrīvijaya and a series of ports in Sumatra and the Malay peninsula; Rājendra’s inscriptions list Kaḍāram (Kedah), Śrīvijaya, Malaiyūr, Takkolam, Mānakkavāram (the Nicobars) and others. Historians debate the motives—whether the raid aimed to protect Tamil merchants’ access to the Straits and the China trade, to punish Śrīvijayan restrictions, or to display royal power—but agree that it was a raid rather than a lasting conquest (Kulke et al. 2009). Tamil merchant guilds were active in the region before and after: a Tamil inscription of the Maṇigrāmam at Takua Pa in southern Thailand dates from the ninth century, and a Tamil inscription of the “Five Hundred” merchant body, dated 1088, was found at Barus in Sumatra.

docs.title: 13.1.4 Indian Merchants in China and the Straits
docs.text: Indian merchants also reached China. At Quanzhou, the great port of southern China in the Song and Yuan periods, a Tamil inscription dated 1281 records the founding of a Śiva temple by a Tamil merchant, and Hindu sculptures from temples of this period survive in the city. In the fifteenth century Malacca became the main entrepôt of the Straits; the Portuguese apothecary Tomé Pires, writing shortly after the Portuguese conquest of the city in 1511, reported that Gujarati merchants were the most numerous and important of the foreign traders there, alongside merchants from the Coromandel coast (the Keling) and Bengal. Indian cloth was the principal commodity exchanged for the spices of the archipelago.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Socotra and the Red Sea
docs.text: Indian sailors and merchants were present in the western Indian Ocean in the Roman period. The Periplus reports that the island of Dioscorida (Socotra) was inhabited by a mixture of Arabs, Indians and Greeks (Casson 1989). In the cave of Hoq on Socotra, explorers in 2000–01 found more than two hundred inscriptions and drawings left by visiting sailors between about the first and the fifth centuries CE; most are in Indian Brāhmī script and Indian languages, many by sailors from Gujarat (Strauch 2012). At the Egyptian Red Sea ports of Berenike and Myos Hormos (Quseir al-Qadim), excavations have found sherds with short Tamil-Brāhmī inscriptions, Indian pottery and large quantities of black pepper (Tomber 2008).

docs.title: 13.2.2 East Africa
docs.text: The Periplus lists Indian cloth, grain, rice, ghee, sesame oil and sugar among the goods brought to the Horn of Africa and the East African coast (Azania), and ivory, tortoise-shell and rhinoceros horn among the exports from there. In the medieval period the Swahili towns of the East African coast traded with Arabia, Persia and India. A recent study of ancient DNA from medieval Swahili burials found that their Asian ancestry came mainly from Persia, with a smaller contribution from India (Brielle et al. 2023). From the sixteenth century, and especially in the nineteenth, Gujarati merchants and financiers were established in Mombasa, Zanzibar and other East African ports (Pearson 2003).

docs.title: 13.2.3 The Arabian Sea
docs.text: India’s links with the Gulf and Arabia are among the oldest of all: Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf, and Mesopotamian texts of the later third millennium BCE name a land called Meluhha, usually identified with the Indus region. In the medieval period Indian ships, merchants and goods were familiar in Aden, Hormuz and the Red Sea, and Arab, Persian and Jewish merchants lived in the ports of Gujarat and Malabar. The documents of the Cairo Geniza include letters of Jewish merchants of the eleventh and twelfth centuries who traded between Egypt, Aden and India and settled on the Malabar coast.

docs.title: 13.3 Central Asia and the Silk Roads
docs.text:
Overland, the north-west of the subcontinent was part of a wider world that included Afghanistan, Bactria and the oasis cities of the Tarim basin. Under the Kuṣāṇas (first to third centuries CE) an empire stretched from Bactria to the Gangetic plain. Buddhist monasteries spread along the routes north of the Hindu Kush, and Indian scripts and languages travelled with them: Gāndhārī Prakrit in Kharoṣṭhī script was used for administration in the kingdom of Kroraina in the Tarim basin in the third and fourth centuries, and Sanskrit Buddhist manuscripts have been found at Gilgit, Bamiyan, Kucha, Turfan and Dunhuang (Neelis 2011). The colossal Buddhas of Bamiyan, destroyed in 2001, stood on the route between Bactria and Gandhāra.

Indian merchants, monks and craftsmen took part in this traffic, along with Sogdian, Bactrian, Chinese and Persian traders. The knowledge it generated is preserved mainly in Chinese and Central Asian sources and in archaeology; Indian texts say comparatively little about the lands beyond the mountains. In later centuries the overland link continued through the trade of Multani and Punjabi merchants in Central Asia and Iran (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 13.4 The Question of the Americas
docs.text: Some popular books claim that Indian sailors reached the Americas before Columbus. The arguments usually rest on the presence of certain plants in both hemispheres, on supposed resemblances between Mesoamerican and Asian art or calendars, or on speculative readings of texts. There is no secure evidence for such contact. Some plants did cross between the hemispheres before 1492—the sweet potato reached Polynesia from South America, and the bottle gourd appears to have spread naturally or with the earliest human settlers—but these cases involve Polynesian voyaging or natural dispersal, not India. No Indian artefact has been found in a securely pre-Columbian context in the Americas, nor any American artefact in pre-Columbian India. The question should be regarded as settled in the negative unless new evidence appears.

docs.title: 13.5 Buddhist Monks Abroad
docs.text:
The transmission of Buddhism from India to Central Asia, China, Korea, Japan, Tibet and Southeast Asia was carried in large part by monks who travelled in both directions. Indian and Central Asian monks went to China as translators; Chinese, Korean and later Tibetan monks came to India as pilgrims and students (Chapter 6).

  • Kumārajīva (conventionally 344–413), born in Kucha to an Indian father and a Kuchean mother, was carried off from Kucha by a Chinese general in the 380s, held for many years at Liangzhou, and reached Chang’an only in 401, where he became one of the greatest translators of Buddhist texts into Chinese.

  • Paramārtha (499–569), from Ujjayinī, reached China in 546 and translated works of the Yogācāra school.

  • Bodhidharma, the legendary founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China, is said to have come from southern India around 500; his biography is largely legendary, and the stories linking him with martial arts are much later inventions.

  • Śāntarakṣita and, according to tradition, Padmasambhava went to Tibet in the eighth century; Atiśa Dīpaṅkara Śrījñāna (982–1054), from Bengal and Vikramaśīla, went to Tibet in 1042 and spent his last years there.

These journeys produced knowledge of routes and places in both directions. Tibetan records of Indian teachers, Chinese records of Indian monks, and the travel accounts of Chinese pilgrims together form a body of geographical knowledge of Buddhist Asia (Sen 2003). When Buddhism declined in India after the twelfth century, Indian Buddhist teachers continued to travel to Tibet and Nepal, and Tibetan pilgrims, such as Dharmasvāmin in the 1230s, continued to visit India.

docs.title: 13.5.1 Sri Lanka, Burma and the Theravāda Networks
docs.text: Monastic connections across the Bay of Bengal continued long after Buddhism declined in India. Sri Lanka became the centre of Theravāda Buddhism, and monks travelled between Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand and Cambodia to obtain valid ordination lineages and texts; in the eleventh century King Anawrahta of Pagan in Burma and King Vijayabāhu I of Sri Lanka exchanged monks and scriptures, and in the fifteenth century monks from Pegu were sent to Sri Lanka for reordination. These networks kept alive the memory of the Buddhist sacred places of India, to which pilgrims and royal missions continued to travel (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 13.5.2 Scholars
docs.text: Scholars travelled too. In the eighth century an Indian astronomer brought a Sanskrit astronomical text to the court of the caliph al-Manṣūr at Baghdad, where its Arabic version carried Indian methods and the meridian of Ujjayinī into Islamic astronomy (Section 3.2). How Sanskrit texts themselves named the peoples and lands beyond the subcontinent is described with the literary “conquest of the quarters” in Section 12.3.4.

docs.title: 13.6 Memory and Diplomacy
docs.text: The long history of Indian Ocean connections has become a resource for modern diplomacy and cultural policy. India’s Ministry of Culture launched Project Mausam in 2014 to study and promote the shared maritime heritage of the countries of the Indian Ocean, and governments of the region regularly invoke the monsoon trade, the spread of Buddhism and the Cōḻa voyages in speeches and exhibitions. Such uses of the past are understandable, but historians have cautioned against presenting the ancient connections as a story of Indian influence radiating outward. The evidence surveyed in this chapter shows a world of exchange in many directions, in which Indians were one group of travellers among many, and in which the peoples of Southeast Asia, East Africa and Arabia were active partners rather than passive recipients (Kulke et al. 2009).

docs.title: 13.7 Indian Travellers and Their Accounts
docs.text:
Pre-modern India produced few travel narratives of the kind written by Faxian or Ibn Baṭṭūṭa. Knowledge of distant lands was carried by merchants, sailors and pilgrims, but rarely written down as a personal narrative. The pilgrimage literature described in Chapter 4 is an exception of a different kind. From the eighteenth century, however, Indians began to write accounts of journeys abroad, first in Persian and later in English, Urdu, Bengali, Marathi and other languages (Khan 1998; Fisher 2004).

  • Mīrzā Iʿtiṣām al-Dīn, a Mughal official, travelled to Britain in 1765–68 as part of a mission to George III and described the journey in Persian in Shigarf-nāma-yi Wilāyat (“The Wonder-Book of Europe”).

  • Sake Dean Mahomed (1759–1851), from Patna, served in the East India Company’s army, moved to Ireland and England, and published The Travels of Dean Mahomet (1794), the first book written in English by an Indian.

  • Mīrzā Abū Ṭālib Khān (1752–c. 1805), from Lucknow, travelled through Europe in 1799–1803 and wrote a Persian account of Britain, Ireland and France, translated into English in 1810.

  • Nawab Sikandar Begum of Bhopal (r. 1860–68) made the Hajj in 1863–64 and wrote an account of the journey and of conditions in Arabia, published in English translation as A Pilgrimage to Mecca (1870)—one of the few pre-modern travel accounts by a woman from South Asia.

  • Pandita Ramabai (1858–1922), the Marathi scholar and reformer, travelled to Britain and the United States in the 1880s and published a Marathi account of American society (1889).

These writers looked at other lands from an Indian standpoint, comparing institutions, manners and religions. Their works are part of the history of Indian geographical knowledge as much as the foreign accounts of India discussed in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 13.7.1 Lascars
docs.text: From the seventeenth century many Indian seamen—known to Europeans as lascars, from the Persian lashkar—served on European ships, including those of the East India Company. By the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries thousands of them sailed to Britain and elsewhere each year; some were stranded in British ports, and small communities of Indian seamen grew up in London and other cities. They were poorly paid and often harshly treated, and their experiences are known mainly from official records and the reports of charities. They too were Indian travellers, whose knowledge of the sea and of distant ports was rarely written down (Fisher 2004).

docs.title: 13.7.2 Migration
docs.text: From the nineteenth century, migration carried millions of Indians abroad: as indentured labourers to Mauritius, the Caribbean, Fiji, Natal and Malaya (1834–1917), as soldiers of the British Indian army, as traders and professionals in East Africa and Southeast Asia, and later to the Gulf, Britain and North America. Letters, songs and memoirs of migrants record their own geography of distant places, often a painful one. Sunil Amrith has traced how, across the Bay of Bengal alone, millions of labourers moved between India, Burma, Malaya and Ceylon in the century before 1940, under the same monsoon that had governed the older trade (Amrith 2013). This later history lies beyond the scope of this volume.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On Southeast Asia: Coedès (1968) and Kulke et al. (2009). On the western Indian Ocean: Strauch (2012), Tomber (2008) and Pearson (2003). On Buddhist travel: Sen (2003). On Indian travellers to Europe: Khan (1998) and Fisher (2004).

docs.title: Chapter 14: Surveying the Subcontinent: Colonial Mapping and Its Legacy
docs.text: Between the 1760s and the 1880s the East India Company and then the British Crown carried out a series of surveys that produced, for the first time, a map of the whole subcontinent based on measurement. The Survey of India, which traces its origin to 1767, is still the national mapping agency. The story of these surveys has often been told as a heroic tale of European science. Recent historians have told it differently: as the making of an empire on paper, in which maps helped to define and control territory, and as a joint enterprise in which Indian assistants, informants, computers and explorers played essential roles that were long left out of the record (Edney 1997; Raj 2007). This chapter follows that history and then considers the place of the older traditions in modern India.

docs.title: 14.1 James Rennell and the First Maps of British India
docs.text:
James Rennell (1742–1830) was appointed Surveyor General of Bengal in 1767, the date from which the Survey of India counts its history. He surveyed the rivers and districts of Bengal and Bihar by compass traverse and measured distances, and published a Bengal Atlas (1779–81). He then compiled a Map of Hindoostan (1782) with an accompanying Memoir (1783, enlarged in later editions), which brought together everything he could find: his own surveys, the route surveys of army officers, astronomical observations of latitude and longitude, earlier European maps, and Indian sources, including the Āʾīn-i Akbarī’s lists of provinces and distances and itineraries supplied by Indian informants (Rennell 1783).

Rennell’s map was a compilation, not a survey: its accuracy varied greatly from region to region, and large areas were filled with information from itineraries. Kapil Raj has argued that it should be seen as the product of an encounter in which Indian knowledge of routes and places, provided by munshīs, guides and local officials, was essential, and in which the categories of the Mughal revenue administration shaped the map of British territory (Raj 2007).

docs.title: 14.2 Colin Mackenzie and the Mysore Survey
docs.text: After the defeat of Tipu Sultan in 1799, Colin Mackenzie (1754–1821) conducted a survey of the former Mysore territories that combined triangulation and topographical mapping with the collection of statistical, historical and ethnographic information. Assisted by a team of Indian scholars, notably the Brahmin brothers Kavali Venkata Borayya and Lakshmayya, he collected thousands of manuscripts, inscriptions, local histories and plans, now known as the Mackenzie Collection. In 1815 he became the first Surveyor General of India. His work shows how closely surveying was tied to the gathering of knowledge about Indian history and society for the purposes of government (Edney 1997).

docs.title: 14.3.1 Lambton
docs.text: In 1802 William Lambton (c. 1753–1823), an infantry officer with a training in mathematics, measured a baseline near Madras and began a triangulation of southern India. His aim was not only to map the territory but to measure the length of a degree of the meridian at Indian latitudes and so contribute to knowledge of the shape of the earth. From a series of triangles running north from Cape Comorin along a meridian close to 78° E, he and his successors built the “Great Arc” (Figure 14.1). Distances were derived from measured baselines and angles taken with great theodolites, the largest weighing about half a tonne. From 1818 the work was known as the Great Trigonometrical Survey. Lambton died in the field at Hinganghat in central India in 1823 (Keay 2000).

docs.title: 14.3.2 Everest
docs.text:
George Everest (1790–1866) took charge of the survey in 1823 and became Surveyor General in 1830. He introduced improved instruments and methods, re-measured baselines, and carried the Great Arc north to the foothills of the Himālaya near Dehra Dun, completing it in the early 1840s. The arc, some 2,400 km long, was the longest meridian arc measured up to that time and a major contribution to geodesy. Everest also planned a grid of further chains of triangles across northern India.

Figure 14.1. The Great Arc of the meridian, measured by Lambton and Everest between 1802 and the early 1840s from Cape Comorin to the Himalayan foothills near Dehra Dun and Mussoorie, about 2,400 km. In reality it was a chain of triangles some tens of kilometres wide, with measured baselines along its length; it is drawn here as a single line close to 78° E. The coastline is simplified.

docs.title: 14.3.3 Radhanath Sikdar and the Height of Peak XV
docs.text: The calculations of the survey were carried out by a staff of “computers”, many of them Indian. Radhanath Sikdar (1813–1870), a Bengali mathematician trained at the Hindu College in Calcutta, joined the survey in 1831, became chief computer, and later headed the meteorological work of the survey in Calcutta. In the early 1850s the computing office reduced observations of the Himalayan peaks taken from the plains and found that Peak XV was the highest yet measured; tradition credits Sikdar with the calculation. In 1856 the Surveyor General Andrew Waugh announced its height as 29,002 feet and proposed naming it after his predecessor, George Everest, against the survey’s own rule of using local names. The mountain is known in Tibetan as Chomolungma and was given the Nepali name Sagarmāthā in the twentieth century (Keay 2000).

docs.title: 14.3.4 Measuring the Himālaya
docs.text: Before the survey reached the Himālaya, it was widely believed in Europe that the Andes contained the world’s highest mountains. Observations of the Himalayan peaks from the plains in the early nineteenth century showed that several were higher; for some decades Dhaulagiri and then Kangchenjunga were thought the highest, until the calculations for Peak XV were completed in the 1850s. Because Nepal and Tibet were closed to British surveyors, the heights were computed from observations taken from stations in India more than a hundred kilometres away, with corrections for the curvature of the earth and for atmospheric refraction—a difficult problem that later surveys refined. The figure of 29,002 feet announced in 1856 was close to later values; the height now generally accepted is 8,848.86 m, announced jointly by Nepal and China in 2020.

docs.title: 14.3.5 The Survey’s Indian Staff
docs.text:
The work of the Great Trigonometrical Survey depended on large numbers of Indian employees whose names are rarely recorded: the khalāsīs who carried the instruments and erected the signal towers, the flag-men and lamp-men who stood on distant hills at night so that their lights could be observed, the clerks and draughtsmen, the computers who reduced the observations, and the sub-assistants who carried out much of the topographical surveying. The building of towers on the flat plains of northern India, the clearing of lines of sight through forests, and the measurement of baselines with chains laid end to end required thousands of labourers. Recent historians have emphasised that the Survey was an Indian as well as a British enterprise, though its credit and its purposes were overwhelmingly British (Edney 1997; Raj 2007).

The Great Trigonometrical Survey: Key Dates

  • 1767: Rennell appointed Surveyor General of Bengal.

  • 1802: Lambton measures his first baseline near Madras.

  • 1815: Colin Mackenzie becomes first Surveyor General of India.

  • 1818: the name “Great Trigonometrical Survey” is adopted.

  • 1823: death of Lambton; Everest takes charge.

  • 1830–43: Everest Surveyor General; the Great Arc completed in the early 1840s.

  • 1856: height of Peak XV (Everest) announced.

  • 1878: the trigonometrical, topographical and revenue surveys united in the Survey of India.

docs.title: 14.4 The Pundits: Indian Explorers of Tibet and Central Asia
docs.text: British officers could not travel openly in Tibet, Central Asia or much of the Himalayan borderland in the mid-nineteenth century. From 1863 Thomas Montgomerie of the Great Trigonometrical Survey trained Indian men from the Himalayan borderlands to travel in disguise as pilgrims or traders and to record routes, distances, altitudes and positions. They were known in the survey’s reports by code names and initials and collectively as the “pundits” (Waller 1990).

docs.title: 14.4.1 Methods
docs.text: The pundits were trained to walk at a fixed pace and to count their steps, using a Buddhist rosary of 100 beads instead of the usual 108, slipping one bead for every hundred paces. Notes were hidden in prayer wheels; compasses and thermometers were concealed in walking staffs and luggage. Latitude was found with a sextant at night, and altitude by measuring the boiling point of water with a thermometer, since water boils at lower temperatures at greater heights. The data were reduced by the survey’s computers in Dehra Dun.

docs.title: 14.4.2 Nain Singh and His Successors
docs.text:
• Nain Singh Rawat (1830–1882), a schoolteacher from Milam in Kumaon, travelled in 1865–66 from Kathmandu to Lhasa, fixing its position, and returned along the upper Tsangpo and past Mānasarovar; in 1867 he visited the gold fields of Thok Jalung in western Tibet; and in 1874–75 he travelled from Leh across the Tibetan plateau to Lhasa and down to Assam. He received the Patron’s Medal of the Royal Geographical Society in 1877.

  • Kishen Singh (“A-K”), his cousin, made a four-year journey (1878–82) from Lhasa to the north-east of the Tibetan plateau and back through western China.

  • Kinthup (“K-P”), a tailor from Sikkim, spent four years (1880–84) on a mission to test whether the Tsangpo was the Brahmaputra, including releasing marked logs into the river; his report was at first disbelieved and later largely vindicated.

  • Sarat Chandra Das (1849–1917), a Bengali scholar, travelled to Shigatse and Lhasa in 1879 and 1881–82, collected Tibetan texts, and later compiled a Tibetan–English dictionary.

The pundits’ journeys were dangerous and poorly rewarded, and several of them were not properly recognised in their lifetimes. Their work depended on their knowledge of languages, of Buddhist and Hindu pilgrimage practice, and of the trade routes of the Himalaya—exactly the kinds of knowledge described in earlier chapters. Their reports also served the strategic interests of British India in the “Great Game” with Russia, which is why the survey paid for them.

docs.title: 14.5 Gazetteers, Censuses and Surveys of People
docs.text:
Maps were only one part of the colonial effort to describe India. District gazetteers, compiled from the 1860s, described the physical geography, history, population, agriculture, castes, religions and antiquities of each district. W. W. Hunter’s Imperial Gazetteer of India (first edition 1881; the expanded edition of 1907–09 runs to twenty-six volumes, including an atlas) summarised them for the whole of British India. The census, taken in parts of India from the 1860s and on a synchronous all-India basis from 1881, counted people by place, religion, caste and occupation. George Grierson’s Linguistic Survey of India (1894–1928) mapped the languages and dialects of most of British India.

These projects produced an enormous body of geographical information, much of it still used. They also shaped the categories through which India was understood and governed: the census in particular fixed and ranked caste categories in ways that had lasting social and political effects. Like the maps of the surveyors, they were made with the help of many Indian clerks, informants and scholars, and they reflected the interests of the state that commissioned them.

docs.title: 14.5.1 Statistical Surveys of Districts
docs.text:
The gazetteers had precursors in the statistical surveys of the early Company period. Francis Buchanan (later Buchanan-Hamilton) travelled through Mysore, Canara and Malabar in 1800–01, after the fall of Tipu Sultan, with instructions to report on agriculture, crafts, commerce, the condition of the people and their religions; his account was published in three volumes in 1807. Between 1807 and 1814 he carried out a survey of the districts of Bihar and northern Bengal, recording the land and its uses, the crops and manufactures, the castes and their occupations, and the antiquities and natural history of each district. Much of it was published only in an edited and abridged form by Montgomery Martin in 1838, and the manuscript reports remain an important source for the social and economic geography of eastern India on the eve of colonial change.

W. W. Hunter, who became the first Director General of Statistics to the Government of India, standardised the form in the 1870s. His Statistical Account of Bengal (twenty volumes, 1875–77) treated each district under a fixed set of headings—physical aspects, population, agriculture, natural calamities, commerce, administration, health—and became the model for the district gazetteers of other provinces and for the Imperial Gazetteer. The uniformity was the point: every district of India could be described, compared and tabulated in the same terms. The method also had its blind spots. The headings came from the needs of revenue and administration, local knowledge entered only as the officials recorded it, and Adivasi and pastoral peoples who did not fit the categories of settled agriculture were described mainly as problems of order.

docs.title: 14.5.2 The Census as a Map of Society
docs.text:
Provincial counts were made in the 1860s, and a census of most of British India was taken between 1867 and 1872, though not on a single date. The census of 1881 was the first taken simultaneously across British India and most of the princely states, and a census has been held every ten years since. The census was geographical in a double sense. It divided the whole country into enumeration blocks, villages, towns, districts and provinces, so that every person was counted in a place; and it produced, decade by decade, tables and maps of the distribution of population, language, religion, caste and occupation that were the raw material for the regional geography of India.

Its categories were contested from the start. The census of 1901, under Herbert Risley, attempted to rank castes in each province by “social precedence”. Caste associations responded with petitions claiming higher places and new names, and the census itself became an arena in which communities sought recognition (Cohn 1987; Dirks 2001). Caste was last enumerated in full in 1931, although in 2025 the government decided to include it again in the next census. The censuses of independent India, beginning in 1951, recorded only the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes among the castes and communities, while expanding the geographical apparatus: district census handbooks with village directories and maps, and census atlases. The language returns of the census, building on Grierson’s survey, supplied the data on which the linguistic states were drawn (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 14.6 Maps, Territory and the Nation
docs.text:
Matthew Edney has argued that the surveys did not simply record a pre-existing India; they helped to create “British India” as a single bounded and measurable territory, an idea that the colonial state then administered and that nationalists inherited (Edney 1997). Ian Barrow has shown how British maps also told a history, presenting the growth of Company territory as the natural progress of an orderly state (Barrow 2003), and Manu Goswami how railways, statistics and maps together produced the idea of India as a single national economy and space by the late nineteenth century (Goswami 2004). The outline map of India became a familiar image in schoolrooms and newspapers.

Nationalist imagination gave the map a sacred meaning. Bankimchandra Chattopadhyay’s song Vande Mātaram (composed in the 1870s and published in his novel Ānandamaṭh in 1882) addresses the land as a mother, “well-watered, fruitful, cool with the breezes from the Malaya hills, dark with crops”. In the early twentieth century, painters and printmakers depicted Bhārat Mātā (Mother India) as a goddess whose body filled or stood upon the outline of the map. Sumathi Ramaswamy has studied how these images combined the cartographic outline produced by colonial surveying with the older language of the sacred land (Ramaswamy 2010). The images were powerful but not neutral: some Muslims and others objected to the identification of the nation with a Hindu goddess, and the debate over Vande Mātaram was part of the politics of the independence movement.

docs.title: 14.7 Mapping in Independent India
docs.text:
After 1947 the Survey of India continued as the national mapping agency. A National Atlas Organisation, founded in 1956 and later renamed the National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO), produced national and thematic atlases. The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), founded in 1969, built a remote-sensing programme beginning with the experimental Bhaskara satellites (1979 and 1981) and the IRS series (from 1988), and later the Cartosat mapping satellites (from 2005). Satellite data are now used for land use, agriculture, forests, water resources, flood and disaster mapping, urban planning and archaeology. India’s regional satellite navigation system (NavIC) and online geoportals make geographical information widely available.

Remote sensing has also been applied to historical questions, such as the mapping of palaeochannels in the Ghaggar–Hakra basin (Chapter 9) and the detection of archaeological sites. These are valuable tools; their results, like all evidence, need careful interpretation, and they cannot by themselves confirm or refute the descriptions of ancient texts.

docs.title: 14.7.1 Maps and the State after 1947
docs.text: For several decades after independence, large-scale topographical maps of India were treated as restricted documents for reasons of security, particularly in border and coastal areas, and the depiction of India’s external boundaries on maps has remained a matter of law and diplomacy. A National Map Policy in 2005 created separate series of defence and open maps, and guidelines issued in 2021 liberalised the acquisition and use of most geospatial data by Indian companies and individuals. The history of mapping in independent India thus continues to show the close connection between geographical knowledge and the power of the state that the colonial surveys revealed.

docs.title: 14.8 The Recovery of Historical Geography
docs.text:
The study of India’s ancient geography as a discipline began in the nineteenth century. Alexander Cunningham, founder of the Archaeological Survey of India (1861), used Xuanzang’s itinerary and the Greek sources to identify ancient sites and published The Ancient Geography of India (1871) (Cunningham 1871). Nundo Lal Dey’s Geographical Dictionary of Ancient and Mediaeval India (1899; second edition 1927) gathered the identifications of thousands of place-names from Sanskrit, Pali and other sources (Dey 1927). Śaṅkara Bālakṛṣṇa Dīkṣita’s history of Indian astronomy, written in Marathi (1896), included a detailed account of the astronomers’ geography (Dikshit 1969). In the twentieth century, scholars such as Bimala Churn Law, D. C. Sircar and V. S. Agrawala used Pali, Sanskrit and epigraphic sources to reconstruct the regions, peoples and places of early India (Law 1954; Sircar 1971; Agrawala 1953).

This scholarship is the foundation on which modern accounts, including this volume, rest. Its methods—the careful comparison of texts, inscriptions, coins, archaeological sites and travellers’ accounts—remain the right ones for a subject in which wishful identification is a constant temptation.

docs.title: 14.9 Geography as a Modern Discipline
docs.text:
Geography entered the Indian classroom through the colonial school curriculum, largely as the memorising of capes, rivers and provincial capitals, and only slowly became a university discipline. Geographical societies with their own journals were founded at Madras and Calcutta between the wars, teachers of geography were trained, and university departments were established from the 1930s and 1940s at Aligarh, Calcutta, Madras, Banaras and elsewhere; they multiplied after independence.

Three strands shaped the new discipline. The first was regional geography in the manner of Spate’s India and Pakistan: the division of the subcontinent into natural and cultural regions, each described physically and historically (Section 12.1). Its fullest expression by Indian geographers is the collective India: A Regional Geography, edited by R. L. Singh at Banaras (Singh 1971). The second was the atlas. S. P. Chatterjee of Calcutta, the first director of the National Atlas Organisation founded in 1956, made the national atlas and its thematic sheets a central project of Indian geography, and the census added its own atlases and village maps. In 1968, while Chatterjee was president of the International Geographical Union, the International Geographical Congress met in New Delhi. The third strand, from the 1970s, was the study of planning, regional development and inequality, associated above all with Moonis Raza and the Centre for the Study of Regional Development at Jawaharlal Nehru University, which brought geography close to economics and history and to the question of who benefits from development.

The new discipline had little to say about the traditions described in the earlier chapters of this volume. The Purāṇic and Siddhāntic material was left to Sanskritists and historians of science, the Persian gazetteers to historians of the Mughal empire, and the knowledge of pilgrims, sailors and herders to anthropologists. Bringing these together, as this volume tries to do, is a recent undertaking, helped by the history of cartography and by the inclusion of Indian knowledge systems in the curriculum (Section 14.13).

docs.title: 14.10 Exploration in Independent India
docs.text: Independent India has continued the tradition of exploration in new forms. Indian mountaineers took part in the exploration and ascent of the Himalayan peaks; Tenzing Norgay, who with Edmund Hillary made the first ascent of Everest in 1953, had made his home in Darjeeling, and Indian expeditions climbed the mountain from 1965. Since 1981 India has sent scientific expeditions to Antarctica and has maintained research stations there—Dakshin Gangotri (1983), Maitri (1989) and Bharati (2012)—as well as a station in the Arctic, at Ny-Ålesund in Svalbard. The National Institute of Oceanography and other bodies survey the seas around India, and satellites map the land from space (see above). These enterprises belong to a modern, international science; they continue, in very different circumstances, the long history of Indians travelling to the edges of the known world and bringing back knowledge of it.

docs.title: 14.11 The Legacy of the Older Traditions
docs.text:
What remains of the geographical traditions described in this volume?

  • Mathematical geography: the Siddhānta tradition lives on in the traditional almanacs (pañcāṅga), still calculated for local latitudes and longitudes and still, in many cases, reckoned from the meridian of Ujjain. Its history is an important part of the history of science (Plofker 2009).

  • Sacred geography: pilgrimage has grown enormously with railways, roads and air travel, and the sacred places described in the Purāṇas and māhātmyas are visited by more people than ever (Eck 2012).

  • Names: Purāṇic and classical names for the land and its features—Bhārata, Himālaya, Gaṅgā, Narmadā, Malaya, Sahyādri—remain in use.

  • Local knowledge: the practical knowledge of farmers, herders, fishers and forest peoples is increasingly studied for its relevance to the management of water, forests and coasts.

docs.title: 14.11.1 Sacred Groves and Tanks
docs.text:
Two institutions are often cited as examples of traditional conservation. Sacred groves—patches of forest dedicated to a deity and protected by custom, called devrāī in Maharashtra, kāvu in Kerala, devarakāḍu in Karnataka, oraṇ in Rajasthan and sarnā among Adivasi communities of central India—have been shown to preserve remnants of native forest and rare species. Madhav Gadgil and V. D. Vartak’s study of the sacred groves of the Western Ghats (1976) began their scientific study (Gadgil and Vartak 1976). Village tank systems in South India, described in Chapter 9, stored water and recharged groundwater for centuries.

Both institutions are valuable, but they should not be romanticised. Many sacred groves have shrunk or been converted to temple compounds; tank systems depended on collective labour often organised along lines of caste, and many decayed under colonial and post-colonial administration. Where tanks have been revived in recent decades, the question of who controls the water has proved as important as the engineering.

docs.title: 14.12 The Politics of Names
docs.text: Place-names are part of geography, and in modern India they have been a subject of politics. After independence, many colonial spellings were replaced by forms closer to local pronunciation, and states were reorganised on linguistic lines from 1956. Several major cities have been officially renamed: Bombay as Mumbai (1995), Madras as Chennai (1996), Calcutta as Kolkata (2001), Bangalore as Bengaluru (2014) and Allahabad as Prayagraj (2018). Some renamings restored names already in local use; others revived older or sacred names. They show how the language of geography continues to express ideas about history and identity, as the names Bhārata and Hindustan did in earlier centuries (Chapter 1).

docs.title: 14.13 Geography and Indian Knowledge Systems in Education
docs.text: The National Education Policy of 2020 recommends that Indian knowledge systems be integrated into school and university curricula. For geography, the material of this volume offers much that is worth teaching: the Vedic and Tamil descriptions of landscapes; the cosmologies of the Purāṇas, Jains and Buddhists as examples of how cultures imagine the world; the mathematical geography of the Siddhāntas and its place in the history of science; the sacred geography of pilgrimage; maps, routes and travel accounts as historical sources; and the knowledge of local communities. Taught honestly—with dates, sources and evidence, with the limits of each tradition acknowledged, and without claims that ancient texts anticipated modern discoveries—it can give students a richer understanding both of India and of geography as a human enterprise.

docs.title: 14.14 Conclusion
docs.text:
The geographical traditions of India are many, not one. The Vedic hymns named rivers and praised the earth. The Purāṇas, and the Jain and Buddhist texts, built cosmologies in which the known land had its place at the centre of an immense and ordered universe. The astronomers worked with a spherical earth, estimated its size in their own units, and computed latitudes and time differences. Pilgrims, merchants, sailors and herders accumulated a vast practical knowledge of routes, seasons and places, much of it never written down. Mughal administrators described the empire’s provinces in detail; Jain artists painted the cosmos; Rajput and Maratha courts drew plans of cities and forts. Foreign travellers recorded what they saw, and Indian travellers began to describe the world beyond. Finally, colonial surveyors, with Indian colleagues whose role was long obscured, measured the subcontinent trigonometrically.

These traditions should be studied with respect and with care: neither dismissed as the “absence of geography” nor inflated into claims that ancient texts anticipated modern science. Read in their own terms, they reveal a long and varied engagement with the land, its waters and the wider world, which is one of the richest chapters in the history of geographical thought.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Edney (1997) and Raj (2007) on colonial surveying; Keay (2000) on the Great Trigonometrical Survey; Waller (1990) on the pundits; Ramaswamy (2010) on maps and the nation; Cohn (1987) and Dirks (2001) on the census and caste; Gadgil and Vartak (1976) on sacred groves.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Terms are Sanskrit unless marked (Pa. = Pali, Pk. = Prakrit, Ta. = Tamil, Mar. = Marathi, Gu. = Gujarati, Ar. = Arabic, Pe. = Persian, Hi. = Hindi).

Term Meaning aḍhāī dvīpa (Pk./Hi.) “Two and a half continents”: in Jain cosmography, the region of the universe where human beings live; also a painted diagram of it akam, puṟam (Ta.) “Interior” and “exterior”: the two genres of classical Tamil poetry, on love and on public life akṣa, akṣāṃśa Terrestrial latitude aṅgula Finger-breadth; the smallest common unit of length ānūpa Wet, marshy land Āryāvarta “Abode of the Āryas”: in normative texts, the land between the Himālaya and the Vindhya aṭavī, āṭavika Forest country and its peoples, distinguished in Aśokan and Gupta inscriptions from the settled subjects of a kingdom bhogabhūmi “Land of enjoyment”: a region where beings enjoy the fruits of past merit without acting (contrast karmabhūmi) bhūgola The earth-sphere of the astronomers bhukti A territorial division in inscriptions: a province in Gupta and Pāla Bengal, a small unit in the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Deccan bhuvanakośa “Treasury of the world”: the cosmographical section of a Purāṇa; also a section of Bhāskara II’s Golādhyāya cara Ascensional difference: the correction for the length of day at a given latitude catuḥsīmā The four boundaries by which a land grant describes the land it conveys cāturmāsya The four months of the rainy season, during which Jain (and other) ascetics stay in one place chauth, sardeśmukhī (Mar.) The quarter and the additional tenth of the revenue claimed by the Marathas from territories outside their home lands dakṣiṇāpatha “Southern road”; the route to the south and the Deccan itself dām (Pe.) Mughal copper coin, forty to the rupee; the unit in which revenue was assessed dargāh (Pe.) Tomb-shrine of a Sufi saint deśa Region, country deśāntara “Difference of place”: longitude correction relative to the reference meridian dhām (Hi.) “Abode”; especially one of the four great pilgrimage centres dhanus “Bow”: a unit of length of four cubits dharmaśālā Rest-house for pilgrims and travellers digvijaya “Conquest of the quarters”: a king’s ideal campaign in all directions, a literary form that lists peoples and places dikpāla Guardian deity of a direction dṛggaṇita “Computation in accordance with sight”: astronomical parameters revised to agree with observation dvīpa Island; in cosmography, a ring-shaped continent ghāṭ (Hi.) Steps leading to water; also a mountain pass, especially in the Western Ghats gola Sphere; golādhyāya, the chapter on the sphere in an astronomical treatise goruta “Cow’s call”: a unit of distance, a quarter of a yojana in the Arthaśāstra grāmadevatā Village deity, often a goddess guarding the settlement huṇḍī Bill of exchange used by Indian merchants iqlīm (Ar.) One of the seven east–west “climes” into which Islamic geographers divided the inhabited world iqṭāʿ (Ar.) Assignment of the revenue of a territory to a military commander under the Delhi Sultanate jamʿ (Pe.) The assessed revenue of a territorial unit in the Mughal records Jambūdvīpa “Rose-apple continent”: the central continent of Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist cosmography, containing Bhāratavarṣa janapada Territory of a people; an early state jāṅgala Dry, open country (the origin of English “jungle”) jarīb (Pe.) Measuring chain used in the Mughal land survey jyotirliṅga One of twelve shrines where Śiva is worshipped as a column of light kamāl (Ar.) Simple navigational instrument for measuring the altitude of stars karmabhūmi “Land of action”: a region where deeds bear fruit and liberation is possible khagola The celestial sphere kos mīnār (Hi./Pe.) Masonry pillar marking distances along Mughal roads kos, krośa A unit of road distance; values varied widely kṣetra Sacred field or territory; in Jain cosmography, a region of a continent kulaparvata One of the seven principal mountain ranges of Bhāratavarṣa Kūrmavibhāga “Division of the tortoise”: Varāhamihira’s arrangement of the regions of India in nine groups lamba Co-latitude Laṅkā (astronomy) The point on the equator under the reference meridian of Ujjain lokapuruṣa “Cosmic person”: the Jain universe imagined in human shape madhyadeśa The “Middle Country” of the Gaṅgā–Yamunā region mahājanapada “Great janapada”: one of the sixteen states listed in early Buddhist texts māhātmya Text praising a sacred place Majjhimadesa (Pa.) The “Middle Country” of the Buddhist monastic code maṇḍala (politics) The “circle” of states in the Arthaśāstra maṇḍala (territory) A territorial division in inscriptions; Tamil maṇḍalam, a major region such as the Cōḻamaṇḍalam manzil (Pe.) A day’s stage on a journey mauẓaʿ, mauzā (Ar./Pe.) A village as a unit of revenue administration Meru The golden mountain at the centre of the cosmos mleccha “Barbarian”: a person outside the Brahmanical social order mukti-kṣetra A sacred place where death brings liberation, such as Kāśī nadī River nāḍu (Ta.) A cluster of villages forming an agrarian locality; the basic territorial unit of medieval Tamil inscriptions palabhā The noon shadow of a twelve-unit gnomon at the equinox, used to find latitude pāḷaiyam (Ta.) A fortified camp; the territory of a pāḷaiyakkārar (“poligar”) chief pālkhī (Mar.) Palanquin; the procession carrying the sandals of a saint to Paṇḍharpur pañcāṅga Traditional almanac, computed for a particular place pargana (Pe.) A sub-district made up of a cluster of villages; the basic local unit of Sultanate and Mughal administration parikramā, pradakṣiṇā Circumambulation, keeping the sacred object on one’s right pātāla The netherworlds of Purāṇic cosmography patwārī, qānūngo (Pe.) Village accountant and sub-district record-keeper in the Mughal revenue system pīṭha “Seat”; especially a seat of the Goddess (śākta pīṭha) pratyanta Frontier; the frontier kingdoms of Samudragupta’s Prayāga inscription qibla (Ar.) The direction of Mecca, toward which Muslims pray rahmānī (Gu.) Book of sailing directions used by pilots of western India sandeśakāvya “Messenger poem”, modelled on the Meghadūta, describing a route saṅgama Confluence of rivers saṅkalpa Declaration of intent at the start of a ritual, naming time and place śaṅku Gnomon: a vertical rod whose shadow is used to find directions, time and latitude sarāy (Pe.) Roadside inn for travellers and caravans sarkār (Pe.) A district of a Mughal province sārtha, sārthavāha Caravan; caravan leader setu Embankment, dam or bridge; also Rāma’s bridge to Laṅkā sīmā Boundary, especially of a village śreṇī Guild of merchants or artisans ṣūba (Pe.) Province of the Mughal empire Śulbasūtra Vedic manual of altar construction using cords Suvarṇabhūmi, Suvarṇadvīpa “Land of gold”, “Island of gold”: names for parts of Southeast Asia svarājya (Mar.) “Own rule”: the home territory of the Maratha state tahsīl, tāluk (Ar./Pe.) A revenue sub-division of a district in British and modern India tiṇai (Ta.) Landscape or situation in classical Tamil poetics tīrtha Ford; sacred place, especially one associated with water tīrthayātrā Pilgrimage to sacred places uttarāpatha “Northern road”; the north-west and the route to it vaḷanāḍu (Ta.) A group of nāḍus; a division of the Cōḻa kingdom vārī (Mar.) The annual walking pilgrimage of the Vārkarīs to Paṇḍharpur varṣa One of the regions of Jambūdvīpa vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala Square grid of deities used in planning buildings viṣaya District; a territorial unit of the inscriptions vyāhṛti The sacred utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, naming the three worlds wāqiʿa-nawīs (Pe.) News-writer posted by the Mughal government in a province or district yātrā Journey; pilgrimage yojana The largest common unit of distance; its length varied, most estimates falling between about 7 and 15 km zabṭ (Pe.) The Mughal system of revenue assessment based on the measurement of fields zīj (Ar./Pe.) Astronomical handbook with tables zilā (Ar./Pe.) District; from Arabic ḍilaʿ, through Persian ziyārat (Ar.) Pilgrimage to a saint’s shrine
